Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 1

Pharmacokinetics and Routes of Administration

Pharmacokinetics refers to how medications travel through the body. They undergo a variety of biochemical processes that result in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Pharmacokinetics = ADME: Absorption (route-dependent), Distribution (blood flow + protein binding), Metabolism (mostly hepatic via P450), Excretion (mostly renal). First-pass effect reduces oral bioavailability. Half-life guides dosing interval. Therapeutic index (TI) — low TI drugs (digoxin, lithium, warfarin) need close monitoring.

The four phases (ADME)

  • Absorption: GI tract, IM, SC, IV, etc. — IV is 100% bioavailable
  • Distribution: lipid solubility, blood flow, plasma protein binding (albumin)
  • Metabolism: liver enzymes (CYP450) — first-pass effect with oral route
  • Excretion: primarily kidneys — adjust dose for renal impairment

Key concepts

  • Half-life: time for drug concentration to drop by 50%
  • Steady state: reached after 4–5 half-lives
  • Peak/trough: monitor for low-TI medications
  • Onset, peak, duration: nurse times assessments accordingly

Important kinetic concepts

  • Bioavailability: Fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation; IV = 100%; PO varies widely
  • First-pass effect: Hepatic metabolism on first GI absorption — reduces oral bioavailability (e.g., nitroglycerin given SL/IV/patch to bypass)
  • Loading dose: Higher initial dose to rapidly reach therapeutic level (faster than waiting 4–5 half-lives)
  • Prodrug: Inactive until metabolized (e.g., codeine → morphine; enalapril → enalaprilat)
  • Routes ranked by absorption speed: IV (instant) > inhaled > SL > IM/SC > PO > topical
  • Z-track IM injection: For irritating meds (iron dextran, hydroxyzine) — pull skin laterally, inject, hold 10 sec, release
  • Enterohepatic recirculation: Prolongs half-life of some drugs (digoxin, OCPs); antibiotics that disrupt gut flora can decrease this
Rank the major routes of administration from fastest to slowest onset, and identify which gives 100% bioavailability.
IV (instantaneous, 100% bioavailability) > inhaled > sublingual > IM/SC > PO > topical. PO bioavailability varies widely because of the first-pass effect (hepatic metabolism before reaching systemic circulation). Nitroglycerin is given SL/IV/patch precisely to bypass this.
Which IM injection technique is used for irritating medications like iron dextran or hydroxyzine — and what are the four steps?
Z-track technique prevents medication leakage into subcutaneous tissue. Steps: (1) pull skin laterally ~1 inch before injecting, (2) inject the medication slowly, (3) hold needle in place 10 seconds, (4) release skin as you withdraw the needle. The skin movement seals the tract.
Which medications are classic examples of a low therapeutic index (low TI) requiring close blood-level monitoring?
Digoxin, lithium, warfarin — the classic trio. Small dose changes can swing between subtherapeutic and toxic. Also commonly monitored: phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin. Peak/trough levels are routine for these.

Absorption & Routes of Administration

Absorption is the transmission of medication from the site of administration to the bloodstream. The rate determines onset; the amount determines intensity. Route choice depends on the medication's properties, the urgency of effect, and client factors.

Oral (PO) and enteral

Most common

Tablets, capsules, liquids, suspensions, elixirs, lozenges. Convenient and inexpensive but absorption is variable.

Absorption pattern

  • Varies greatly with stability, solubility, GI pH, emptying time, food presence
  • Enteric-coated tablets and sustained-release forms — do not crush or chew
  • First-pass effect through the liver reduces oral bioavailability

Nursing considerations

  • Hold for NPO, dysphagia, vomiting
  • Verify swallowing ability
  • Check for crushing/splitting compatibility

Sublingual / Buccal

Rapid systemic action

Dissolves under tongue (SL) or against cheek (buccal). Bypasses first-pass effect — rapid systemic absorption.

Pattern

  • Quick absorption through highly vascular mucous membranes
  • Swallowing before dissolution allows gastric pH to inactivate the medication
  • Common examples: nitroglycerin (SL), buprenorphine (buccal)

Teaching

  • Do not swallow until fully dissolved
  • Avoid eating, drinking, or smoking during dissolution

Other mucous membranes (rectal, vaginal)

Suppositories and vaginal applications produce both local and systemic effects depending on the medication.

Absorption

  • Easy absorption with both local and systemic effects
  • Stool in the rectum or infectious material in the vagina limits tissue contact

Uses

  • Rectal: antiemetics (promethazine), laxatives, hemorrhoid preparations
  • Vaginal: antifungals (miconazole), hormonal therapy

Inhalation

Direct delivery to lungs

Medication delivered via metered-dose inhaler (MDI), dry powder inhaler (DPI), or nebulizer. Local effect for respiratory conditions; some systemic absorption.

Absorption pattern

  • Rapid absorption through alveolar capillary network
  • Barrier: inadequate inspiratory effort
  • Use a spacer with MDI to ↑ drug delivery to lungs, ↓ deposition in oropharynx

MDI with spacer technique

  • Remove cap; shake inhaler 5–6 times
  • Insert MDI into spacer end
  • Exhale completely; seal lips around mouthpiece
  • Press inhaler and begin slow, deep inhalation (3–5 sec)
  • Hold breath for 10 seconds; exhale slowly through pursed lips

Intradermal, topical, transdermal

Local and slow systemic

Topical creams/ointments treat skin conditions; transdermal patches deliver steady systemic medication over hours to days.

Patterns

  • Slow, gradual absorption
  • Effects primarily local, but systemic possible with lipid-soluble drugs (passes through SC fat)

Transdermal patch teaching

  • Apply to clean, dry, hairless skin (do not shave — use scissors if needed)
  • Rotate sites; do not place on same site as old patch
  • Remove old patch before applying new — never two patches at once
  • Wash hands after applying
  • Avoid direct heat (heating pads, hot tubs) — accelerates absorption (especially dangerous with fentanyl)

Subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM)

Parenteral

Injection into subcutaneous fat (SC) or muscle (IM). Bypasses GI tract; useful when oral route unavailable or for medications inactivated by GI environment (insulin).

Absorption

  • Capillary walls have large gaps — no significant barrier
  • Highly soluble medications absorb in 10–30 min; poorly soluble drugs absorb slowly
  • ↑ blood perfusion at injection site = ↑ rate of absorption

IM sites & technique

  • Vastus lateralis: Preferred for infants < 1 year
  • Ventrogluteal: Preferred for IM injections and volumes > 2 mL
  • Deltoid: Smaller muscle; max 1 mL typically; common for vaccines
  • Z-track method for irritating drugs (iron dextran): pull skin laterally, inject, hold 10 sec, release

Intravenous (IV)

Most rapid and complete

Direct infusion into the vein. 100% bioavailability and immediate onset. Carries the highest risk for adverse effects and toxicity.

Properties

  • No barriers — immediate and complete
  • Enters blood directly; reaches systemic circulation in entirety
  • Allows precise titration and rapid effect

Risks

  • Cannot be reversed easily once given
  • Risk of infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, infection, air embolism, fluid overload
  • Some medications are vesicants (chemo, dopamine, vasopressors) — extravasation causes tissue necrosis
  • Always verify patency; flush before/after med administration per protocol

Distribution

Distribution is the transportation of medication to sites of action by bodily fluids. Three primary factors affect distribution: circulation, cell membrane permeability, and plasma protein binding.

Circulation

Conditions that inhibit blood flow or perfusion delay distribution.

Conditions that impair distribution

  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Cardiac disease (heart failure, shock)
  • Edema and inflammation in target tissue

Permeability of cell membranes

The medication must cross tissues and membranes to reach its target. Lipid solubility and transport systems determine penetration.

What crosses easily

  • Lipid-soluble medications (cross blood-brain barrier and placenta)
  • Small uncharged molecules
  • Medications with active transport systems

Implications

  • Pregnancy: assume the medication crosses the placenta unless proven otherwise
  • CNS effects: lipid-soluble drugs (most psychotropics, opioids) cross BBB

Plasma protein binding

Medications compete for protein binding sites in the blood — primarily albumin. Only the unbound (free) fraction is active.

Key concepts

  • Two medications competing for the same binding site → ↑ free fraction → ↑ effect/toxicity
  • Low albumin (malnutrition, liver disease, older adults) → ↑ free drug → ↑ effect
  • Highly protein-bound drugs (warfarin, phenytoin) are most affected by displacement

Metabolism (biotransformation)

Metabolism converts medications into more active, less active, or inactive forms via enzymatic action. Occurs primarily in the liver but also kidneys, lungs, intestines, and blood.

Factors affecting metabolism

Multiple factors alter the rate at which the body metabolizes medications, requiring dosage adjustments.

Factors that ↓ metabolism (require ↓ dose)

  • Liver failure — decreased enzyme activity
  • Aging — hepatic metabolism declines, accumulation possible
  • Concurrent medications metabolized by the same enzyme pathway
  • Infants — immature liver enzymes

Factors that ↑ metabolism (require ↑ dose)

  • Concurrent enzyme-inducing medications (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John's wort)
  • Increased medication-metabolizing enzymes
  • Smoking ↑ metabolism of theophylline

First-pass effect

Oral medications absorbed in the GI tract pass through the liver before reaching systemic circulation. The liver metabolizes a portion, reducing the amount that reaches systemic circulation (oral bioavailability).

Routes that bypass first-pass effect

  • IV, IM, SC, sublingual, buccal, transdermal, inhaled
  • Example: Nitroglycerin is given SL, IV, transdermal, or buccal — never PO standard tablet (almost completely destroyed in first pass)

Prodrugs

Inactive medications that become active after metabolism.

Examples

  • Codeine → morphine (CYP2D6)
  • Enalapril → enalaprilat
  • Levodopa → dopamine
  • Clopidogrel requires CYP2C19 activation

Excretion

Excretion is the elimination of medication from the body, primarily via the kidneys. Other routes include bile/feces, lungs (volatile substances), sweat, saliva, and breast milk.

Renal excretion

The kidneys filter most medications and their metabolites. Renal function determines elimination rate.

Key points

  • ↓ glomerular filtration rate (GFR) → ↑ medication accumulation → ↑ risk of toxicity
  • Renal impairment: ↓ dose for renally-cleared drugs (digoxin, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, lithium, metformin)
  • Older adults: assume some degree of reduced renal function
  • Monitor creatinine clearance (CrCl) and BUN/creatinine for renally-cleared drugs

Other routes of excretion

Some medications use additional or alternative routes.

Routes

  • Bile/feces — enterohepatic recirculation prolongs effect of some drugs
  • Lungs — volatile drugs and gases (anesthetics, alcohol)
  • Breast milk — drugs may transfer to nursing infant
  • Sweat, saliva, tears — small amounts

Half-life, Steady State, and Therapeutic Index

Half-life determines dosing frequency. Steady state determines when full effect is reached. Therapeutic index determines how closely the drug must be monitored.

Half-life (t½)

The time required for the medication concentration to decrease by 50%. Determines dosing frequency.

Implications

  • Short half-life → multiple daily doses (e.g., ibuprofen QID)
  • Long half-life → once daily dosing (e.g., phenobarbital, levothyroxine)
  • Time to clear drug: approximately 4–5 half-lives
  • Time to reach steady state: approximately 4–5 half-lives with regular dosing

Steady state

When the amount of medication entering the body equals the amount eliminated. Therapeutic effect plateaus.

Loading dose

  • A larger initial dose to reach therapeutic level quickly
  • Used when waiting 4–5 half-lives is impractical (e.g., digoxin, amiodarone, antiretrovirals)
  • Followed by smaller maintenance doses

Therapeutic index (TI)

The ratio of toxic to therapeutic dose. A high TI means a wide safety margin; a low TI means a narrow margin where toxicity is close to therapeutic levels.

Low-TI medications (require monitoring)

  • Digoxin — therapeutic 0.5–2.0 ng/mL
  • Lithium — therapeutic 0.6–1.2 mEq/L
  • Warfarin — monitored via INR (2–3 standard)
  • Phenytoin — therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL
  • Theophylline — therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL
  • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — peak and trough levels
  • Vancomycin — trough levels

Peak vs trough monitoring

  • Peak: Highest concentration — typically drawn 30 min after IV finishes (or per drug-specific timing)
  • Trough: Lowest concentration — drawn immediately before the next scheduled dose
  • Trough below the toxic threshold confirms safe dosing interval

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Therapeutic Procedure. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is showing a client how to use a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) with a spacer. What should the nurse include in the instructions? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Therapeutic Procedure to complete this item.

Show key

Indications

  • Medication absorption pattern: Rapid absorption through the alveolar capillary network. A spacer keeps the medication in the device longer, increasing the amount delivered to the lungs and decreasing the amount deposited in the oropharynx.
  • Barrier to absorption: Inadequate respiratory effort.

Client Education — Steps for MDI with Spacer

  • Remove the covers from the mouthpieces of the inhaler and of the spacer
  • Insert the MDI into the end of the spacer
  • Shake the inhaler five or six times
  • Exhale completely, then close your mouth around the spacer's mouthpiece
  • Tilt your head back slightly, press the inhaler, and at the same time begin a slow, deep inhalation
  • Continue to breathe in slowly and deeply for 3 to 5 seconds to facilitate delivery to the air passages
  • Hold your breath for 10 seconds to allow the medication to deposit in your airways
  • Take the mouthpiece out of your mouth and slowly exhale through pursed lips
  • Resume normal breathing

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 1 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A provider prescribes phenobarbital for a client who has a seizure disorder. The medication has a long half-life of 4 days. How many times per day should the nurse expect to administer this medication?

  1. A. One
  2. B. Two
  3. C. Three
  4. D. Four
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. Medications with long half-lives remain at their therapeutic levels between doses for long periods. The nurse should expect to administer this medication once a day.

B. A medication administered twice a day would have a shorter half-life. An example is vancomycin.

C. A medication administered three times a day would have a shorter half-life. An example is zidovudine.

D. A medication administered four times a day would have a shorter half-life. An example is ibuprofen.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q2

A nurse educator is reviewing medication metabolism at an in-service presentation. Which of the following factors should the educator include as a reason to administer lower medication dosages? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Increased renal excretion
  2. B. Increased medication-metabolizing enzymes
  3. C. Liver failure
  4. D. Peripheral vascular disease
  5. E. Concurrent use of medication that the same pathway metabolizes
Show rationale ▾

A. Increased renal excretion decreases the concentration of the medication, requiring an INCREASED dosage.

B. Increased metabolism decreases the concentration of the medication, requiring an INCREASED dosage.

C. CORRECT. Liver failure decreases metabolism and thus increases the concentration of a medication. This requires decreasing the dosage.

D. PVD impairs distribution, but the medication remains in circulation longer at lower levels, often requiring an INCREASED dosage to reach target tissues.

E. CORRECT. When the same pathway metabolizes two medications, they compete for metabolism, thereby increasing the concentration of one or both medications. This requires decreasing the dosage.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions
Q3

A nurse is preparing to administer eye drops to a client. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Have the client lie on one side
  2. B. Ask the client to look up at the ceiling
  3. C. Tell the client to blink when the drops enter the eye
  4. D. Drop the medication into the client's conjunctival sac
  5. E. Instruct the client to close the eye gently after instillation
Show rationale ▾

A. The client should be sitting or in a supine position to facilitate the instillation of eye drops.

B. CORRECT. The client should look upward to keep the drops from falling onto the cornea.

C. Ideally, the client should not blink so that they do not eject the eye drops. If they do blink, repeat the instillation.

D. CORRECT. Dropping medication into the conjunctival sac promotes distribution.

E. CORRECT. Closing the eye gently promotes distribution of the medication.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q4

A nurse is teaching a client about transdermal patches. Which of the following statements should the nurse identify as an indication that the client understands?

  1. A. "I will clean the site with an alcohol swab before I apply the patch."
  2. B. "I will rotate the application sites weekly."
  3. C. "I will apply the patch to an area of skin with no hair."
  4. D. "I will place the new patch on the site of the old patch."
Show rationale ▾

A. The site should be clean and dry, but alcohol swabs are not necessary and can irritate the skin.

B. Rotation should occur with each new patch application — typically every 24–72 hours depending on the patch — not weekly.

C. CORRECT. A hairless area allows good adhesion and consistent absorption. If hair is present, use scissors to trim — do not shave (causes skin trauma → variable absorption).

D. Sites should be rotated to prevent skin irritation and ensure consistent absorption.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q5

A nurse reviewing a client's medical record notes a new prescription for verifying the trough level of the client's medication. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?

  1. A. Obtain a blood specimen immediately prior to administering the next dose of medication
  2. B. Verify that the client has been taking the medication for 24 hr before obtaining a blood specimen
  3. C. Ask the client to provide a urine specimen after the next dose of medication
  4. D. Administer the medication, and obtain a blood specimen 30 min later
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. Trough levels reflect the lowest concentration of medication in the blood, which is just before the next dose. This is used to verify the medication has not accumulated to toxic levels.

B. Trough levels are obtained once steady state has been reached, which typically takes 4–5 half-lives — usually longer than 24 hours.

C. Medication levels are measured in blood (serum), not urine.

D. This would measure the peak level, not the trough level.

Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 2

Safe Medication Administration and Error Reduction

Safe medication administration begins with the rights of medication administration, requires careful error reduction strategies, and recognizes adverse effects, allergic reactions, and medication interactions.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Six rights: right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation (plus reason, response). Verify by checking three times against the MAR. Use two patient identifiers. High-alert medications (insulin, opioids, heparin, KCl) require independent double-check. ISMP do-not-use abbreviations cause errors.

Rights of medication administration

  • Right patient (two identifiers)
  • Right medication (read label 3 times)
  • Right dose (calculate, verify with another nurse for high-alert)
  • Right route
  • Right time
  • Right documentation
  • Right reason and right response

Error prevention

  • Use barcode scanning (BCMA)
  • Compute calculations independently
  • Question unclear or unusual orders
  • Never crush enteric-coated or sustained-release tablets
  • Do not leave meds at bedside (unless ordered)
  • Report all errors per facility policy

Controlled substances, errors & reporting

  • Controlled substance schedules (DEA):
  • • Schedule I: No accepted medical use (heroin, LSD, marijuana federally)
  • • Schedule II: High abuse potential, accepted medical use — morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methylphenidate, amphetamines
  • • Schedule III: Moderate potential — buprenorphine, ketamine, anabolic steroids
  • • Schedule IV: Lower potential — benzodiazepines, tramadol, zolpidem
  • • Schedule V: Lowest potential — pregabalin, low-dose codeine cough preparations
  • Controlled substance documentation: Count at every shift change with another nurse; document discrepancies immediately
  • Wasting: Two licensed staff witness disposal of unused portions
  • ISMP do-not-use abbreviations: U/u (use "units"), IU (use "international units"), Q.D./QD (use "daily"), Q.O.D./QOD (use "every other day"), MS/MSO4/MgSO4 (use full name), trailing zero (10.0 mg → 10 mg), leading zero (.5 mg → 0.5 mg)
  • Tall-man lettering distinguishes look-alike drug names (hydrOXYzine vs hydrALAzine; predniSONE vs predniSOLONE; vinBLAStine vs vinCRIStine)
  • Medication reconciliation required at admission, transfer, and discharge — compare current meds with new orders
  • Error reporting: Complete incident/occurrence report per facility policy — used for system improvement, NOT punishment; near-misses also reported
  • Just culture: Distinguishes human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior; supports learning from errors
Name the four classic high-alert medications that require independent double-check by two licensed nurses before administration.
Insulin, opioids, heparin, KCl. ISMP designates these high-alert because errors carry high risk of serious harm. The independent double-check means each nurse calculates separately (not just "verify what I did") and signs off.
A provider writes "10.0 mg" and another writes ".5 mg". Which is correct ISMP convention, and why?
Trailing zero forbidden: "10.0 mg" → write 10 mg (decimal point can be missed → 100 mg overdose). Leading zero required: ".5 mg" → write 0.5 mg (missed decimal → 5 mg overdose). Both rules exist because of real fatal errors.
Quick-recall: place these in the correct DEA schedule — morphine, alprazolam, buprenorphine, pregabalin.
Schedule II: morphine (high abuse potential, accepted medical use — also fentanyl, oxycodone, methylphenidate). Schedule III: buprenorphine (also ketamine, anabolic steroids). Schedule IV: alprazolam (also other benzos, tramadol, zolpidem). Schedule V: pregabalin (lowest potential — also low-dose codeine cough preps).

Six Rights of Medication Administration

The foundational checks performed every time a medication is given. Use them at three checkpoints: when removing the medication, when preparing it, and at the bedside before administration.

The 6 (or 8) Rights

Verify every dose

The classic six rights protect against medication errors. Many facilities now add right reason, right response, and right documentation.

Core six rights

  • Right patient — verify with two identifiers (name, DOB, MR#); scan barcode
  • Right medication — read label three times: when removing, when preparing, before administering
  • Right dose — verify calculation; independent double-check for high-alert (insulin, heparin, opioid drips, chemo)
  • Right route — confirm the prescribed route; never assume
  • Right time — within 30 minutes of scheduled time (per facility); first-dose and STAT promptly
  • Right documentation — after administration, not before; include any deviations

Additional rights

  • Right reason — understand why this client needs this medication now
  • Right response — assess for therapeutic effect and adverse reactions
  • Right to refuse — clients can decline; document and notify provider

Two patient identifiers

Use two unique identifiers before administering any medication. Room number is NOT an identifier.

Acceptable identifiers

  • Full name and date of birth
  • Medical record number
  • Hospital armband barcode (scan)
  • Government-issued photo ID (outpatient)

Special situations

  • Unconscious/non-verbal: armband + family confirmation
  • Children: ask the parent to state the child's name and DOB
  • Cognitively impaired adults: armband + family member or caregiver

Error Prevention

Medication errors are preventable. Use technology, double-checks, and standardized practices to reduce risk. Errors are reported as part of a Just Culture — focus is on system improvement, not punishment.

Technology safeguards

Bedside technology has substantially reduced errors but is not a substitute for nursing vigilance.

Tools

  • Barcode medication administration (BCMA): Scan client armband and medication; system flags mismatches
  • Smart pumps: Built-in drug libraries with dose-range limits; flag potentially unsafe rates
  • eMAR (electronic medication administration record): Real-time updates; allergy alerts
  • Override functionality should be used cautiously and documented

Communication safeguards

Many errors trace back to communication breakdowns.

Best practices

  • Read back verbal/telephone orders; have the prescriber repeat
  • SBAR communication for handoffs (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
  • Bedside handoff with the off-going nurse
  • Question any unclear or unusual orders before administering
  • Never accept a verbal order in a non-emergency situation if avoidable

Special formulation cautions

Certain medication forms have administration restrictions that prevent errors.

Do NOT crush or chew

  • Enteric-coated tablets
  • Sustained-release / extended-release (ER, XR, XL, SR, CR)
  • Sublingual or buccal tablets
  • Capsules (unless specifically labeled to open)
  • Crushing changes pharmacokinetics — can cause toxicity (release entire dose at once) or therapeutic failure

Other cautions

  • Never leave medication at bedside (unless ordered, e.g., nitroglycerin within client reach)
  • Never administer a medication someone else prepared (except pharmacy)
  • Never recap needles routinely
  • Dispose of sharps in approved containers

Tall-man lettering

A system of mixed-case letters that highlights distinguishing letters in look-alike drug names. Prevents wrong-drug errors.

Common tall-man pairs

  • hydrOXYzine (antihistamine, anxiolytic) vs hydrALAzine (antihypertensive)
  • predniSONE (oral) vs predniSOLONE (different potency)
  • vinBLAStine vs vinCRIStine (chemotherapy — fatal if confused)
  • DAUNOrubicin vs DOXOrubicin
  • cycloSERINE vs cycloSPORINE

ISMP Do-Not-Use abbreviations

The Institute for Safe Medication Practices (ISMP) maintains a list of dangerous abbreviations that should not be used. The Joint Commission requires elimination of these from prescribing.

Common forbidden abbreviations

  • U or u → use "units" (mistaken for 0, 4, or cc)
  • IU → use "international units"
  • QD or Q.D. → use "daily"
  • QOD or Q.O.D. → use "every other day"
  • Trailing zero (10.0 mg) → use 10 mg (decimal point can be missed)
  • Missing leading zero (.5 mg) → use 0.5 mg (decimal point can be missed)
  • MS, MSO4, MgSO4 → use full name (morphine sulfate vs magnesium sulfate confusion)
  • SC, SQ → use "subcut" or "subcutaneously"

Controlled Substances

The DEA classifies certain medications with abuse potential into five Schedules. Schedule I has no accepted medical use; Schedules II–V are prescribed but require special handling, documentation, and security.

DEA Schedules

Schedule classification determines prescribing restrictions, refills allowed, and storage requirements.

Schedule II — high abuse potential, accepted medical use

  • No refills allowed; written or electronic prescription required (some states allow phone for emergency, with written follow-up)
  • Examples: morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl, methadone, methylphenidate, amphetamines, cocaine

Schedule III — moderate abuse potential

  • Refills allowed (up to 5 in 6 months)
  • Examples: buprenorphine, ketamine, anabolic steroids, codeine combination products, testosterone

Schedule IV — lower abuse potential

  • Refills allowed (up to 5 in 6 months)
  • Examples: benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, lorazepam), tramadol, zolpidem, eszopiclone, modafinil

Schedule V — lowest abuse potential

  • Some available OTC (state-dependent); refills similar to Schedule IV
  • Examples: pregabalin, low-dose codeine in cough preparations, diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil)

Handling and documentation

Controlled substances require strict accountability to prevent diversion.

Nursing responsibilities

  • Count at every shift change with another licensed nurse — both sign
  • Any discrepancy: investigate immediately; do not give the next dose until resolved
  • Document on the controlled substance record at the time of administration
  • Wasting: Two licensed staff witness disposal of unused portions (e.g., a partial vial of morphine) and both sign
  • Lock storage in a double-locked cabinet or automated dispensing machine (e.g., Pyxis)
  • Report suspected diversion through facility chain of command

Medication Reconciliation & Pregnancy Categories

Reconciliation prevents discrepancies between what the client takes and what is prescribed. Pregnancy categories (now replaced by detailed labeling) guide safety decisions.

Medication reconciliation

A formal process required at every transition of care to prevent omissions, duplications, dosing errors, and interactions.

When to reconcile

  • On admission to a healthcare facility
  • At each transfer (e.g., ICU to floor, ED to admission)
  • At discharge
  • After each provider visit

What to include

  • Prescription medications (name, dose, route, frequency, last dose)
  • Over-the-counter medications
  • Herbal supplements and vitamins
  • Recreational substances if disclosed
  • Compare with new orders; reconcile any discrepancies with the provider

Pregnancy categories (older FDA system)

The FDA pregnancy categories (A, B, C, D, X) were the standard until 2015. The newer Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) replaces these with narrative summaries, but the letter categories still appear on many references.

FDA letter categories

  • A — adequate human studies show no fetal risk (rare; example: levothyroxine, prenatal vitamins)
  • B — animal studies show no risk OR animal toxicity not confirmed in humans (acetaminophen, most penicillins, metformin, ondansetron)
  • C — animal studies show harm OR no adequate studies; use only if benefits outweigh risks (most drugs)
  • D — evidence of human fetal harm; may be used if benefit outweighs risk in serious illness (phenytoin, lithium, paroxetine)
  • X — contraindicated; risks clearly outweigh any benefit (warfarin, isotretinoin, methotrexate, statins, thalidomide, misoprostol)

PLLR (current) sections

  • Pregnancy: includes risk summary and clinical considerations
  • Lactation: information on drug transfer to milk and infant effects
  • Females and Males of Reproductive Potential: contraception requirements, fertility effects

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is preparing to administer a medication to a client. List the steps a nurse should take to verify the right client. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill to complete this item.

Show key

Description of Skill — Verifying the Right Client

  • Use two unique identifiers before each medication administration
  • Acceptable identifiers: full name, date of birth, medical record number
  • Compare the medication administration record (MAR) against the client's identification armband
  • Scan the client's armband and the medication barcode when available
  • Ask the client to state their name and date of birth (when able)
  • For unconscious/non-verbal clients, verify with armband and a family member

Indications for Use of Two Identifiers

  • Reduces wrong-patient errors
  • Required by The Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goal
  • Used at every medication administration, blood transfusion, specimen collection

Considerations

  • Never use room number or location as an identifier
  • If barcode scanning fails, do not bypass — re-verify manually and troubleshoot
  • Document any deviation from standard process per facility policy

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 2 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is preparing to administer medications. Which of the following actions should the nurse take to prevent medication errors?

  1. A. Read the medication label three times: when removing the container, when preparing the medication, and at the bedside before administering it
  2. B. Crush the enteric-coated tablet to make it easier to swallow
  3. C. Leave the medication at the bedside for the client to take when they are ready
  4. D. Document medication administration immediately before giving the medication
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. Reading the label three times is the standard safety practice that catches errors at each handling step. This is a foundational principle of medication safety.

B. Crushing enteric-coated tablets destroys the protective coating and can cause GI irritation, drug instability, or release of the entire dose at once.

C. Medications should not be left at the bedside (unless specifically ordered, like nitroglycerin) — they may be missed, misplaced, or taken by another person.

D. Documentation should occur AFTER the medication is administered, not before. Documenting first risks omission if the client refuses or the medication is held.

NCLEX · Safety and Infection Control · Medication Administration · Error Prevention
Q2

A nurse is reviewing the ISMP list of error-prone abbreviations. Which of the following abbreviations should the nurse identify as appropriate to use in a medication order? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. "units" instead of "U"
  2. B. "daily" instead of "QD"
  3. C. "morphine sulfate" instead of "MS"
  4. D. "0.5 mg" instead of ".5 mg"
  5. E. "5.0 mg" instead of "5 mg"
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — "U" can be misread as "0," "4," or "cc," leading to massive overdose. Always write out "units."

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — "QD" can be misread as "QID" (four times a day) or "QOD" (every other day). Write out "daily."

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — "MS" or "MSO4" can be confused with "MgSO4" (magnesium sulfate). Always write the full name.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Always use a leading zero before a decimal point so the decimal is not missed. ".5 mg" can look like "5 mg" (10× overdose).

E. INCORRECT — Trailing zeros should be removed. "5.0 mg" can be misread as "50 mg" if the decimal point is missed.

NCLEX · Safety and Infection Control · Reporting of Incident/Event
Q3

A nurse on a medical unit is signing out a controlled substance for administration. Which of the following actions is the priority?

  1. A. Wait until the end of shift to count and verify with another nurse
  2. B. Document the dose on the MAR before administering it
  3. C. Verify the count with another licensed nurse before removing the dose
  4. D. Discard any unused portion in the sharps container
Show rationale ▾

A. Controlled substance counts occur at shift change, but discrepancies for a current dose must be addressed immediately, not at the end of shift.

B. Document AFTER administering, not before. This is true for all medications, but especially important for controlled substances where wasted doses must be accounted for.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Controlled substance counts must be verified by two licensed staff. Discrepancies must be investigated immediately, before continuing administration.

D. Unused portions must be wasted in front of a second licensed witness who co-signs the wasting documentation. Discarding alone or in the wrong container does not provide accountability.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q4

A nurse is performing medication reconciliation for a newly admitted client. Which of the following should the nurse include?

  1. A. Only prescription medications taken regularly
  2. B. Prescription medications, OTC products, and herbal supplements
  3. C. Only medications the client took in the past 24 hours
  4. D. Medications listed in the discharge summary from the previous admission
Show rationale ▾

A. Reconciliation must include ALL substances the client takes — prescription, OTC, herbal, vitamins — because all can interact.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Complete reconciliation includes all medications and supplements. Herbals especially can have major interactions (e.g., St. John's wort with antidepressants, antiretrovirals, anticoagulants).

C. A 24-hour window misses medications taken every other day, weekly, or as needed. Reconciliation looks at the client's full current regimen.

D. Discharge summaries are a useful reference but the client's current regimen may differ. Confirm with the client and/or caregiver.

NCLEX · Management of Care · Continuity of Care
Q5

A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about FDA pregnancy categories. Which of the following medications should the nurse identify as Category X (contraindicated in pregnancy)? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Warfarin
  2. B. Acetaminophen
  3. C. Isotretinoin
  4. D. Methotrexate
  5. E. Insulin
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Warfarin is a known teratogen causing fetal warfarin syndrome (skeletal abnormalities, CNS defects). Use heparin or LMWH in pregnancy instead.

B. Acetaminophen is Category B and considered safe at therapeutic doses throughout pregnancy. It is the first-line analgesic/antipyretic in pregnancy.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Isotretinoin (Accutane) is a potent teratogen causing severe craniofacial and cardiac defects. Requires the iPLEDGE program with strict contraception requirements.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Methotrexate is an abortifacient and teratogen. Used to terminate pregnancy in some cases; contraindicated when continued pregnancy is desired.

E. Insulin is Category B and is the preferred treatment for diabetes in pregnancy. Most oral antidiabetic agents are avoided.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 3

Dosage Calculation

Dosage calculation requires accuracy. Nurses use three methods — ratio and proportion, formula, and dimensional analysis — to safely calculate oral, parenteral, IV, and weight-based pediatric doses.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Three methods: ratio-proportion, formula method (Desired/Have × Volume), dimensional analysis. Pediatric doses: mg/kg/day (always weight-based). IV flow rates: gtt/min = (mL × gtt/mL) ÷ min. Always double-check calculations for high-alert drugs.

Standard formulas

  • Tablet/capsule: Desired ÷ Have = number of units
  • Liquid: (Desired ÷ Have) × Volume = mL
  • IV rate: mL/hr = total volume ÷ time in hours
  • IV drip: (mL × drop factor) ÷ minutes = gtt/min

Pediatric calculations

  • Doses always based on weight (kg)
  • Verify safe range: dose × weight = total daily dose
  • Compare to recommended dose range — call provider if outside range
  • Use age-appropriate measurement devices (oral syringes)

Common calculation formulas

  • Tablets: Desired ÷ Have = number of tablets
  • Liquid: (Desired ÷ Have) × Volume on hand = mL
  • Pediatric weight-based: Convert lb to kg (lb ÷ 2.2); then mg/kg × kg = total daily dose; divide by # of doses/day
  • IV continuous: mL/hr = total volume (mL) ÷ time (hr)
  • IV drip (gtt/min): (Volume × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes
  • Drop factors (gtt/mL): Macrodrip 10/15/20; microdrip = 60 (1 mL = 60 gtt; mL/hr = gtt/min for micro)
  • Safe dose verification: Calculate dose × weight = expected; compare to ordered; hold and call provider if outside safe range
  • Round per facility policy; pediatric — usually to nearest tenth; high-alert (insulin, heparin) — independent double-check
When the drop factor is microdrip (60 gtt/mL), what is the shortcut for converting mL/hr to gtt/min?
With a microdrip set (60 gtt/mL): mL/hr = gtt/min directly (no math required). Reason: (mL/hr × 60 gtt/mL) ÷ 60 min/hr cancels to mL/hr. Macrodrip factors are 10, 15, or 20 gtt/mL and require the full formula: gtt/min = (mL × gtt/mL) ÷ min.
A child weighing 22 lb is prescribed amoxicillin 90 mg PO q8h. The safe range is 20–40 mg/kg/day. Is this dose safe?
Step 1: 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg. Step 2: total daily dose = 90 mg × 3 doses = 270 mg/day. Step 3: safe range = 10 kg × 20–40 = 200–400 mg/day. 270 mg/day is within safe range → administer. Always: convert weight → calculate total daily dose → compare to safe range. If outside range, hold and call provider.

Three Methods of Dosage Calculation

Three commonly-taught methods produce the same answer: ratio-proportion, formula method (desired over have), and dimensional analysis. Choose the method you find clearest — what matters is accurate calculation.

Ratio-proportion method

Universal applicability

Set up known and unknown ratios as equivalent fractions, then solve for the unknown.

Steps

  • Step 1: Write the known ratio (what you have)
  • Step 2: Write the unknown ratio (what you want)
  • Step 3: Cross-multiply and solve for x
  • Example: Order = 750 mg; on hand = 500 mg/tab → 500/1 = 750/x → x = 1.5 tabs

Formula method (Desired ÷ Have × Quantity)

Most common

Use when the units match. Quantity is the volume or number of units per dose.

Formula

  • (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = amount to administer
  • Example: Desired = 25 mg; have = 100 mg/2 mL → (25 ÷ 100) × 2 = 0.5 mL
  • Always check that units cancel correctly — if not, conversions are needed

Dimensional analysis

Best for multi-step conversions

Set up a chain of conversion factors so unwanted units cancel and only the desired unit remains. Particularly useful for weight-based and IV drip calculations.

Steps

  • Step 1: Write the desired unit (left side of equation = X with appropriate unit)
  • Step 2: Find a factor with the same unit on top (right side starts there)
  • Step 3: Add factors so unwanted units cancel diagonally (numerator-denominator)
  • Step 4: Multiply across; the only remaining unit should be the desired unit
  • Example: 8 mg/kg/day × 10 kg × 1 day = 80 mg/day total

Key Formulas

Memorize these common formulas. They cover the majority of clinical dosage calculations: tablets, liquids, IV continuous rates, IV drip rates, and pediatric doses.

Tablets and capsules

Solid oral dosage forms. Always confirm whether the tablet can be cut, crushed, or split.

Formula

  • Number of tablets = Desired dose ÷ Available dose per tablet
  • Example: Order = 750 mg; on hand = 250 mg tabs → 750 ÷ 250 = 3 tabs
  • Avoid splitting tablets when possible (uneven doses); never split capsules or sustained-release

Liquid medications

Oral suspensions, solutions, and parenteral medications. Always verify with marked oral syringe (oral) or appropriate volumetric measure.

Formula

  • Volume = (Desired dose ÷ Available concentration) × Volume of one dose
  • Example: Order = 40 mg; on hand = 100 mg/5 mL → (40 ÷ 100) × 5 = 2 mL
  • Always use oral syringe for oral liquids (never a parenteral syringe)
  • Never use household teaspoons — they vary widely

IV continuous infusion

Calculate the rate for IV pump programming. Pumps deliver in mL/hr.

Formula

  • mL/hr = Total volume (mL) ÷ Time (hours)
  • Example: 1000 mL over 8 hr → 125 mL/hr
  • Verify with pump programming; double-check high-alert infusions

IV drip rate (gtt/min) — gravity infusion

For gravity drips without a pump. Requires the drop factor (gtt/mL), found on the tubing package.

Formula

  • gtt/min = (Volume × Drop factor) ÷ Time in minutes
  • Example: 1000 mL over 8 hr, drop factor 15 gtt/mL → (1000 × 15) ÷ 480 min ≈ 31 gtt/min
  • Drop factors: Macrodrip = 10, 15, or 20 gtt/mL; Microdrip = 60 gtt/mL
  • Microdrip shortcut: mL/hr = gtt/min (one-to-one)

IV bolus / push

Direct injection of a medication into an IV line.

Considerations

  • Verify drug-specific push rate (per pharmacy or drug reference) — many drugs over 1–5 minutes
  • Hold timer; do not exceed maximum rate (e.g., furosemide ≤ 20 mg/min, vancomycin not given as push)
  • Flush before and after with appropriate solution

Pediatric Dose Calculations

Children's doses are ALWAYS weight-based (mg/kg or mg/kg/day) because they vary so dramatically by age and size. Verify the calculated dose is within the safe range for the medication and the child's weight.

Weight-based dosing

Always convert pounds to kilograms first: kg = lb ÷ 2.2. Some medications use mg/m² (body surface area) but most pediatric drugs use mg/kg.

Standard process

  • Step 1: Convert weight to kg (lb ÷ 2.2)
  • Step 2: Calculate total daily dose (mg/kg/day × weight in kg)
  • Step 3: Divide total daily dose by number of doses per day to get per-dose amount
  • Step 4: Convert from mg to mL using the available concentration
  • Step 5: Verify against safe dose range — if outside range, hold and call provider

Example

  • Order: cefixime 8 mg/kg/day PO divided q12h to toddler weighing 22 lb
  • 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg
  • 8 mg/kg/day × 10 kg = 80 mg/day total
  • 80 mg ÷ 2 doses = 40 mg per dose
  • On hand: 100 mg/5 mL → (40 ÷ 100) × 5 = 2 mL per dose

Safe dose verification

Critical safety check

Before administering ANY pediatric medication, verify the order is within the safe dose range. Hold the medication and call the provider if outside the range.

Verification steps

  • Look up the recommended dose range (mg/kg/day) from a drug reference
  • Calculate the safe range for this client (range × weight in kg)
  • Compare the ordered dose to the safe range
  • Within range: Administer
  • Outside range: Hold medication, call provider, document

Rounding rules

Follow facility policy and the medication's package insert.

Common pediatric rounding

  • Most pediatric oral liquids: round to nearest 0.1 mL (1/10)
  • Many IV medications: round to nearest 0.01 mL for small infants
  • Tablets: avoid splitting beyond scored lines; choose liquid form when available
  • Use appropriate measurement device (oral syringe for liquids — never household teaspoon)

High-Alert Medications & Verification

High-alert medications cause significant harm when used in error. They require additional safety measures even when used correctly.

High-alert medication classes

These categories have the highest risk profile. ISMP maintains the official list.

Examples

  • Insulin (all forms — especially U-500 concentration)
  • Anticoagulants (heparin IV, warfarin, DOACs)
  • Opioids (especially IV; concentrated forms)
  • Concentrated electrolytes (KCl, NaCl > 0.9%, MgSO4)
  • Chemotherapy (all forms)
  • Neuromuscular blockers (succinylcholine, rocuronium, vecuronium)
  • Digoxin, lithium, sedatives (moderate sedation)

Independent double-check

Two qualified individuals separately calculate and verify the medication and dose. Each person performs the calculation independently — not just "looks over" the other's work.

When required (per ISMP and facility policy)

  • Insulin IV infusions and bolus doses
  • Heparin IV infusions and bolus
  • Opioid IV continuous infusions, PCA programming
  • Chemotherapy preparations
  • IV potassium and other concentrated electrolytes
  • Neonatal and pediatric high-alert medications

Process

  • Each nurse independently calculates the dose
  • Each nurse independently verifies the medication, concentration, pump settings, line tracing
  • Both sign documentation only after agreement
  • If disagreement: stop, recalculate, involve a third party if needed

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is preparing to administer cefixime 8 mg/kg/day PO divided every 12 hours to a toddler who weighs 22 lb. Available is cefixime suspension 100 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse administer per dose? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill to complete this item.

Show key

Description of Calculation Steps

  • Step 1: Convert weight — 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg
  • Step 2: Calculate total daily dose — 8 mg/kg/day × 10 kg = 80 mg/day
  • Step 3: Divide by doses per day — 80 mg ÷ 2 doses (q12h) = 40 mg per dose
  • Step 4: Calculate volume — (40 mg ÷ 100 mg) × 5 mL = 2 mL per dose
  • Answer: 2 mL per dose

Safety Considerations

  • Verify the order is within the safe dose range (5–10 mg/kg/day for cefixime in pediatrics — 8 mg/kg/day is within range)
  • Use an oral syringe — not a household teaspoon
  • Independent double-check is not required for cefixime but is good practice for any pediatric calculation
  • Document administration on the MAR after giving

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 3 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is preparing to administer digoxin 0.125 mg PO to a client. The medication is available in scored 0.25 mg tablets. How many tablets should the nurse administer?

  1. A. 0.25 tablet
  2. B. 0.5 tablet
  3. C. 1 tablet
  4. D. 2 tablets
Show rationale ▾

A. Incorrect calculation — this would deliver only 0.0625 mg, not 0.125 mg.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — (0.125 ÷ 0.25) × 1 tablet = 0.5 tablet. The tablet is scored, so it can be safely split.

C. One tablet would deliver 0.25 mg — twice the ordered dose. This would be a serious medication error in a narrow-therapeutic-index drug.

D. Two tablets would deliver 0.5 mg — four times the ordered dose. Digoxin toxicity is dangerous.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Dosage Calculation
Q2

A provider prescribes 1000 mL 0.9% NaCl to infuse over 8 hours. The IV tubing drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. How many gtt/min should the nurse set the infusion at? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

  1. A. 21 gtt/min
  2. B. 31 gtt/min
  3. C. 42 gtt/min
  4. D. 125 gtt/min
Show rationale ▾

A. This would be too slow — would not deliver the volume in 8 hours.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — (1000 mL × 15 gtt/mL) ÷ (8 hr × 60 min/hr) = 15,000 ÷ 480 = 31.25 ≈ 31 gtt/min.

C. Too fast — would deliver the volume in less than 8 hours.

D. 125 is the mL/hr rate, not gtt/min. Confusing the two leads to massive over-infusion.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Dosage Calculation
Q3

A nurse is preparing to administer amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day PO divided every 8 hours to a child who weighs 33 lb. Available is amoxicillin suspension 250 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse administer per dose? (Round to the nearest whole number.)

  1. A. 3 mL
  2. B. 5 mL
  3. C. 7 mL
  4. D. 10 mL
Show rationale ▾

A. Recalculate. 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg; 50 mg × 15 = 750 mg/day; ÷ 3 doses = 250 mg/dose; (250 ÷ 250) × 5 = 5 mL.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — 33 lb ÷ 2.2 = 15 kg → 50 mg/kg/day × 15 kg = 750 mg/day → 750 ÷ 3 doses = 250 mg/dose → (250 mg ÷ 250 mg) × 5 mL = 5 mL.

C. Too high — recheck the conversion and division by 3 doses per day.

D. This would deliver double the prescribed dose. Recalculate carefully.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Pediatric Dosage Calculation
Q4

A nurse is administering heparin IV bolus 80 units/kg to a client who weighs 154 lb. Heparin is available 5,000 units/mL. How many mL should the nurse administer? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

  1. A. 0.8 mL
  2. B. 1.1 mL
  3. C. 1.6 mL
  4. D. 2.0 mL
Show rationale ▾

A. Recalculate the bolus dose and the volume.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg → 80 units/kg × 70 kg = 5,600 units → 5,600 ÷ 5,000 × 1 mL = 1.12 mL ≈ 1.1 mL.

C. Recheck the conversion to kg and the multiplication.

D. Recheck — would be approximately 10,000 units, much higher than the prescribed dose.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Parenteral/Intravenous Therapies
Q5

A nurse is reviewing strategies to prevent calculation errors with high-alert medications. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Perform an independent double-check with another qualified nurse before administration
  2. B. Use a calculator rather than mental math for all dose calculations
  3. C. Avoid leading zeros on decimal doses (e.g., write ".5 mg" instead of "0.5 mg")
  4. D. Confirm the dose is within the safe range for the client
  5. E. Use trailing zeros on whole-number doses (e.g., write "5.0 mg" instead of "5 mg")
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Independent double-checks for insulin, heparin, opioids, chemotherapy, and concentrated electrolytes catch errors before they reach the client.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Mental math is a common source of error. A calculator (with the result verified) is safer and faster for complex calculations.

C. INCORRECT — Always include a leading zero before a decimal (0.5 mg, not .5 mg). The decimal point can be missed without a leading zero.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Verifying the calculated dose against the safe range is a fundamental check, especially for pediatric and high-alert medications.

E. INCORRECT — Trailing zeros should be avoided. "5.0 mg" can be misread as "50 mg" if the decimal point is missed.

NCLEX · Safety and Infection Control · Reporting of Incident/Event
Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 4

Intravenous Therapy

Intravenous (IV) therapy delivers fluids, electrolytes, medications, blood products, and nutritional support directly into the venous system. The nurse maintains IV access, infuses solutions, and monitors for complications.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Crystalloids (isotonic NS/LR, hypo 0.45% NS, hyper D5NS) treat dehydration and maintenance. Colloids (albumin, dextran) expand volume. Check site for infiltration, phlebitis, infection. Central lines for irritants, vesicants, TPN, hyperosmolar solutions. IV push: always over correct time.

IV solution types

  • Isotonic (0.9% NS, LR) — fluid replacement, blood compatible
  • Hypotonic (0.45% NS) — cellular hydration
  • Hypertonic (D5NS, 3% NS) — pulls fluid into vascular space
  • Add electrolytes (KCl) carefully — never IV push K+

Complications

  • Infiltration: cool, swelling, no blood return
  • Phlebitis: redness, warmth, pain along vein
  • Extravasation: leakage of vesicant → tissue damage
  • Infection: site redness, fever, purulent drainage
  • Air embolism, fluid overload: assess regularly

IV complications & monitoring

  • Infiltration (non-vesicant solution leaks into tissue): Swelling, cool, blanched/pale, decreased flow, fluid leakage; stop IV, remove catheter, elevate limb, warm compress (cool for some); restart at different site
  • Extravasation (vesicant solution — chemo, dopamine, vasopressors leaks): Tissue damage/necrosis possible; stop infusion immediately, try to aspirate residual from catheter, give antidote per protocol, do NOT remove catheter until done
  • Phlebitis (vein inflammation): Redness, warmth, pain along the vein, possible palpable cord; remove IV, warm compress, may need culture; common with peripheral IV > 72–96 hr
  • Air embolism: Sudden chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension; turn client left side, Trendelenburg (keeps air in right ventricle); O2
  • Catheter embolism: Tip of catheter breaks off; emergency — tourniquet above site, X-ray to locate
  • Circulatory overload (TACO): Crackles, dyspnea, hypertension, JVD; slow rate, sit client up, O2, diuretic
  • Central line complications: CLABSI (bloodstream infection); pneumothorax (after subclavian/jugular insertion); air embolism; thrombosis
  • Tubing change: Continuous IV q96h; intermittent/secondary q24h; TPN q24h; blood/blood products with each unit; lipids q24h
  • IV bag/bottle: Maximum hang time 24 hr (less for blood, TPN, lipids); date and time when hung
  • Site rotation: Peripheral IV typically rotated q72–96h per CDC; can be longer if needed
Differentiate isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic IV solutions — and what each is used to treat.
Isotonic (0.9% NS, LR): same osmolarity as plasma → fluid replacement, blood-compatible. Hypotonic (0.45% NS): pulls fluid into cells → cellular hydration (e.g., hypernatremia, DKA after initial resuscitation). Hypertonic (D5NS, 3% NS): pulls fluid into vascular space → severe hyponatremia, cerebral edema. Never IV push K⁺.
A nurse notes the IV site is swollen, cool, blanched, with no blood return. Is this infiltration or extravasation — and what is the key action difference?
Infiltration = a non-vesicant solution leaks into surrounding tissue (cool, swelling, pale, no blood return). Action: stop IV, remove catheter, elevate limb, warm or cool compress. Extravasation = a vesicant (chemo, dopamine, vasopressors) leaks → tissue necrosis. Action: stop infusion immediately, try to aspirate residual through the catheter, give antidote per protocol, do NOT remove catheter until done.
A client with a central line suddenly reports chest pain, dyspnea, and becomes hypotensive. Air embolism is suspected. What is the immediate positioning?
Turn client to LEFT lateral side and Trendelenburg (head down). Rationale: traps the air in the right ventricle so it can be absorbed gradually rather than entering the pulmonary circulation. Also: clamp the line, give 100% O₂, notify provider. Distinguish from catheter embolism (tip breaks off — apply tourniquet above site, X-ray).

IV Solutions

IV fluids are categorized by tonicity (osmolality compared to plasma). Choosing the right tonicity for the clinical situation prevents dangerous fluid shifts. Crystalloids contain water-soluble solutes; colloids contain larger molecules that pull fluid into the vascular space.

Isotonic solutions

Same osmolality as plasma

Fluid stays in the vascular space — used for volume expansion and replacement. No fluid shift between compartments.

Examples & uses

  • 0.9% sodium chloride (NS, normal saline) — fluid replacement; compatible with blood products
  • Lactated Ringer's (LR) — surgical and trauma resuscitation; contains K+, Ca++, lactate (becomes bicarbonate); avoid in liver failure (impaired lactate metabolism), hyperkalemia
  • D5W (5% dextrose in water) — technically isotonic in the bag, but becomes hypotonic once dextrose is metabolized; treats hypernatremia, vehicle for medications
  • Uses: Hypovolemia, shock, blood/blood product administration (NS only), surgical fluid replacement

Cautions

  • Risk of fluid overload — circulatory overload, CHF, pulmonary edema
  • Monitor lung sounds, weight, JVD, edema

Hypotonic solutions

Lower osmolality than plasma

Fluid shifts from the vascular space into cells — rehydrates cells. Used carefully — too much can cause cellular swelling and cerebral edema.

Examples & uses

  • 0.45% NS (half-normal saline) — most common hypotonic; cellular dehydration, hypernatremia, DKA after initial resuscitation
  • 0.225% NS, 0.33% NS — less common

Risks

  • Do NOT give: Increased ICP (worsens cerebral edema), burns, trauma, liver disease
  • Monitor closely; can cause hypotension if vascular space depletes

Hypertonic solutions

Higher osmolality than plasma

Pulls fluid from cells into the vascular space. Used for severe hyponatremia and to reduce cerebral edema.

Examples & uses

  • 3% NS, 5% NS — severe symptomatic hyponatremia, cerebral edema (raises serum osmolality, reduces brain swelling)
  • D5NS, D5LR, D5 ½ NS — provides calories with electrolytes; post-op
  • D10W, D20W, D50W — concentrated dextrose; hypoglycemia (D50W IV push)

Cautions

  • Risk of fluid overload and pulmonary edema
  • Risk of cellular dehydration and crenation
  • Hypertonic saline (3%) requires central line for prolonged administration; intensive monitoring
  • Rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)

Colloids

Volume expanders

Large molecules that remain in the vascular space, pulling fluid in by osmotic pressure. Useful when blood products are not available or appropriate.

Examples & uses

  • Albumin (5% and 25%) — burns, hypovolemia, hypoalbuminemia, large-volume paracentesis
  • Dextran, hetastarch — synthetic plasma expanders; trauma
  • Blood products (whole blood, PRBCs, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate)

Cautions

  • Risk of fluid overload
  • Hetastarch and dextran: bleeding risk, possible renal effects
  • Albumin: anaphylaxis (rare), fluid overload

IV Access

Peripheral IV catheters are the standard short-term access. Central venous catheters allow long-term access, irritating medications, TPN, and frequent blood draws.

Peripheral IV

Standard short-term

Catheter inserted in a peripheral vein, usually in the hand or forearm. Limited to short courses (typically < 5–7 days) and non-vesicant solutions.

Site selection

  • Use most distal site that will accept the catheter (preserves proximal sites for future use)
  • Avoid: areas of flexion (antecubital limited), affected side post-mastectomy, dialysis fistula limb, paralyzed limb
  • Hand veins for shorter dwell times; forearm veins for longer dwell times
  • Avoid lower extremity in adults (risk of DVT, infection)

Catheter sizing

  • 18 gauge: Blood/blood products, surgery, trauma
  • 20 gauge: Standard adult IV fluids and most medications
  • 22 gauge: Older adults, fragile veins, pediatric
  • 24 gauge: Neonates, infants, fragile veins

Rotation

  • Per CDC: peripheral IV may stay in place if functioning and site shows no complications
  • Per facility policy: typically replaced every 72–96 hours; sooner if complications

Central venous access

Long-term, irritant, TPN

Catheter terminates in the superior vena cava (or other large central vein). Allows infusion of irritants, vesicants, hyperosmolar solutions, TPN, and frequent blood draws.

Types

  • PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter): Inserted in upper arm, threads to SVC; weeks to months; nurse-inserted with proper certification
  • Tunneled catheter (Hickman, Broviac, Groshong): Surgically tunneled under skin; long-term (months to years); chemotherapy, TPN
  • Implanted port (Port-a-cath): Subcutaneous reservoir; longest-term; accessed with Huber needle
  • Non-tunneled central line: Inserted in jugular, subclavian, or femoral; short-term ICU use

Maintenance

  • Sterile technique for all dressing changes, access
  • Confirm placement with X-ray before initial use
  • Flush per facility protocol (often heparin lock for ports; NS for PICC/CVC)
  • Change dressing per protocol (typically q7d for transparent; q2d for gauze)
  • CLABSI prevention bundle: Hand hygiene, max sterile barriers at insertion, chlorhexidine skin prep, optimal site selection, daily review of necessity

IV Complications

Early recognition of IV complications prevents tissue damage and systemic harm. Inspect the site at every assessment.

Infiltration

Non-vesicant leak

Solution leaks into surrounding tissue (extravascular). Most common IV complication.

Signs

  • Swelling, coolness, pallor at the site
  • Slowed or stopped flow
  • Tenderness without erythema
  • Possible fluid leakage at insertion site

Interventions

  • Stop the infusion immediately
  • Remove the IV catheter
  • Elevate the extremity
  • Apply warm compress (for most solutions) or cool compress (per facility protocol/specific medication)
  • Restart IV at a different site, preferably proximal to original site
  • Document size of affected area, appearance, intervention

Extravasation

Vesicant leak — emergency

A VESICANT solution (chemotherapy, dopamine, vasopressors, calcium chloride, hypertonic saline) leaks into surrounding tissue, causing severe tissue damage and necrosis.

Signs

  • Severe burning or pain at site
  • Swelling and erythema
  • Skin discoloration
  • Tissue necrosis can develop over days

Interventions (emergency)

  • Stop the infusion immediately — but leave the IV catheter in place initially
  • Attempt to aspirate residual fluid through the catheter
  • Administer the antidote through the catheter (if available — e.g., hyaluronidase, phentolamine, sodium thiosulfate depending on vesicant)
  • Remove catheter only after antidote given
  • Apply warm or cold compress per the vesicant's protocol
  • Mark and measure affected area; photograph if facility policy
  • Notify provider and follow protocol for tissue specialist consult

Phlebitis / Thrombophlebitis

Vein inflammation

Inflammation of the vein wall, often with thrombus formation. Caused by chemical irritation, mechanical movement of catheter, or infection.

Signs

  • Redness and warmth along the vein
  • Pain or tenderness
  • Palpable cord along the vein course
  • Possible fever, purulent drainage (if infectious)

Interventions

  • Stop infusion and remove IV
  • Apply warm compress
  • Elevate extremity
  • Culture site/catheter tip if infectious phlebitis suspected
  • Restart IV in opposite extremity if possible
  • Document grade per facility scale (0–4)

Air embolism

Life-threatening

Air enters the circulation through the IV line.

Signs

  • Sudden dyspnea, chest pain
  • Hypotension, tachycardia
  • Confusion, anxiety
  • Wheezing, cyanosis

Interventions (emergency)

  • Position client on left side in Trendelenburg (traps air in right atrium/ventricle apex)
  • Administer 100% oxygen
  • Call rapid response / provider
  • Monitor vital signs continuously
  • Prevent: prime tubing fully; secure all connections; avoid letting bags run dry

Circulatory overload (TACO)

Volume overload

Too much IV fluid given too quickly overwhelms cardiovascular system.

Signs

  • Dyspnea, crackles (rales), tachypnea
  • Hypertension
  • Jugular vein distention (JVD)
  • Bounding pulse, S3 heart sound
  • Productive cough with pink frothy sputum (pulmonary edema)

Interventions

  • Slow the infusion to a keep-vein-open (KVO) rate
  • Position client upright (Fowler's or high Fowler's)
  • Administer oxygen
  • Notify provider; expect order for diuretic (furosemide IV)
  • Risk factors: older adults, infants, renal impairment, heart failure — use slower rates and smaller volumes

Catheter embolism

Catheter fragment travels

Tip of catheter breaks off and travels in the bloodstream.

Recognition & response

  • Suspect when partial catheter is withdrawn during removal
  • Apply tourniquet above insertion site
  • Notify provider immediately
  • X-ray to locate fragment; possible surgical retrieval
  • Prevention: never reinsert needle/stylet into a catheter; remove catheter intact

Infection / CLABSI

Bloodstream infection

Central line-associated bloodstream infection. Significant morbidity and mortality risk.

Signs

  • Fever, chills, elevated WBC
  • Erythema, warmth, purulent drainage at site
  • Positive blood cultures (especially from line vs peripheral)
  • Signs of sepsis: hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status

Prevention bundle (CLABSI bundle)

  • Hand hygiene before all line interactions
  • Maximum sterile barriers at insertion
  • Chlorhexidine skin antisepsis
  • Optimal site selection (subclavian preferred over femoral)
  • Daily review of line necessity — remove ASAP

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who has an IV infusion and notes that the IV site is cool, swollen, and pale, with decreased flow. What actions should the nurse take? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Nursing Skill to complete this item.

Show key

Description of Complication — Infiltration

  • Infiltration is the leakage of a non-vesicant solution into the tissue surrounding the IV catheter
  • Signs: coolness, swelling, pallor, decreased flow, possible fluid leakage
  • Caused by catheter displacement, vein wall puncture, or vein fragility

Nursing Actions

  • Stop the IV infusion immediately
  • Remove the IV catheter
  • Elevate the extremity to promote venous return
  • Apply warm compress to most non-irritant solutions (or cool compress per specific solution protocol)
  • Restart IV in a different site, preferably proximal to or in the opposite extremity
  • Document site appearance, size, intervention, and time
  • Notify provider if significant infiltration

Differentiation from Extravasation

  • Infiltration = non-vesicant solution; manage with stop/remove/warm compress
  • Extravasation = vesicant solution (chemo, dopamine, vasopressors) — emergency; leave catheter in place to administer antidote first

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 4 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is preparing to administer 0.9% NaCl IV to a client who is hypovolemic. Which of the following statements describes 0.9% NaCl?

  1. A. It is a hypotonic solution that shifts fluid into cells
  2. B. It is an isotonic solution that expands intravascular volume
  3. C. It is a hypertonic solution that pulls fluid from cells
  4. D. It is a colloid solution containing large molecules
Show rationale ▾

A. 0.9% NaCl is isotonic, not hypotonic. It has the same osmolality as plasma and does not shift fluid between compartments.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is isotonic. Fluid stays in the intravascular space, expanding circulating volume — making it ideal for hypovolemia and shock.

C. 0.9% NaCl is isotonic. Hypertonic saline (3% or 5%) pulls fluid from cells.

D. 0.9% NaCl is a crystalloid (small dissolved solutes), not a colloid (large molecules like albumin).

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Parenteral/Intravenous Therapies
Q2

A nurse is monitoring a client who is receiving IV fluids and notices the insertion site is swollen and cool with decreased flow. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?

  1. A. Apply warm compresses to the site
  2. B. Stop the IV infusion
  3. C. Administer the antidote
  4. D. Elevate the client's arm
Show rationale ▾

A. Warm compresses are an appropriate eventual intervention, but the first action is to stop the infusion.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — The signs (swelling, coolness, decreased flow) indicate infiltration. The first action is to stop the infusion to prevent further leakage into tissue.

C. Administering an antidote is for extravasation of a vesicant solution. This appears to be infiltration of a non-vesicant.

D. Elevation helps after stopping the infusion, but is not the priority first action.

NCLEX · Reduction of Risk Potential · System-Specific Assessments
Q3

A nurse is caring for a client who develops sudden dyspnea, chest pain, and hypotension during IV fluid administration. The nurse suspects air embolism. Which of the following positions should the nurse place the client in?

  1. A. High-Fowler's position
  2. B. Left lateral Trendelenburg
  3. C. Right lateral position
  4. D. Supine with head of bed flat
Show rationale ▾

A. High-Fowler's is appropriate for fluid overload but worsens air embolism.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Positioning the client on the LEFT side in Trendelenburg traps air in the apex of the right atrium/ventricle, preventing it from entering the pulmonary circulation. This is the priority intervention for suspected air embolism.

C. Right lateral position would allow air to enter the pulmonary circulation, worsening the embolism.

D. A simple supine position is insufficient. The left Trendelenburg position is required.

NCLEX · Reduction of Risk Potential · Therapeutic Procedures
Q4

A nurse is monitoring a client receiving IV chemotherapy via a peripheral IV. The nurse notes severe burning at the site, swelling, and erythema. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?

  1. A. Discontinue the IV catheter immediately
  2. B. Stop the infusion and aspirate residual vesicant from the catheter
  3. C. Apply ice and elevate the extremity
  4. D. Document the findings and continue monitoring
Show rationale ▾

A. For chemotherapy extravasation (vesicant), the catheter should remain in place initially to attempt aspiration of residual vesicant and to administer the antidote.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Chemotherapy is a vesicant; this is an extravasation emergency. Stop infusion, attempt to aspirate any residual vesicant through the catheter, and prepare to administer the antidote. The catheter stays in place until the antidote has been given.

C. Cold or warm compresses depend on the specific vesicant — not the first action. Stop the infusion and aspirate first.

D. This is a tissue-threatening emergency. Documentation occurs after intervention.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q5

A nurse is preparing to administer IV fluids to a client. Which of the following are appropriate uses for lactated Ringer's (LR)? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Surgical fluid replacement
  2. B. Trauma resuscitation
  3. C. Treating hyperkalemia
  4. D. A client with severe liver failure
  5. E. Co-infusing with blood products
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — LR is commonly used for surgical and post-operative fluid replacement because of its balanced electrolyte composition.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — LR is preferred for trauma resuscitation because it more closely matches body fluids than NS and reduces risk of hyperchloremic acidosis.

C. INCORRECT — LR contains potassium (4 mEq/L); avoid in clients with hyperkalemia.

D. INCORRECT — LR contains lactate, which is converted to bicarbonate by the liver. In severe liver failure, lactate accumulates and worsens acidosis.

E. INCORRECT — LR contains calcium, which can cause clotting when co-infused with citrated blood products. Use 0.9% NaCl with blood transfusion.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Parenteral/Intravenous Therapies
Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 5

Adverse Effects, Interactions, and Contraindications

Adverse drug reactions range from common side effects to life-threatening events. Recognizing toxicity, allergic responses, anaphylaxis, and drug-drug or drug-food interactions is a core nursing skill.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Adverse effects range from minor (nausea) to severe (anaphylaxis, organ toxicity). Allergic reaction = immune-mediated; side effect = predictable, dose-related. Anaphylaxis: epinephrine first, then antihistamine + steroid. Drug interactions: check before adding any new med. Grapefruit + many CYP450 substrates = danger.

Types of adverse reactions

  • Side effects: predictable, dose-related (nausea, drowsiness)
  • Adverse effects: harmful, unintended responses
  • Toxic effects: from accumulation, overdose, or low-TI drug
  • Idiosyncratic: unexpected (genetic factor)
  • Allergic: immune-mediated, can escalate to anaphylaxis
  • Carcinogenic / teratogenic: long-term harm

Anaphylaxis management

  • Epinephrine IM first (lateral thigh)
  • Call for help, position supine, elevate legs
  • Oxygen, IV access, fluids
  • Diphenhydramine, methylprednisolone
  • Monitor for biphasic reaction (4–24 hr after)

Adverse effects — additional concepts

  • Black Box Warning: FDA strongest warning — review before administration; common examples: NSAIDs (CV), antipsychotics (death in dementia), SSRIs (suicide < 25 yo), LABA monotherapy in asthma
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / TEN: Life-threatening skin reaction — fever, blisters, mucosal involvement; STOP drug immediately; common culprits: sulfa drugs, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin), allopurinol
  • Naranjo scale: Tool to determine probability that an adverse drug reaction is actually caused by the suspected drug
  • Pregnancy categories (older system, being phased out): A (safe), B (probably safe), C (caution — animal harm or unknown), D (evidence of human harm but benefits may outweigh), X (contraindicated)
  • 2015 FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule: Replaced letter categories with narrative summaries for pregnancy, lactation, and reproductive potential
  • Drug-drug interaction mechanisms: Pharmacokinetic (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and pharmacodynamic (additive/synergistic/antagonistic effects)
  • CYP450 inducers (↓ levels of substrates): Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John's wort, smoking
  • CYP450 inhibitors (↑ levels of substrates): Erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, fluconazole, grapefruit juice, cimetidine
In anaphylaxis, what is the FIRST drug, route, and site — and why this first?
Epinephrine IM into the lateral thigh (vastus lateralis) — first, before anything else. Reverses bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and capillary leak via α₁ and β agonism. IM thigh gives faster, more reliable absorption than SC or deltoid. THEN: oxygen, IV fluids, antihistamine (diphenhydramine), steroid (methylprednisolone), and continue monitoring.
After successful epinephrine treatment for anaphylaxis, why must the client be monitored for hours afterward?
Biphasic reaction — a second wave of anaphylactic symptoms can occur 4–24 hours (sometimes up to 72 hr) after initial resolution, even without re-exposure to the trigger. Monitor in a clinical setting for at least 4–6 hr; longer if severe initial reaction. Teach client/family to seek care immediately if symptoms return.
Which medication classes are the classic culprits for Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / TEN — and what is the immediate action?
Classic culprits: sulfa drugs, anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin), allopurinol, NSAIDs. Presentation: fever + painful blistering rash + mucosal involvement (lips/eyes/genitals). STOP the offending drug immediately — this is the most important intervention. Then ICU/burn-unit-level supportive care. HLA-B*1502 screening recommended for carbamazepine in Asian descent.
Name five common CYP450 inducers and explain the clinical implication.
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John's wort, smoking (also phenobarbital, chronic alcohol). Inducers ↓ levels of CYP-metabolized drugs → loss of therapeutic effect. Clinical: warfarin INR drops; OCP fails; immunosuppressants underdosed; antiretrovirals fail. Often requires dose increase or alternative agent.
Name five common CYP450 inhibitors and explain why grapefruit juice is on the list.
Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole), grapefruit juice, cimetidine, ritonavir/protease inhibitors. Inhibitors ↑ levels of CYP substrates → toxicity.
