Grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 — even one glass can elevate levels of many statins, calcium channel blockers, immunosuppressants, and some benzodiazepines for up to 72 hours.

Types of Adverse Reactions — Overview

Not all adverse events are the same. Recognizing the type guides nursing response — some require dose adjustment, others require stopping the drug and never giving it again.

Side effect

Predictable

An expected, dose-related effect at therapeutic doses. Usually mild; often resolves with continued use or dose reduction.

Examples

  • Nausea with opioids
  • Drowsiness with antihistamines
  • Dry mouth with anticholinergics

Nursing actions

  • Educate client to expect
  • Offer comfort measures (mints, fluids, slow position changes)
  • Notify provider if intolerable

Adverse effect

Unintended, harmful

Noxious, unintended response at normal doses. More serious than side effects; may require dose adjustment or discontinuation.

Examples

  • Aplastic anemia with chloramphenicol
  • Pulmonary fibrosis with amiodarone
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome with sulfa drugs

Nursing actions

  • Monitor for early signs
  • Stop drug, notify provider
  • Document and report (MedWatch)

Toxic effect

Dose-related danger

Effect from accumulation, overdose, or low therapeutic index. Watch for in renal/hepatic impairment, drug interactions, and high-alert medications.

High-risk drugs

  • Digoxin (therapeutic 0.5–2.0 ng/mL)
  • Lithium (0.6–1.2 mEq/L)
  • Warfarin (INR 2–3)
  • Phenytoin (10–20 mcg/mL)
  • Aminoglycosides (peak/trough)
  • Theophylline (10–20 mcg/mL)

Nursing actions

  • Monitor serum drug levels
  • Renal/hepatic function tests
  • Recognize early toxicity signs specific to each drug
  • Know the antidote (Digibind, vitamin K, etc.)

Idiosyncratic effect

Unpredictable

Unusual, unexpected response that cannot be predicted by the drug's pharmacology. Often genetic basis (e.g., CYP450 polymorphism).

Examples

  • Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency with sulfa drugs, nitrofurantoin, primaquine
  • Paradoxical excitation in older adults with benzodiazepines
  • Carbamazepine hypersensitivity in HLA-B*1502 (Asian descent)

Allergic reaction

Immune-mediated

Hypersensitivity reaction from prior sensitization. Severity ranges from mild rash to fatal anaphylaxis.

Types

  • Type I (immediate): IgE-mediated — anaphylaxis, urticaria, bronchospasm (PCN, latex, contrast)
  • Type II: Cytotoxic — hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia (PCN, methyldopa)
  • Type III: Immune complex — serum sickness, glomerulonephritis
  • Type IV (delayed): Cell-mediated — contact dermatitis, drug rash (sulfa, anticonvulsants)

Nursing actions

  • Always ask about allergies and the SPECIFIC REACTION
  • Document; alert band
  • Severe reaction = stop drug, support airway/breathing/circulation
  • Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM first

Teratogenic, carcinogenic, mutagenic

Long-term harm

Effects on fetal development, cancer risk, or DNA. Most relevant for pregnancy planning and chronic therapy.

Known teratogens (avoid in pregnancy)

  • Warfarin (fetal bleeding, malformation)
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs (renal damage)
  • Isotretinoin (severe defects)
  • Methotrexate (abortifacient, malformation)
  • Valproate (neural tube defects)
  • Statins (Category X)
  • Tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (bone/teeth)
  • Lithium (Ebstein anomaly — 1st trimester)

Anaphylaxis — Recognition and Response

A severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that can occur within minutes to hours of drug exposure. Most commonly: penicillins, contrast media, NSAIDs, latex, neuromuscular blockers.

Recognition

Multi-system

Manifestations

  • Skin: Generalized urticaria, flushing, pruritus, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat)
  • Respiratory: Hoarseness, stridor, wheezing, dyspnea, throat tightness
  • Cardiovascular: Tachycardia, hypotension, shock, dysrhythmias
  • GI: Nausea, vomiting, cramping, diarrhea
  • Neuro: Anxiety, sense of impending doom, dizziness, loss of consciousness

Biphasic reaction

  • Can recur 4–24 hours after the initial reaction resolves
  • Even without re-exposure to the trigger
  • Observe for at least 4–6 hours post-event

Treatment sequence

Time-critical

Immediate actions

  • 1. Stop the offending drug immediately
  • 2. Epinephrine IM in the vastus lateralis (anterolateral thigh) — first-line, no contraindications in anaphylaxis
  • 3. Call for help / rapid response
  • 4. Position supine with legs elevated (or sitting if respiratory distress dominates)
  • 5. Oxygen, IV access, IV fluids (crystalloids)

Secondary medications

  • Diphenhydramine IV (H1 blocker)
  • Famotidine or ranitidine (H2 blocker)
  • Methylprednisolone or hydrocortisone IV
  • Albuterol nebulizer for bronchospasm
  • Repeat epinephrine every 5–15 min if no improvement
  • Glucagon if on beta blocker (epinephrine may be less effective)

Drug Interactions — Mechanisms

Two or more drugs taken together can produce effects that neither would produce alone. Categorized by mechanism (pharmacokinetic vs pharmacodynamic) and outcome (synergistic, antagonistic, novel).

Pharmacokinetic interactions

ADME-based

Absorption

  • Antacids ↓ absorption of fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines (separate by 2 hr)
  • Bile acid sequestrants bind many drugs — separate by 4 hr
  • Food affects absorption (levothyroxine, bisphosphonates need empty stomach)

Distribution

  • Protein-binding competition — sulfonamides displace warfarin → ↑ bleeding
  • Cleared when drugs are taken concurrently with similar high protein binding

Metabolism — CYP450 inducers (↓ drug levels)

  • Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital
  • Rifampin, rifabutin
  • St. John's wort
  • Smoking
  • Chronic alcohol use

Metabolism — CYP450 inhibitors (↑ drug levels)

  • Erythromycin, clarithromycin
  • Ketoconazole, fluconazole, itraconazole
  • Cimetidine
  • Grapefruit juice
  • Acute alcohol intake
  • Many antidepressants (fluoxetine, paroxetine)

Excretion

  • NSAIDs ↓ renal excretion of lithium → toxicity
  • Probenecid ↓ excretion of penicillins (intentional — prolongs effect)
  • Loop diuretics ↑ excretion of potassium → hypokalemia

Pharmacodynamic interactions

Effect-based

Additive / synergistic (effects ↑)

  • CNS depressants (alcohol + benzodiazepine + opioid) — respiratory depression
  • Multiple antihypertensives — hypotension
  • NSAID + warfarin — bleeding
  • SSRI + MAOI — serotonin syndrome

Antagonistic (effects ↓)

  • Beta blockers + beta agonists (oppose each other)
  • Vitamin K + warfarin
  • Naloxone + opioids (overdose reversal)
  • Flumazenil + benzodiazepines

Pregnancy and Lactation Considerations

All medications cross the placenta to some extent. Risk varies by trimester, dose, and individual drug. The 2015 FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule replaced the older A/B/C/D/X letter categories with narrative summaries — but the letters are still commonly used and tested.

Legacy FDA Pregnancy Categories

Still used clinically

Categories

  • A: Adequate studies show no risk (vitamins at RDA, levothyroxine)
  • B: Animal studies show no risk, but no adequate human studies (acetaminophen, amoxicillin, metformin, insulin)
  • C: Animal studies show adverse effect; risk cannot be ruled out (most drugs default here)
  • D: Evidence of human risk, but benefits may outweigh (lithium, phenytoin, valproate sometimes)
  • X: Contraindicated — risks outweigh benefits (isotretinoin, methotrexate, warfarin, statins, thalidomide, misoprostol)

Lactation

Most drugs cross to milk

Generally safe

  • Acetaminophen, ibuprofen (most NSAIDs)
  • Most antibiotics (avoid sulfonamides near birth — kernicterus)
  • Insulin, levothyroxine
  • Heparin, LMWH (don't cross to milk)
  • SSRIs (sertraline preferred)

Avoid in lactation

  • Lithium (high transfer)
  • Amiodarone (very long half-life)
  • Ergot alkaloids
  • Antineoplastics (chemotherapy)
  • Radioactive iodine
  • Chloramphenicol (gray baby syndrome)

Active Learning Scenario · Gentamicin + Naproxen

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is planning care for a client who is receiving gentamicin IV bolus twice daily. The client has a history of musculoskeletal pain and takes naproxen daily for relief. What information should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication to complete this item.

Show key

Therapeutic uses

  • Gentamicin is a narrow-spectrum aminoglycoside antibiotic prescribed to treat serious infections caused by aerobic bacilli.

Complications

  • Gentamicin can injure cells of the proximal renal tubules (nephrotoxicity).
  • Gentamicin is ototoxic — can cause permanent hearing loss and vestibular damage.
  • Naproxen and other NSAIDs can independently cause renal insufficiency.
  • The glomerular filtration rate of the kidneys decreases with advanced age, ↑ risk for nephrotoxicity.
  • Combining gentamicin with naproxen significantly increases the risk of acute kidney injury.

Nursing interventions — labs to monitor

  • BUN and serum creatinine (baseline and periodically)
  • Peak and trough gentamicin levels (peak 30 min after IV completion; trough just before next dose)
  • Specific gravity of urine; urinalysis for proteinuria, casts
  • Audiometry if long-term therapy (baseline + periodic)

Nursing interventions — actions

  • Monitor intake and output; report urine output < 30 mL/hr
  • Daily weights to track fluid status
  • Encourage adequate fluid intake (unless contraindicated)
  • Hold naproxen if possible during gentamicin therapy; collaborate with provider
  • Educate client to report hearing changes, tinnitus, dizziness, decreased urine output

Practice · Application Exercises (Set 1)

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 5 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse in a clinic is caring for a group of clients. The nurse should contact the provider about a potential contraindication to a medication for which of the following clients? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. A client at 8 weeks of gestation who asks for an influenza immunization
  2. B. A client who takes prednisone and has a possible fungal infection
  3. C. A client who has chronic liver disease and is taking hydrocodone/acetaminophen
  4. D. A client who has peptic ulcer disease, takes sucralfate, and has started taking OTC aluminum hydroxide
  5. E. A client who has a prosthetic heart valve, takes warfarin, and reports a suspected pregnancy
Show rationale ▾

A. The influenza vaccine is recommended for all clients > 6 months and is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy (the inactivated injection — only the live intranasal is contraindicated).

B. CORRECT. Glucocorticoids (prednisone) are immunosuppressive and should not be given to a client with a possible systemic fungal infection — they can worsen the infection. Notify the provider.

C. CORRECT. Acetaminophen is hepatotoxic and contraindicated in chronic liver disease. Notify the provider to prescribe a non-acetaminophen analgesic.

D. No absolute contraindication exists here. Sucralfate and aluminum hydroxide should be taken 30 min apart for full effect, but both can be used. Verify the provider is aware.

E. CORRECT. Warfarin is Pregnancy Category X — it causes severe fetal defects (warfarin embryopathy). Notify the provider; the client will likely be switched to LMWH (heparin or enoxaparin), which does not cross the placenta.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q2

A nurse is preparing to administer an IM dose of penicillin to a client who has a new prescription. The client states when they took penicillin 3 years ago, they developed a rash. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?

  1. A. Administer the prescribed dose.
  2. B. Withhold the medication.
  3. C. Ask the provider to change the prescription to an oral form.
  4. D. Administer an oral antihistamine at the same time.
Show rationale ▾

A. Do not administer. A previous rash with penicillin indicates allergic sensitization. Future doses can produce more severe reactions (anaphylaxis).

B. CORRECT. Withhold the medication and notify the provider. The client has a documented allergic reaction to penicillin. The provider will likely prescribe an alternative antibiotic.

C. Changing the route does not address the allergy — the drug is the issue, not the route.

D. Pretreating with an antihistamine does not prevent anaphylaxis and is not standard practice. The drug must be avoided.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects
Q3

A nurse is providing discharge instructions for a client who has a new prescription for an antihypertensive medication. Which of the following statements should the nurse give?

  1. A. "Be sure to limit your potassium intake while taking the medication."
  2. B. "You should check your blood pressure every 8 hours while taking this medication."
  3. C. "Your medication dosage will be increased if you develop tachycardia."
  4. D. "Change positions slowly when you move from sitting to standing."
Show rationale ▾

A. Whether to limit potassium depends on the specific antihypertensive. Loop and thiazide diuretics ↓ K (eat more K-rich foods); K-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs ↑ K (limit K-rich foods).

B. Checking BP every 8 hours at home is excessive and not recommended.

C. Tachycardia is not the expected dose-adjustment trigger; reflex tachycardia from some antihypertensives may even suggest the dose is too high or that a beta blocker should be added.

D. CORRECT. Orthostatic hypotension is a common adverse effect of nearly all antihypertensive medications. Teaching slow position changes reduces the risk of falls and syncope.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects
Q4

A nurse is reviewing a client's health record and notes that the client experienced permanent extrapyramidal effects caused by a previous medication. The nurse should recognize that the medication affected which of the following systems in the client?

  1. A. Cardiovascular
  2. B. Immune
  3. C. Central nervous
  4. D. Gastrointestinal
Show rationale ▾

A. Extrapyramidal effects (EPS) are not cardiovascular in origin.

B. EPS are not immune-mediated.

C. CORRECT. Extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia) arise from dopamine blockade in the basal ganglia — part of the central nervous system. Common with first-generation antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) and metoclopramide.

D. EPS affect movement, not the GI tract.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects
Q5

A nurse is caring for a client who is taking oral oxycodone. The client is also taking ibuprofen in three recommended doses daily. The nurse should identify that an interaction between these two medications will cause which of the following findings?

  1. A. A decrease in blood levels of ibuprofen, possibly leading to a need for increased doses
  2. B. A decrease in blood levels of oxycodone, possibly leading to a need for increased doses
  3. C. An increase in the expected therapeutic effect of both medications
  4. D. An increase in expected adverse effects for both medications
Show rationale ▾

A. The combination does not decrease ibuprofen levels.

B. The combination does not decrease oxycodone levels.

C. CORRECT. This is a beneficial synergistic interaction. Opioids and NSAIDs work through different mechanisms (opioid receptor activation vs. COX inhibition), so combining them provides greater analgesia than either alone — and often allows lower doses of each, reducing adverse effects.

D. While both medications have adverse effects, this combination is generally used because the synergy allows for LOWER doses of each, often reducing adverse effects.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Pharmacological Pain Management

Adverse Reactions — Common Patterns

Adverse effects range from mild side effects to life-threatening reactions. Recognizing the pattern helps decide whether to continue, modify, or stop the medication.

Side effect

Expected, dose-related

An effect that is part of the medication's pharmacological action but is unwanted. Usually predictable, mild, and dose-related.

Examples

  • Drowsiness with antihistamines
  • Dry mouth with anticholinergics
  • GI upset with NSAIDs
  • Headache with nitrates

Management

  • Often tolerable — continue medication
  • Dose reduction may help
  • Time-related (often improves as body adjusts)
  • Teach client to expect and report severity

Allergic reaction (hypersensitivity)

Immune-mediated

An immunologic response to a medication. May be immediate (Type I, IgE-mediated, e.g., anaphylaxis) or delayed (Type IV, T-cell mediated, e.g., contact dermatitis).

Manifestations (mild → severe)

  • Itching, hives, rash
  • Wheezing, dyspnea, swelling of lips/tongue
  • Anaphylaxis: hypotension, laryngeal edema, bronchospasm, shock

Management

  • STOP medication immediately
  • Document allergy with reaction description
  • Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM (first), O2, IV fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids
  • Update allergy band/list
  • NEVER re-administer

Idiosyncratic reaction

Unpredictable

An unexpected reaction unique to the individual, often genetic. Cannot be predicted from the medication's known pharmacology.

Examples

  • Aplastic anemia with chloramphenicol
  • Malignant hyperthermia with halothane/succinylcholine
  • Hemolysis with sulfa in G6PD deficiency

Approach

  • Discontinue medication
  • Report to FDA MedWatch
  • Document for future avoidance

Toxic effect

Dose-related serious harm

Damage caused by excessive medication levels — either overdose or accumulation due to impaired metabolism/excretion.

Common examples

  • Acetaminophen → hepatotoxicity (antidote: acetylcysteine)
  • Aminoglycosides → nephro/ototoxicity
  • Digoxin → arrhythmias, visual changes
  • Vancomycin → red man syndrome, nephrotoxicity

Management

  • Hold further doses
  • Antidote if available
  • Supportive care; monitor levels

Serious & Special Reactions

Certain adverse effects are particularly severe, often requiring immediate intervention and permanent discontinuation.

Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / TEN

Dermatologic emergency

A severe mucocutaneous reaction characterized by fever, skin pain, then widespread blistering and sloughing. Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is the most severe form (> 30% body surface).

Common triggers

  • Sulfa drugs (TMP/SMX)
  • Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin)
  • Allopurinol
  • NSAIDs, penicillins, nevirapine

Management

  • STOP medication immediately
  • Transfer to burn unit (severe cases)
  • IV fluid replacement, electrolyte correction
  • Wound care
  • Genetic testing (HLA-B*1502 in Asian descent before carbamazepine)

Black Box Warning

FDA highest warning

The FDA's strongest warning, indicating a medication has serious or life-threatening risks. Required on the label and prescribing information.

Examples

  • SSRIs: Suicidal ideation in < 25 yo
  • NSAIDs: CV thrombotic events, GI bleeding
  • Antipsychotics: Increased mortality in elderly with dementia
  • LABA (e.g., salmeterol): Asthma death (monotherapy)
  • Fluoroquinolones: Tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy
  • Methotrexate: Severe toxicities; teratogenic

Nursing responsibility

  • Review black box warnings before administration
  • Teach client about specific risks
  • Monitor for early signs
  • Document risk-benefit discussion

Teratogenic effects

Pregnancy harm

Medications that can cause fetal malformations or developmental harm. The FDA replaced the A/B/C/D/X categories in 2015 with detailed narrative labeling (PLLR).

Known teratogens (avoid in pregnancy)

  • Warfarin — fetal warfarin syndrome
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs — fetal renal damage (esp. 2nd-3rd trimester)
  • Isotretinoin — severe craniofacial/cardiac defects
  • Methotrexate — abortifacient + teratogen
  • Statins — congenital anomalies
  • Tetracyclines — teeth/bone effects (also < 8 yo)
  • Lithium — Ebstein cardiac anomaly (1st trimester)
  • Valproate — neural tube defects
  • Thalidomide — limb defects (REMS program)

Nursing actions

  • Pregnancy test before initiating known teratogen
  • Contraception counseling for women of childbearing potential
  • Document pregnancy status
  • For high-risk drugs (isotretinoin), iPLEDGE program required

Drug Interactions — CYP450 and Foods

Medications can interact with other drugs, foods, and supplements. Interactions may be pharmacokinetic (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) or pharmacodynamic (additive, synergistic, antagonistic effects).

CYP450 enzyme interactions

Major mechanism

The cytochrome P450 enzyme system in the liver metabolizes most drugs. Inducers increase enzyme activity (→ less drug); inhibitors decrease activity (→ more drug).

CYP inducers (↓ substrate levels)

  • Anticonvulsants: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital
  • Rifampin
  • St. John's wort
  • Smoking (↑ theophylline metabolism)
  • Chronic alcohol use
  • Effect: ↓ levels of OCPs, warfarin, antiretrovirals, digoxin

CYP inhibitors (↑ substrate levels)

  • Macrolides: Erythromycin, clarithromycin (NOT azithromycin)
  • Azole antifungals: Ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole
  • Grapefruit juice (calcium channel blockers, statins)
  • Cimetidine
  • Protease inhibitors
  • Effect: ↑ levels of warfarin, statins, digoxin → toxicity

Food interactions

Foods can alter absorption, metabolism, and pharmacological effect of medications.

Common food-drug interactions

  • Warfarin + vitamin K foods (leafy greens) → ↓ INR; keep intake CONSISTENT
  • MAOI + tyramine foods (aged cheese, cured meats, wine) → hypertensive crisis
  • Tetracyclines/quinolones + dairy/calcium → ↓ absorption (separate by 2 hr)
  • Levothyroxine + food/calcium/iron → ↓ absorption (empty stomach AM, 1 hr before food)
  • Grapefruit juice + statins/CCBs/many others → ↑ levels (CYP3A4 inhibition)

Pharmacodynamic interactions

When drugs with similar or opposing effects are combined, effects may be additive, synergistic, or antagonistic.

Additive/synergistic (dangerous combinations)

  • CNS depressants: Opioids + benzodiazepines + alcohol → respiratory depression
  • Serotonergic agents: SSRI + MAOI/St. John's wort/triptan → serotonin syndrome
  • Anticoagulants: Warfarin + aspirin/NSAIDs/clopidogrel → bleeding
  • QT-prolonging drugs: Multiple combined → torsades de pointes

Antagonistic

  • Naloxone reverses opioids
  • Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines
  • Vitamin K reverses warfarin
  • Protamine reverses heparin
  • Therapeutic in overdose; problematic if drugs given together accidentally

Active Learning Scenario · Warfarin + St. John's Wort

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who is taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation. The client reports taking St. John's wort for mild depression. What action should the nurse take? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication to complete this item.

Show key

Interaction Identification

  • St. John's wort is a CYP450 inducer (CYP3A4 and others)
  • It will ↓ warfarin levels → ↓ anticoagulation effect → ↑ risk of thrombosis/stroke
  • St. John's wort also interacts with: OCPs, antiretrovirals, digoxin, antidepressants (serotonin syndrome)

Nursing Actions

  • Notify the provider of the supplement use
  • Educate client to discontinue St. John's wort or monitor INR closely
  • Document the interaction
  • Recheck INR within 1 week of stopping the supplement (may need warfarin dose adjustment)

Client Education

  • Always inform providers about ALL supplements, including "natural" and herbal products
  • "Natural" does NOT mean "safe" — supplements have real drug interactions
  • Read labels; bring all supplements to medication reconciliation visits

Practice · Application Exercises (Set 2)

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 5 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is reviewing the medication list of a client and notes they are prescribed warfarin and have just been started on TMP/SMX (Bactrim). Which of the following should the nurse anticipate?

  1. A. No interaction is expected
  2. B. Increased INR and bleeding risk requiring close monitoring
  3. C. Decreased warfarin effectiveness
  4. D. No change to monitoring needed
Show rationale ▾

A. A significant interaction exists: TMP/SMX inhibits warfarin metabolism and displaces it from protein binding, increasing INR and bleeding risk.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Sulfamethoxazole inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9) AND displaces warfarin from albumin → ↑ free warfarin → ↑ INR. Close monitoring with possible warfarin dose reduction is needed.

C. The interaction increases warfarin effect, not decreases it.

D. Closer INR monitoring is essential when starting this combination.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q2

A nurse is caring for a client who develops fever, painful red rash, and oral mucosa blistering 1 week after starting a sulfa antibiotic. Which of the following is the priority action?

  1. A. Apply topical hydrocortisone to the rash
  2. B. Stop the antibiotic and notify the provider immediately
  3. C. Continue the antibiotic and treat the rash with antihistamines
  4. D. Decrease the antibiotic dose to reduce the rash
Show rationale ▾

A. Topical steroids do not address the systemic emergency. The medication must be stopped.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — These signs indicate Stevens-Johnson Syndrome — a life-threatening reaction. Immediately stop the offending drug and notify the provider. SJS may progress to TEN with high mortality.

C. Continuing the offending medication can be fatal in SJS/TEN.

D. Dose reduction does not stop the immunologic reaction. The drug must be discontinued.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q3

A nurse is reviewing medications with a client who is pregnant. Which of the following medications should the nurse instruct the client to avoid? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Acetaminophen
  2. B. Warfarin
  3. C. Isotretinoin
  4. D. Insulin
  5. E. Lisinopril
Show rationale ▾

A. Acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic in pregnancy (Category B).

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Warfarin is teratogenic (Category X) — causes fetal warfarin syndrome.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial and cardiac defects. Requires the iPLEDGE program.

D. Insulin is Category B and is the preferred treatment for diabetes in pregnancy.

E. CORRECT. CORRECT — ACE inhibitors cause fetal renal damage in 2nd/3rd trimester. Class effect.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q4

A client receiving IV penicillin develops sudden onset wheezing, swelling of the lips, and hypotension. Which of the following is the priority intervention?

  1. A. Administer epinephrine IM
  2. B. Administer diphenhydramine IV
  3. C. Administer methylprednisolone IV
  4. D. Slow the rate of penicillin infusion
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — This is anaphylaxis. Epinephrine IM is the first-line treatment. Standard adult dose is 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL concentration) in the anterolateral thigh.

B. Diphenhydramine is given AFTER epinephrine. It is an adjunct, not first-line.

C. Corticosteroids prevent biphasic anaphylaxis but are not first-line and have slower onset than epinephrine.

D. STOP the penicillin entirely — do not slow it. This is a life-threatening allergic reaction.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q5

A nurse is teaching a client about food-drug interactions. Which of the following statements by the client indicates understanding? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. "I should keep my intake of leafy green vegetables consistent while taking warfarin."
  2. B. "I should avoid grapefruit juice while taking my statin."
  3. C. "I can take my levothyroxine with breakfast for better absorption."
  4. D. "I should avoid aged cheese and cured meats while taking my MAOI."
  5. E. "I should take my doxycycline with a glass of milk."
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Vitamin K (in leafy greens) antagonizes warfarin. Consistent intake — not avoidance — is key so dose can be adjusted appropriately.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4, leading to ↑ statin levels and risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis.

C. Levothyroxine should be taken on an EMPTY stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast. Food (especially calcium, iron, fiber) decreases absorption.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, wine, beer) can cause hypertensive crisis when combined with MAOIs.

E. Dairy (calcium) decreases doxycycline absorption. Take with water; separate from dairy by 2 hours.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Unit 1 · Pharmacological Principles · Chapter 6

Individual Considerations of Medication Administration

Medication response varies across the lifespan and across populations. Pediatric, older adult, pregnant, and breastfeeding clients require careful dose adjustment and increased monitoring.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Pediatrics: organ immaturity affects every phase of ADME. Always weight-based (mg/kg). Older adults: ↓ renal/hepatic function = ↑ drug levels; polypharmacy is a hazard. Pregnancy: avoid teratogens (warfarin, ACE inhibitors, statins, retinoids); use FDA pregnancy risk categories. Lactation: most drugs cross into milk but at low levels.

Pediatric considerations

  • Doses always per kg of body weight
  • Immature hepatic enzymes — slower metabolism
  • Higher % body water — affects distribution
  • Watch for paradoxical reactions (some get excited from sedatives)

Older adult considerations

  • Start low, go slow
  • Watch for polypharmacy and interactions
  • Beers Criteria flags potentially inappropriate medications
  • ↓ glomerular filtration = renal clearance reduction
  • ↓ albumin = more free (active) drug

Pregnancy & lactation

  • Teratogens to AVOID: warfarin, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins, isotretinoin, valproic acid, lithium (most)
  • Safer alternatives exist for nearly every category
  • Lactation: check LactMed before any new med

Lifespan-specific cautions

  • Pediatric weight-based dosing is universal — always mg/kg
  • Children's drug response differs: Slower hepatic metabolism (especially neonates), ↑ % body water, immature blood-brain barrier (more CNS effects)
  • NEVER: Aspirin in children with viral illness (Reye); tetracyclines < 8 yo (teeth); fluoroquinolones < 18 yo (cartilage); codeine < 12 yo (variable metabolism, deaths)
  • Older adult considerations: ↓ GFR (renal-cleared drugs accumulate), ↓ hepatic metabolism, ↓ serum albumin (more free drug), ↑ body fat (lipid-soluble drugs persist), polypharmacy
  • Beers Criteria: List of potentially inappropriate medications for adults > 65 yo — examples: long-acting benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, NSAIDs (long-term), 1st-gen antihistamines
  • STOPP/START criteria: Tool to identify potentially inappropriate prescribing in elderly
  • Pregnancy: Avoid teratogens — warfarin, ACE/ARB, statins, isotretinoin, methotrexate, valproate, lithium (mostly), tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones
  • Breastfeeding: Most drugs cross to milk in small amounts; check LactMed; some absolutely contraindicated (chemotherapy, lithium, ergotamine, amiodarone)
  • Genetics/pharmacogenomics: CYP2D6 variability affects codeine, tamoxifen, antidepressants; HLA-B*5701 → abacavir reaction; HLA-B*1502 → carbamazepine SJS
Name four medications that should NEVER be used in specific pediatric populations and the reason for each.
(1) Aspirin in viral illness → Reye syndrome (encephalopathy + liver failure). (2) Tetracyclines < 8 yo → permanent tooth discoloration + enamel hypoplasia. (3) Fluoroquinolones < 18 yo → cartilage/tendon damage. (4) Codeine < 12 yo → variable CYP2D6 metabolism causes unpredictable opioid effect; deaths reported.
List the classic teratogenic medications to AVOID in pregnancy.
Warfarin (use heparin/LMWH instead — they don't cross placenta). ACE inhibitors and ARBs (renal/skull defects). Statins (fetal development). Isotretinoin (severe malformations — iPLEDGE program). Valproic acid (neural tube defects). Lithium (Ebstein cardiac anomaly). Methotrexate. Tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones.
What five physiologic changes in older adults affect drug response — and what is the practical implication for dosing?
(1) ↓ GFR → renal-cleared drugs accumulate (digoxin, gentamicin). (2) ↓ hepatic metabolism → CYP-metabolized drugs persist. (3) ↓ serum albumin → ↑ free (active) drug fraction. (4) ↑ body fat → lipid-soluble drugs (benzos) accumulate, prolonged effect. (5) Polypharmacy → interaction risk. Practical rule: "Start low, go slow"; Beers Criteria flags inappropriate meds.

Pediatric Considerations

Children are not small adults. Pharmacokinetics differs by age, organ maturity, body composition, and metabolism. Dosing is universally weight-based (mg/kg).

Pharmacokinetic differences

Age-related

Infants and young children have unique absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion patterns.

Key differences

  • Absorption: Gastric pH higher in neonates; oral absorption variable
  • Distribution: Higher % body water; lower body fat; immature blood-brain barrier (more CNS effects)
  • Metabolism: Immature hepatic enzymes — slower metabolism in neonates and young infants
  • Excretion: Renal function reaches adult levels by ~1 year

Implications

  • Higher mg/kg doses needed for some drugs (children metabolize faster than adults after infancy)
  • Lower mg/kg for neonates due to immature systems
  • Use specific pediatric dose references — never extrapolate from adult doses

Drugs to AVOID in children

High-risk medications

Several medications have specific age cutoffs based on safety concerns.

Absolute avoidance

  • Aspirin in viral illness: Reye syndrome (fatal hepatic encephalopathy)
  • Tetracyclines < 8 yo: Tooth discoloration, bone growth inhibition
  • Fluoroquinolones < 18 yo: Cartilage damage in animals; tendon issues
  • Codeine < 12 yo: Variable metabolism, deaths reported
  • Benzyl alcohol (preservative): Gasping syndrome in neonates

Caution

  • Promethazine < 2 yo (respiratory depression)
  • Cold/cough preparations < 6 yo
  • Pseudoephedrine: variable response in young children

Administration considerations

Technique varies with age and developmental stage.

Pediatric administration tips

  • Liquid oral medications: use oral syringe (not household teaspoon)
  • Tablets: consider crushability or use liquid form when available
  • IM injections: vastus lateralis preferred < 1 year
  • IV: rates calculated by weight and concentration
  • Involve caregivers; explain in age-appropriate terms
  • Praise cooperation; avoid threats or comparisons to other children

Older Adult Considerations

Aging changes affect every phase of pharmacokinetics. Combined with polypharmacy and chronic disease, older adults are at significantly higher risk for adverse drug events.

Pharmacokinetic changes

Aging effects

Multiple physiologic changes alter how medications behave in older adults.

Changes & implications

  • ↓ Renal function (GFR): Accumulation of renally-cleared drugs (digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, vancomycin)
  • ↓ Hepatic metabolism: Some drugs accumulate
  • ↓ Serum albumin: More free drug; ↑ effect of highly protein-bound drugs (warfarin, phenytoin)
  • ↑ Body fat / ↓ Body water: Lipid-soluble drugs persist longer (benzodiazepines), water-soluble drugs have higher initial concentrations
  • ↓ Cardiac output: Slower distribution

General principle

  • "Start low, go slow"
  • Use the lowest effective dose
  • Titrate slowly to therapeutic effect
  • Monitor for accumulation and toxicity

Beers Criteria

Avoid in elderly

A list of potentially inappropriate medications for adults > 65 years, maintained by the American Geriatrics Society.

Examples of medications to avoid

  • Benzodiazepines (especially long-acting): falls, sedation, cognitive impairment
  • 1st-generation antihistamines (diphenhydramine): anticholinergic effects, confusion
  • Tricyclic antidepressants: anticholinergic, orthostatic hypotension
  • NSAIDs (chronic use): GI bleed, renal impairment, HF
  • Antipsychotics in dementia: increased mortality (BBW)
  • Muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine, carisoprodol): sedation, falls
  • Sliding-scale insulin alone: risk of hypoglycemia

Application

  • Use only when no safer alternative exists
  • Document risk-benefit decision
  • Monitor closely if used

Polypharmacy

Multiple medications

Older adults often take many medications, increasing risk of interactions, errors, and non-adherence.

Strategies

  • Medication review at every visit
  • Deprescribing: Stop medications that are no longer needed
  • Simplify dosing schedules (once daily preferred)
  • Use pill organizers and reminder systems
  • Involve caregivers in administration when needed
  • STOPP/START criteria: Tool to identify inappropriate prescriptions and missing beneficial ones

Pregnancy & Lactation

Most medications cross the placenta and many enter breast milk. Decisions require weighing maternal benefit against fetal/infant risk.

Pregnancy

The FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR, 2015) replaced the A/B/C/D/X categories with narrative labeling, though letter categories still appear on many references.

Generally safe in pregnancy

  • Acetaminophen (preferred analgesic/antipyretic)
  • Insulin (preferred for diabetes)
  • Levothyroxine
  • Penicillins, cephalosporins (most)
  • Heparin/LMWH (does not cross placenta — preferred over warfarin)
  • Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine (hypertension in pregnancy)

Avoid in pregnancy

  • NSAIDs (esp. 3rd trimester — premature ductus closure)
  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs (renal damage)
  • Warfarin (teratogen)
  • Tetracyclines (teeth)
  • Sulfa drugs (late pregnancy — kernicterus)
  • Lithium (1st trimester cardiac defects)
  • Isotretinoin, methotrexate, statins, valproate (teratogens)

Lactation

Most drugs transfer to breast milk in small amounts. Always check LactMed database before prescribing.

Considerations

  • Check LactMed (NIH database) for specific drugs
  • Time doses to minimize infant exposure (right after feeding)
  • Monitor infant for adverse effects
  • Most antibiotics, acetaminophen, NSAIDs (occasional use) compatible

Avoid during breastfeeding

  • Chemotherapy
  • Lithium
  • Ergotamine, methotrexate
  • Amiodarone
  • Iodine 131 (radioactive)
  • Recreational drugs

Pharmacogenomics

Genetic variation affects how individuals metabolize medications and respond to them. Some medications now require genetic testing before use.

Clinical examples

Several drugs have well-established genetic considerations.

Genetic testing recommendations

  • Abacavir + HLA-B*5701: Test before use; presence → severe hypersensitivity
  • Carbamazepine + HLA-B*1502: Test in Asian descent (Stevens-Johnson risk)
  • Clopidogrel + CYP2C19: Poor metabolizers have reduced antiplatelet effect
  • Warfarin + CYP2C9/VKORC1: Genotype-guided dosing reduces bleeding
  • Codeine + CYP2D6: Ultra-rapid metabolizers → toxic morphine levels; poor metabolizers → no analgesic effect
  • Thiopurines + TPMT: TPMT deficiency → bone marrow suppression

Application

  • Order testing before initiation when indicated
  • Adjust dose based on metabolizer status
  • Document for future reference

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for an 82-year-old client who has multiple chronic conditions and takes 9 different medications daily. The client has fallen twice in the past month and reports feeling dizzy when standing. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder to analyze concerns.

Show key

Risk Factors Identified

  • Polypharmacy (≥ 5 medications) — known fall risk factor
  • Age > 65 — multiple physiologic changes affecting drug response
  • Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension (dizziness on standing)
  • Two recent falls — significantly elevated future fall risk

Common Medication Classes Contributing to Falls

  • Antihypertensives (especially alpha-blockers, ACE inhibitors)
  • Diuretics (volume depletion)
  • Benzodiazepines and sleep aids (Beers Criteria — avoid)
  • Opioids
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (Beers Criteria — avoid)
  • Antihistamines (1st-generation — Beers Criteria)
  • Antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics

Nursing Actions

  • Conduct a comprehensive medication review with the provider
  • Identify potentially inappropriate medications (Beers Criteria)
  • Suggest deprescribing where appropriate
  • Check orthostatic vital signs
  • Implement fall precautions
  • Educate client and family about fall prevention
  • Consider PT consult for gait/balance

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 6 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is administering medications to a 75-year-old client. Which of the following changes in pharmacokinetics should the nurse consider in older adults?

  1. A. Increased renal excretion of medications
  2. B. Decreased metabolism of medications
  3. C. Increased serum albumin levels
  4. D. Decreased body fat
Show rationale ▾

A. Renal function DECREASES with age, slowing excretion and increasing accumulation.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Hepatic metabolism decreases with age, and renal excretion decreases. Both lead to medication accumulation and require dose adjustments.

C. Serum albumin decreases with age and chronic illness, increasing free drug (and effect) for highly protein-bound medications.

D. Body fat actually INCREASES with age, prolonging the effect of lipid-soluble drugs (e.g., benzodiazepines).

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Pharmacological Pain Management
Q2

A nurse is reviewing the medications of an 80-year-old client. Which of the following medications should the nurse identify as inappropriate per the Beers Criteria? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Diphenhydramine for sleep
  2. B. Acetaminophen for mild pain
  3. C. Long-term diazepam for anxiety
  4. D. Amitriptyline for neuropathy
  5. E. Levothyroxine for hypothyroidism
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — 1st-generation antihistamines have strong anticholinergic effects causing confusion, sedation, and increased fall risk.

B. Acetaminophen is appropriate and is the preferred first-line analgesic in older adults.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Long-acting benzodiazepines cause sedation, cognitive impairment, and falls. Avoid in older adults.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — TCAs have strong anticholinergic effects and orthostatic hypotension. Use SNRIs (duloxetine) or gabapentin instead.

E. Levothyroxine is appropriate; older adults may need lower starting doses but the medication itself is not contraindicated.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q3

A pregnant client at 30 weeks gestation reports a headache. Which of the following medications is most appropriate for the nurse to recommend?

  1. A. Ibuprofen 400 mg
  2. B. Acetaminophen 500 mg
  3. C. Aspirin 325 mg
  4. D. Naproxen 220 mg
Show rationale ▾

A. NSAIDs are contraindicated in the 3rd trimester — they can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Acetaminophen (Category B) is the preferred analgesic/antipyretic throughout pregnancy when used at recommended doses.

C. Aspirin is generally avoided in pregnancy (especially 3rd trimester) due to bleeding risk and possible ductal closure.

D. Like ibuprofen, naproxen is an NSAID and is contraindicated in the 3rd trimester.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Pharmacological Pain Management
Q4

A nurse is preparing to administer codeine to a 6-year-old. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

  1. A. Administer the codeine as prescribed
  2. B. Question the order with the provider
  3. C. Give half the prescribed dose
  4. D. Document the medication was given
Show rationale ▾

A. Codeine is contraindicated in children < 12 years due to variable metabolism (CYP2D6) and reports of fatal respiratory depression in ultra-rapid metabolizers.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Codeine carries a black box warning against use in children < 12 years. The nurse should question the order and suggest a safer alternative.

C. Reducing the dose does not address the fundamental safety issue of unpredictable metabolism in children.

D. This would be unsafe practice. Question the order before administration.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q5

A provider is considering prescribing carbamazepine to a client of Asian descent for trigeminal neuralgia. Which of the following actions is most appropriate before initiating therapy?

  1. A. Obtain genetic testing for HLA-B*1502
  2. B. Obtain a complete blood count
  3. C. Order a chest X-ray
  4. D. Administer test dose and monitor for 24 hours
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — HLA-B*1502 allele (more common in Asian descent) is strongly associated with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/TEN with carbamazepine. Testing is recommended before initiation in this population.

B. A CBC may be appropriate as part of overall workup, but the specific concern for this population and medication is the HLA-B*1502 test.

C. A chest X-ray is not specific to carbamazepine initiation.

D. A test dose does not detect the genetic predisposition. The reaction can take days to weeks to manifest.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Expected Actions/Outcomes
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 7

Anxiety and Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders

Anxiety disorders include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, OCD, social anxiety, and PTSD. Pharmacological management uses benzodiazepines (short-term), buspirone, SSRIs, SNRIs, and adjuncts like beta blockers and hydroxyzine.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam, diazepam) — fast relief, short-term only due to dependence. Buspirone — non-sedating, takes weeks to work, no dependence. SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline) — first-line for chronic anxiety. Avoid alcohol with any anxiolytic. Flumazenil reverses benzo overdose.

Benzodiazepines (Alprazolam — prototype)

  • Action: Enhance GABA inhibition in CNS — rapid anxiolysis
  • Uses: GAD, panic disorder, PTSD, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, pre-procedure sedation
  • Adverse: CNS depression, anterograde amnesia, paradoxical excitation (older adults), tolerance/dependence
  • Overdose: Reverse with flumazenil IV
  • Avoid: Alcohol, opioids, other CNS depressants (additive respiratory depression)

Atypical anxiolytics & antidepressants

  • Buspirone: No sedation, no dependence — but takes 3–6 weeks to work
  • SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline, escitalopram): First-line for chronic anxiety — slow onset (4 weeks)
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine): Used for GAD
  • Beta blockers (propranolol): For performance anxiety (somatic symptoms only)
  • Hydroxyzine: PRN; antihistamine with anxiolytic effect

Anxiety — additional therapy details

  • SSRI dosing for anxiety: Often starts lower than depression dosing then titrated up; full effect 4–6 weeks
  • Serotonin syndrome: Mental status changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus); occurs with serotonergic drug combinations
  • Hydroxyzine (Vistaril, Atarax): H1 antihistamine; rapid relief of anxiety; less sedating than diphenhydramine; useful in pregnancy
  • Beta blockers (propranolol): Block somatic symptoms (palpitations, tremor) of performance anxiety; ineffective for cognitive symptoms
  • Alpha-blockers (prazosin): PTSD-related nightmares
  • Pregabalin, gabapentin: Anxiolytic effects; off-label for GAD
  • Withdrawal from benzodiazepines: Can be life-threatening — seizures, agitation, autonomic instability; NEVER abruptly discontinue chronic benzo use — taper slowly over weeks
A client with chronic alprazolam use presents with respiratory depression and CNS depression after intentional overdose. What is the antidote — and what is the catch?
Flumazenil IV — competitively antagonizes benzodiazepine binding at GABA-A. Catch: in clients with chronic benzo use, flumazenil can precipitate withdrawal seizures. Also short half-life (~1 hr) — patient may re-sedate. Used cautiously, often only in pure benzo overdose without chronic use; primary management is supportive (airway, ventilation).
Compare buspirone to benzodiazepines for anxiety: onset, sedation, dependence.
Buspirone: non-sedating, no dependence, no withdrawal — but takes 3–6 weeks for full effect, useless for acute panic. Mechanism: 5-HT1A partial agonist. Benzodiazepines: rapid relief (minutes-hours), but sedating, dependence-forming, and combine dangerously with other CNS depressants. Use buspirone for chronic anxiety in clients at risk for dependence.
Why must chronic benzodiazepine use never be stopped abruptly?
Abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures, severe agitation, autonomic instability, and rebound anxiety — potentially life-threatening, similar to alcohol withdrawal. Always taper slowly over weeks to months, often by 10–25% every 2 weeks. Substituting with a longer-acting benzo (diazepam) before taper can ease the process.

Benzodiazepines

GABA receptor enhancers — provide rapid anxiolysis but carry risks of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal. Used short-term (2–4 weeks) for acute anxiety, panic, alcohol withdrawal, seizures, and pre-procedure sedation.

Prototype: Alprazolam (Xanax)

Schedule IV

Short-acting benzodiazepine. Other examples: lorazepam (Ativan), diazepam (Valium), midazolam (Versed), chlordiazepoxide (Librium), clonazepam (Klonopin), oxazepam, temazepam, triazolam.

Mechanism & uses

  • Enhances GABA inhibition in CNS → rapid anxiolysis, sedation, anticonvulsant, muscle relaxant
  • Uses: GAD, panic disorder, PTSD adjunct, alcohol withdrawal (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam), seizures (lorazepam, diazepam — status epilepticus), pre-procedure sedation, muscle spasm (diazepam)

Adverse effects

  • CNS depression (sedation, dizziness, confusion)
  • Anterograde amnesia
  • Paradoxical excitation (especially elderly)
  • Tolerance and physical dependence with chronic use
  • Respiratory depression (especially with other CNS depressants)
  • Withdrawal can be life-threatening (seizures, autonomic instability)

Nursing actions

  • Antidote: Flumazenil IV for overdose; reverses sedation, may precipitate seizures in chronic users
  • AVOID with alcohol, opioids, other CNS depressants
  • Never abruptly discontinue chronic use — taper over weeks
  • Beers Criteria: Avoid in older adults (falls, cognitive impairment)
  • Educate: short-term use only, do not drive until effect known

Buspirone

Anxiolytic with no sedation, no dependence, no withdrawal — but slow onset (3–6 weeks). Useful for chronic generalized anxiety in clients who cannot tolerate or use benzodiazepines.

Buspirone (BuSpar)

Atypical anxiolytic

5-HT1A partial agonist. Not a CNS depressant. Does not cause sedation or impair cognition. No abuse potential (not scheduled).

Uses

  • Generalized anxiety disorder
  • Adjunctive treatment of depression
  • Useful in clients with substance use history (no abuse potential)

Adverse effects

  • Dizziness, headache, nausea, restlessness
  • Generally well-tolerated

Nursing actions

  • Takes 3–6 weeks for full effect — not for acute anxiety relief
  • AVOID with MAOIs (hypertensive crisis)
  • AVOID grapefruit juice (↑ levels)
  • AVOID alcohol
  • Educate client about delayed onset; do not stop because they don't feel it immediately

Antidepressants for Anxiety

SSRIs and SNRIs are first-line for chronic anxiety disorders. They take 4–6 weeks for full effect but have lower abuse potential and longer-term safety than benzodiazepines.

SSRIs

First-line for chronic anxiety

Examples: paroxetine (Paxil) — prototype for anxiety, sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro), fluoxetine (Prozac), citalopram, fluvoxamine.

Uses

  • Generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety
  • Also approved for depression

Adverse effects

  • Initial: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), headache, jitteriness — often improves in 2 weeks
  • Sexual dysfunction (often persistent)
  • Weight gain
  • Insomnia or sedation (depends on agent)
  • SIADH/hyponatremia (especially older adults)
  • Bleeding risk (↑ with NSAIDs)
  • Serotonin syndrome — autonomic instability, mental status changes, neuromuscular hyperactivity
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Withdrawal syndrome with abrupt discontinuation (paroxetine especially)

Nursing actions

  • 4–6 weeks to full effect — must continue even if not feeling immediate benefit
  • Lower starting dose for anxiety than for depression; titrate up
  • BLACK BOX: Suicidal ideation in < 25 yo — monitor closely first 2–3 months
  • Taper slowly to discontinue (especially paroxetine)
  • Avoid combining with MAOIs (washout 2 weeks); other serotonergic drugs
  • Pregnancy: paroxetine = Cat D (cardiac defects); sertraline often preferred

SNRIs

Also first-line

Examples: venlafaxine (Effexor) — prototype, duloxetine (Cymbalta), desvenlafaxine.

Uses & Effects

  • GAD, panic, social anxiety, depression
  • Similar AE profile to SSRIs PLUS: hypertension (especially venlafaxine), tachycardia
  • Duloxetine: also for diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia

Cautions

  • Monitor BP
  • Withdrawal more severe than SSRIs
  • Hepatotoxicity (duloxetine — avoid in liver disease)

TCAs (older alternative)

Examples: amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine (most effective for OCD).

AE & Cautions

  • Anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision)
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Sedation, weight gain
  • Cardiotoxic in overdose — wide QRS, arrhythmias; narrow therapeutic index
  • Beers Criteria: Avoid in older adults
  • Lower doses for anxiety/pain than depression

Adjunct Medications

Used for specific symptoms or anxiety subtypes when first-line agents are insufficient or contraindicated.

Beta blockers

Performance anxiety

Propranolol — blocks somatic (physical) symptoms of anxiety.

Uses

  • Performance anxiety, social anxiety (acute, situational use)
  • Essential tremor
  • Migraine prophylaxis

Notes

  • Blocks palpitations, tremor, sweating, blushing
  • Does NOT address cognitive symptoms (worry, fear)
  • Take 30 min before anxiety-provoking event
  • AVOID in asthma (bronchospasm); use cautiously in diabetes (masks hypoglycemia)

Hydroxyzine

PRN anxiety

H1 antihistamine with anxiolytic effect — useful for occasional anxiety without dependence.

Properties

  • Sedating but no abuse potential
  • Useful in pregnancy
  • PRN dosing (not scheduled)
  • AE: drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness
  • Less sedating than diphenhydramine

Alpha-blockers

PTSD nightmares

Prazosin — for PTSD-related nightmares.

Notes

  • Bedtime dosing; titrate to effect
  • AE: orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, headache
  • Significant nightmare reduction in many PTSD clients

Gabapentin, pregabalin

Off-label

Anticonvulsants with some anxiolytic effect.

Notes

  • Off-label for GAD; useful adjuncts
  • Pregabalin is Schedule V
  • Sedation, dizziness, weight gain

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has been prescribed paroxetine for generalized anxiety disorder. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication to develop the teaching plan.

Show key

Indications & Expected Pharmacological Action

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
  • Increases serotonin availability in the synaptic cleft
  • Used for: generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety, PTSD, OCD, depression

Adverse Effects to Monitor

  • Initial: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), headache, insomnia — usually improves in 2 weeks
  • Sexual dysfunction (often persistent — sometimes leads to discontinuation)
  • SIADH/hyponatremia (especially older adults)
  • Increased bleeding risk (especially with NSAIDs)
  • Serotonin syndrome (mental status, autonomic, neuromuscular)
  • BLACK BOX: Suicidal ideation in < 25 yo — monitor closely first 2–3 months

Client Education

  • Takes 4–6 weeks for full effect — must continue even if not feeling immediate benefit
  • Take at the same time daily
  • Do NOT abruptly discontinue — paroxetine has worst withdrawal of SSRIs (flu-like, dizziness, irritability); taper over weeks
  • AVOID alcohol, MAOIs, St. John's wort, triptans (serotonin syndrome)
  • Report: worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, unusual bleeding, signs of serotonin syndrome
  • Sexual side effects: discuss with provider — may switch agent
  • Avoid in pregnancy (Category D — cardiac defects); use sertraline if needed

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 7 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed buspirone for generalized anxiety disorder. Which of the following statements by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

  1. A. "I can take this medication as needed when I feel anxious."
  2. B. "I should expect this medication to take several weeks to work."
  3. C. "I can drink alcohol while taking this medication."
  4. D. "I might become physically dependent on this medication."
Show rationale ▾

A. Buspirone is NOT a PRN medication. It must be taken regularly and takes weeks to reach therapeutic effect.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Buspirone has a slow onset of 3–6 weeks. Clients must continue taking it daily even if they do not feel an immediate effect.

C. Alcohol should be avoided with buspirone (CNS depressant interaction).

D. Buspirone does NOT cause dependence — this is one of its advantages over benzodiazepines.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q2

A nurse is caring for a client who has taken an overdose of lorazepam. Which of the following medications should the nurse anticipate administering?

  1. A. Naloxone
  2. B. Flumazenil
  3. C. Acetylcysteine
  4. D. Protamine sulfate
Show rationale ▾

A. Naloxone reverses opioid overdose, not benzodiazepine overdose.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Flumazenil is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose. It is a competitive GABA receptor antagonist. CAUTION: it may precipitate seizures in chronic benzo users.

C. Acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose.

D. Protamine reverses heparin, not benzodiazepines.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q3

A client taking paroxetine for 6 months reports they wish to stop the medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate response from the nurse?

  1. A. "You can stop the medication today since you no longer need it."
  2. B. "You should taper the medication gradually with provider supervision."
  3. C. "You can stop the medication but continue taking it on alternate days."
  4. D. "There is no need to taper an SSRI."
Show rationale ▾

A. Abrupt discontinuation causes withdrawal symptoms (flu-like, dizziness, irritability), especially with paroxetine.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Paroxetine has the worst withdrawal syndrome of SSRIs and must be tapered gradually over weeks under provider supervision.

C. Alternate-day dosing is not an appropriate way to discontinue. Taper according to a structured plan.

D. SSRIs require tapering — paroxetine especially.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q4

A nurse is monitoring a client who is taking multiple serotonergic medications. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as signs of serotonin syndrome? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Confusion and agitation
  2. B. Hyperreflexia and clonus
  3. C. Bradycardia and hypotension
  4. D. Fever and diaphoresis
  5. E. Pupillary constriction
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Mental status changes are part of the serotonin syndrome triad.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor, rigidity) is a hallmark.

C. Serotonin syndrome typically causes TACHYcardia and HYPERtension (autonomic instability).

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Autonomic instability includes hyperthermia and diaphoresis.

E. Pupils typically DILATE (mydriasis) in serotonin syndrome, not constrict.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q5

A nurse is preparing to administer alprazolam to a client with anxiety. Which of the following findings would be a reason to hold the medication?

  1. A. Respiratory rate of 10/min
  2. B. Heart rate of 88/min
  3. C. Blood pressure of 130/85 mmHg
  4. D. Temperature of 98.6°F (37°C)
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Benzodiazepines cause respiratory depression. With an RR of 10/min, hold the medication and notify the provider.

B. A normal heart rate is not a contraindication.

C. A normal-borderline BP is not a contraindication.

D. A normal temperature is not a contraindication.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 8

Depressive Disorders

Depressive disorders are treated primarily with SSRIs, SNRIs, atypical antidepressants (bupropion, mirtazapine), tricyclics (TCAs), and MAOIs. All carry a black box warning for suicidal ideation in clients under 25, and most require 4–8 weeks to reach full effect.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

SSRIs (fluoxetine — prototype) = first-line, fewer side effects. Black box warning: suicidal ideation in clients < 25 yo. 4–8 weeks for full effect. Serotonin syndrome if combined with MAOIs, triptans, or St. John's wort. MAOIs require strict tyramine-free diet — risk of hypertensive crisis.

SSRIs & SNRIs

  • SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram): First-line for depression
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine): Also treat neuropathic pain
  • Common AE: Sexual dysfunction, GI upset, insomnia, weight changes
  • Serotonin syndrome: Confusion, agitation, hyperthermia, tremor, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis
  • Discontinuation syndrome: Taper slowly; flu-like symptoms if stopped abruptly

Atypicals, TCAs, MAOIs

  • Bupropion: No sexual side effects; also for smoking cessation; lowers seizure threshold
  • Mirtazapine: Sedating, appetite increase — give at bedtime
  • TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine): Anticholinergic effects, cardiotoxic in overdose
  • MAOIs (phenelzine): Avoid tyramine foods (aged cheese, wine, cured meats) — risk of hypertensive crisis
  • MAOI washout: 2 weeks before/after switching to/from SSRIs

Black box & safety

  • Suicidal ideation in clients < 25 yo — monitor closely first 4–8 weeks
  • Pregnancy: Paroxetine = Category D (cardiac defects); others Category C
  • Onset = 1–3 weeks; full therapeutic effect = 4–8 weeks

Depression — additional details

  • St. John's wort interactions: CYP3A4 inducer — ↓ OCP, warfarin, digoxin, antiretrovirals; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/MAOIs
  • SSRIs in older adults: First-line for depression; ↓ falls vs. TCAs; SIADH/hyponatremia risk
  • Pregnancy: Untreated depression has its own risks; sertraline often preferred SSRI in pregnancy/lactation; paroxetine = Category D (cardiac defects)
  • ECT (electroconvulsive therapy): Used for severe/resistant depression, suicidal ideation, severe psychotic depression; safe in pregnancy
  • Esketamine (Spravato) intranasal: Treatment-resistant depression; REMS program (monitored use due to abuse/dissociation)
  • Tricyclic overdose triad: Anticholinergic, cardiac (wide QRS), CNS (seizures, coma) — life-threatening; treat with sodium bicarbonate IV
A 19-year-old begins fluoxetine for major depression. What is the time frame for therapeutic effect — and what is the black-box warning to discuss?
Therapeutic effect: 1–3 weeks for initial improvement, 4–8 weeks for full effect. Black box warning: increased suicidal ideation in clients < 25 yo during initial weeks of therapy. Teach client/family to watch for worsening mood, new agitation, suicidal thoughts — and to contact provider immediately. Schedule weekly follow-up for first month.
A client taking phenelzine asks what foods to avoid. Which foods and what is the consequence?
AVOID tyramine-rich foods: aged cheeses, cured/smoked meats, fermented soy (soy sauce, miso), red wine, beer (especially tap), aged or pickled foods, overripe bananas, fava beans. MAOIs prevent tyramine breakdown → massive norepinephrine release → hypertensive crisis (severe headache, neck stiffness, palpitations, possible intracranial hemorrhage). Also requires 2-week washout when switching to/from SSRIs.
A client overdoses on amitriptyline. What is the classic triad of presenting findings, and what is the antidote for cardiac toxicity?
Classic TCA-overdose triad: (1) Anticholinergic toxicity (dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, hyperthermia), (2) Cardiac toxicity — widened QRS on ECG, hypotension, arrhythmias, (3) CNS toxicity (seizures, coma). Treatment for cardiotoxicity: IV sodium bicarbonate (alkalinizes serum → reverses QRS widening). Plus supportive care.

SSRIs — First-Line Antidepressants

Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors are the first-line treatment for depression. They have a more favorable side effect profile than TCAs and MAOIs but share serotonin syndrome and withdrawal concerns.

SSRIs

Most commonly prescribed antidepressants

Prototype: Fluoxetine (Prozac). Other examples: sertraline (Zoloft), paroxetine (Paxil), citalopram (Celexa), escitalopram (Lexapro), fluvoxamine, vilazodone.

Uses

  • Major depressive disorder
  • Anxiety disorders (GAD, panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety)
  • Premenstrual dysphoric disorder
  • Bulimia (fluoxetine FDA-approved)

Adverse effects

  • Initial: GI upset, headache, jitteriness — usually improves in 2 weeks
  • Sexual dysfunction (often persistent — significant quality-of-life issue)
  • Weight gain (less than TCAs, but possible)
  • Insomnia or sedation (depends on agent — fluoxetine activating; paroxetine sedating)
  • Hyponatremia/SIADH (especially older adults — monitor sodium)
  • Bleeding risk (↑ with NSAIDs, anticoagulants)
  • Serotonin syndrome
  • Discontinuation syndrome (paroxetine worst)

Nursing actions

  • 4–6 weeks for full effect — continue even without immediate benefit
  • BLACK BOX: Suicidal ideation in < 25 yo — monitor closely first 2–3 months
  • Taper to discontinue
  • AVOID MAOIs (washout 2 weeks; 5 weeks after fluoxetine due to long half-life)
  • AVOID St. John's wort, triptans, tramadol (serotonin syndrome)
  • Pregnancy: paroxetine Cat D; sertraline often preferred
  • Lactation: most pass into milk in small amounts; sertraline preferred

SNRIs

Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors block reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine. Effective for depression, anxiety, and pain syndromes.

SNRIs

Dual action

Examples: venlafaxine (Effexor) — prototype, duloxetine (Cymbalta), desvenlafaxine (Pristiq), levomilnacipran.

Uses

  • Major depressive disorder, GAD, panic, social anxiety, PTSD
  • Duloxetine: diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain

Adverse effects

  • Similar to SSRIs PLUS:
  • Hypertension (especially venlafaxine — dose-dependent; monitor BP)
  • Tachycardia
  • Insomnia, sweating
  • Hepatotoxicity (duloxetine — avoid in active liver disease)
  • More severe withdrawal than SSRIs
  • Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic agents

Nursing actions

  • Monitor BP regularly — especially venlafaxine
  • Lower starting doses; titrate carefully
  • Taper slowly to discontinue
  • AVOID with MAOIs

Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs)

Older antidepressants with more side effects than SSRIs/SNRIs but useful for specific indications. Effective but cardiotoxic in overdose with a narrow therapeutic index.

TCAs

Second-line — high toxicity in overdose

Prototype: Amitriptyline. Other examples: imipramine, nortriptyline, doxepin, desipramine, clomipramine.

Uses

  • Depression (resistant or specific symptom patterns)
  • Neuropathic pain (amitriptyline, nortriptyline — lower doses than depression)
  • Migraine prevention
  • Insomnia (amitriptyline, doxepin)
  • OCD (clomipramine especially effective)
  • Enuresis in children (imipramine)

Adverse effects

  • Anticholinergic effects: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion (especially elderly)
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Sedation, weight gain
  • Cardiotoxicity: QRS widening, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death; narrow TI
  • Lethal in overdose — small amounts can be fatal

Nursing actions

  • Avoid in older adults (Beers Criteria — anticholinergic effects, falls)
  • Baseline ECG before initiation
  • Monitor for suicidal ideation — limit dispensed quantity if suicide risk
  • AVOID with MAOIs
  • Slow taper to discontinue
  • Treat overdose with sodium bicarbonate IV (cardiac toxicity)

MAOIs and Atypical Antidepressants

MAOIs are reserved for treatment-resistant depression because of food and drug interactions. Atypical antidepressants offer alternatives with unique mechanisms.

MAOIs

Last-line — many restrictions

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors — phenelzine (Nardil), tranylcypromine (Parnate), isocarboxazid, selegiline (transdermal patch).

Uses

  • Treatment-resistant depression
  • Atypical depression
  • Selegiline transdermal (Emsam) — Parkinson disease (low dose), depression

Critical warnings

  • Hypertensive crisis with tyramine foods: Aged cheese, cured/smoked meats, red wine, beer, soy sauce, sauerkraut, fermented foods
  • Hypertensive crisis with sympathomimetics: Decongestants (pseudoephedrine), amphetamines, cocaine
  • Serotonin syndrome: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, meperidine, tramadol, St. John's wort

Nursing actions

  • Extensive client education about food and drug restrictions
  • Washout periods: 2 weeks between MAOI and other antidepressants; 5 weeks after fluoxetine
  • Medical alert bracelet recommended
  • Treat hypertensive crisis: short-acting antihypertensive (phentolamine, nitroprusside)

Atypical antidepressants

Diverse mechanisms outside SSRI/SNRI/TCA classes.

Bupropion (Wellbutrin)

  • Norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake inhibitor
  • Uses: Depression, smoking cessation (as Zyban), seasonal affective disorder
  • AE: Seizure risk (avoid in seizure history, eating disorders, alcohol withdrawal)
  • NO sexual dysfunction (advantage)
  • NO weight gain (advantage)
  • Activating — good for fatigue, low energy

Mirtazapine (Remeron)

  • Alpha-2 antagonist; affects serotonin and norepinephrine
  • Uses: Depression — especially with insomnia, weight loss
  • AE: Significant sedation (give at bedtime); weight gain; agranulocytosis (rare)
  • Few sexual side effects

Trazodone

  • Serotonin modulator
  • Primarily used for INSOMNIA at low doses (not as primary antidepressant)
  • AE: Sedation, orthostatic hypotension, priapism (urologic emergency — male clients)

Esketamine (Spravato)

  • NMDA antagonist intranasal spray
  • Treatment-resistant depression
  • REMS program (sedation, dissociation — administered in office under monitoring)

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who has been prescribed phenelzine (an MAOI) for treatment-resistant depression. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication to develop the teaching plan.

Show key

Foods to AVOID (tyramine-containing) — Risk of Hypertensive Crisis

  • Aged cheeses (cheddar, blue, Swiss, Parmesan, Brie)
  • Cured and smoked meats (salami, pepperoni, prosciutto, hot dogs)
  • Smoked or pickled fish
  • Soy sauce, miso, fermented soybean products
  • Aged or fermented foods (sauerkraut, kimchi)
  • Red wine, sherry, vermouth, draft beer
  • Overripe fruits, fava beans
  • Yeast extracts (Marmite)

Medications to AVOID

  • OTC decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine)
  • Stimulants and amphetamines
  • Other antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs) — serotonin syndrome
  • Triptans (migraine medications)
  • Meperidine, tramadol
  • St. John's wort

Signs of Hypertensive Crisis (Report Immediately)

  • Severe occipital (back of head) headache
  • Stiff neck
  • Sweating, palpitations
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Photophobia
  • Markedly elevated blood pressure

Other Education

  • Effect takes 2–4 weeks to develop
  • Carry a medical alert card or wear medical alert jewelry
  • Inform all providers (dentist, surgeons) of MAOI use
  • Do NOT discontinue suddenly
  • Washout: 2 weeks before starting another antidepressant; 5 weeks if previous medication was fluoxetine

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 8 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed fluoxetine for depression. Which of the following statements by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

  1. A. "I should expect to feel better within a few weeks."
  2. B. "I will take this medication on an empty stomach in the morning."
  3. C. "I can take St. John's wort as a natural booster."
  4. D. "I will not stop the medication without talking to the provider."
Show rationale ▾

A. This is accurate — SSRIs typically take 2–4 weeks to begin showing effect and 4–6 weeks for full effect.

B. Fluoxetine is activating and best taken in the morning. Empty stomach is acceptable.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT (indicates need for further teaching) — St. John's wort + SSRI can cause serotonin syndrome. Do not combine.

D. This is accurate — SSRIs require tapering to prevent withdrawal syndrome.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q2

A nurse is caring for a client who has been taking amitriptyline for chronic neuropathic pain. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as adverse effects of TCAs? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Dry mouth and constipation
  2. B. Orthostatic hypotension
  3. C. Sexual dysfunction
  4. D. Diarrhea
  5. E. Cardiac arrhythmias
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Anticholinergic effects are very common with TCAs.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — TCAs commonly cause orthostatic hypotension, increasing fall risk.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Common with TCAs as with most antidepressants.

D. TCAs cause CONSTIPATION, not diarrhea (anticholinergic).

E. CORRECT. CORRECT — TCAs cause QRS widening and arrhythmias; cardiotoxic in overdose.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q3

A client receiving phenelzine reports a sudden severe headache, palpitations, and neck stiffness after eating dinner at a restaurant. The nurse should identify these findings as a sign of which of the following?

  1. A. Serotonin syndrome
  2. B. Hypertensive crisis from tyramine ingestion
  3. C. Anaphylaxis
  4. D. Migraine headache
Show rationale ▾

A. Serotonin syndrome typically presents with mental status changes, neuromuscular signs (clonus, hyperreflexia), and autonomic instability — different pattern.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — These are classic signs of MAOI-induced hypertensive crisis. The client likely ate tyramine-containing food (aged cheese, cured meat, fermented foods). Treat with phentolamine or nitroprusside.

C. Anaphylaxis presents with hypotension, wheezing, and urticaria — different pattern.

D. These features (sudden onset, neck stiffness, hypertension) are not typical of migraine.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q4

A nurse is preparing to administer bupropion to a client. Which of the following findings would be a contraindication?

  1. A. History of hypertension
  2. B. History of seizure disorder
  3. C. History of insomnia
  4. D. History of obesity
Show rationale ▾

A. Hypertension is not a specific contraindication to bupropion.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in clients with seizure disorders, eating disorders (bulimia, anorexia), or those undergoing alcohol withdrawal.

C. While bupropion can be activating, insomnia is not an absolute contraindication.

D. Bupropion is actually less likely to cause weight gain than other antidepressants.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Contraindications/Precautions
Q5

A nurse is monitoring a client who is starting an SSRI for depression. The client is 22 years old. Which of the following should be the priority assessment?

  1. A. Sexual function changes
  2. B. Suicidal ideation
  3. C. Weight changes
  4. D. Sleep quality
Show rationale ▾

A. Sexual dysfunction is a concern but not a priority over suicide assessment.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — All antidepressants have a BLACK BOX warning for increased suicidal ideation in clients < 25 years, especially during the first 2–3 months of treatment. This is the priority assessment.

C. Weight changes should be monitored but are not priority over suicide risk.

D. Sleep is important but not priority over suicide risk assessment.
