Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 9

Bipolar Disorders

Bipolar disorder is managed with mood stabilizers — lithium remains the prototype, alongside anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) and atypical antipsychotics. Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window (0.6–1.2 mEq/L) requiring strict monitoring.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Lithium = prototype mood stabilizer. Therapeutic range: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (acute: up to 1.5). Toxicity > 1.5 → GI distress, tremor, confusion, ataxia, seizures. Maintain sodium and fluid intake (low sodium = lithium retention = toxicity). Anticonvulsants (valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) also used as mood stabilizers.

Lithium

  • Therapeutic level: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L (maintenance); up to 1.5 acute
  • Toxicity: Mild >1.5 (GI, tremor, polyuria); Moderate 2.0–2.5 (confusion, coarse tremor, ataxia); Severe >2.5 (seizures, coma, death)
  • Common AE: Polyuria, polydipsia, tremor, weight gain, hypothyroidism
  • Interactions: NSAIDs ↑ lithium levels; thiazide diuretics ↑ levels; ACE inhibitors ↑ levels
  • Critical teaching: Maintain steady fluid intake (2–3 L/day); steady sodium intake (low Na = lithium retention); avoid NSAIDs
  • Monitoring: Levels every 1–3 days during initiation, then every 1–3 months; TSH; serum creatinine

Anticonvulsants as mood stabilizers

  • Valproic acid (Depakote): Hepatotoxic; teratogenic (neural tube defects); ↑ ammonia
  • Carbamazepine: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (especially HLA-B*1502); CBC monitoring (agranulocytosis)
  • Lamotrigine: Risk of life-threatening rash (Stevens-Johnson); titrate slowly
  • Topiramate: Cognitive slowing; kidney stones; weight loss

Other agents

  • Atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole) for acute mania
  • Antidepressants used cautiously — can trigger mania

Bipolar — additional

  • Lithium administration: Take with food (decreases GI distress); maintain 2–3 L fluid/day; consistent sodium intake; AVOID NSAIDs and dehydration
  • Lithium and pregnancy: Category D — risk of Ebstein cardiac anomaly in first trimester
  • Lithium pre-treatment workup: Baseline TSH, BUN/Cr, ECG (if > 40 yo or cardiac history), pregnancy test, CBC
  • Why anticonvulsants work as mood stabilizers: Stabilize neuronal membranes by modulating sodium channels and GABA
  • Lamotrigine specifics: Best for bipolar DEPRESSION (less so mania); very slow titration to reduce Stevens-Johnson risk
  • Atypical antipsychotics for bipolar: Olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, lurasidone — used for acute mania and maintenance
  • Treating bipolar depression: AVOID antidepressant monotherapy (can trigger mania) — use mood stabilizer + antidepressant or atypical antipsychotic
A client on lithium has a serum level of 1.8 mEq/L. Is this therapeutic, mild toxicity, or severe toxicity — and what action?
Mild-to-moderate toxicity (>1.5 mEq/L). Therapeutic: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L maintenance (up to 1.5 acute mania). Mild toxicity 1.5–2.0: GI distress, coarse tremor, polyuria, drowsiness. Moderate 2.0–2.5: confusion, ataxia, slurred speech. Severe >2.5: seizures, coma, death. Hold lithium, notify provider, check labs, ensure hydration. Severe → hemodialysis.
Why must a client on lithium maintain steady sodium intake and avoid dehydration?
Lithium and sodium compete for renal reabsorption. Low sodium (or dehydration) → kidney retains more lithium → lithium toxicity. High sodium intake → ↑ lithium excretion → loss of therapeutic effect. Teach client: maintain consistent dietary sodium and 2–3 L fluid/day; AVOID NSAIDs (↑ lithium levels) and thiazide diuretics; report excessive sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea immediately.
What baseline studies should be done before starting lithium?
(1) TSH (lithium causes hypothyroidism). (2) BUN/creatinine (renal function — lithium is renally cleared and can be nephrotoxic). (3) Pregnancy test (lithium category D — Ebstein cardiac anomaly first trimester). (4) CBC (baseline). (5) ECG if > 40 yo or cardiac history. Then trough lithium levels every 1–3 days during titration, every 1–3 months once stable.
Why is lamotrigine titrated slowly when used as a mood stabilizer?
To minimize the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN, which is life-threatening. Rapid titration is the major risk factor. Teach client to stop the medication immediately and seek care for any rash — especially with fever, blistering, or mucosal involvement. Lamotrigine is best for bipolar depression (less effective for mania).

Lithium

The gold standard mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder. Narrow therapeutic index requires careful monitoring, hydration, and consistent sodium intake.

Lithium carbonate (Lithobid, Eskalith)

Mood stabilizer prototype

Mechanism unclear; stabilizes neuronal membranes and alters intracellular signaling. Effective for both acute mania and maintenance.

Uses

  • Acute mania
  • Maintenance therapy for bipolar I and II
  • Prevention of recurrent mood episodes
  • Augmentation of antidepressants in depression

Therapeutic levels

  • Acute mania: 0.8–1.4 mEq/L
  • Maintenance: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L
  • Toxicity: > 1.5 mEq/L
  • Severe toxicity: > 2.0 mEq/L (medical emergency)

Side effects (therapeutic range)

  • GI upset (nausea, diarrhea — usually improves)
  • Fine hand tremor
  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Weight gain
  • Cognitive dulling

Toxicity signs

  • Early (1.5–2.0): N/V, diarrhea, coarse tremor, slurred speech, lethargy, confusion
  • Severe (> 2.0): Hyperreflexia, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse, death

Long-term concerns

  • Thyroid: Hypothyroidism (check TSH q6–12 months)
  • Renal: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD with long-term use (check BUN/Cr q6–12 months)
  • Cardiac: Conduction abnormalities (baseline ECG if > 40 yo)
  • Pregnancy: Category D — Ebstein cardiac anomaly in 1st trimester

Critical client teaching

  • Maintain consistent fluid intake (2–3 L/day) — dehydration → toxicity
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake — low sodium → ↑ lithium retention → toxicity
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors — ↑ lithium levels
  • Take with food (decreases GI upset)
  • Report: vomiting, diarrhea, fever — risk of dehydration → toxicity
  • Monitor for thyroid symptoms (cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue)

Lithium toxicity treatment

  • Mild toxicity: hold lithium, hydrate, monitor levels
  • Severe toxicity: hemodialysis (most effective treatment)

Anticonvulsant Mood Stabilizers

Several anticonvulsants are effective mood stabilizers. They work by stabilizing neuronal membranes through sodium channel modulation or GABA enhancement.

Valproic acid / divalproex (Depakote)

First-line for acute mania, especially with rapid cycling or mixed episodes.

Uses

  • Acute mania, mixed episodes, rapid cycling
  • Bipolar maintenance
  • Seizure disorders
  • Migraine prophylaxis

Adverse effects

  • Hepatotoxicity — baseline LFTs; monitor
  • Pancreatitis — severe abdominal pain, elevated amylase/lipase
  • Thrombocytopenia — check CBC
  • GI upset, sedation, weight gain
  • Hair loss
  • Teratogenicity: Category X — neural tube defects, severe — AVOID in pregnancy

Levels

  • Therapeutic: 50–125 mcg/mL
  • Toxic: > 175 mcg/mL

Lamotrigine (Lamictal)

Best for bipolar depression

More effective for bipolar depression than mania.

Uses

  • Bipolar I maintenance
  • Bipolar depression
  • Seizure disorders

Adverse effects

  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome — life-threatening rash; very slow titration required
  • Headache, dizziness, ataxia
  • Nausea

Nursing actions

  • Slow titration over 6+ weeks to reduce SJS risk
  • Hold and report ANY rash
  • ↓ dose with valproate (valproate ↑ lamotrigine levels)

Carbamazepine (Tegretol)

Used when other agents fail. Many drug interactions.

Uses

  • Bipolar disorder, mania
  • Seizure disorders
  • Trigeminal neuralgia

Adverse effects

  • Agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia — baseline CBC; monitor
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome — HLA-B*1502 testing in Asian descent before initiation
  • SIADH/hyponatremia
  • Sedation, ataxia

Interactions

  • Potent CYP450 inducer — ↓ OCPs (pregnancy risk), warfarin, many other drugs
  • Auto-induces own metabolism (levels may decrease over time)

Atypical Antipsychotics for Bipolar

Several atypical antipsychotics are FDA-approved for bipolar disorder — acute mania, depression, and maintenance.

Atypical antipsychotics

Multiple indications

Examples used in bipolar: olanzapine (Zyprexa), quetiapine (Seroquel), risperidone, aripiprazole (Abilify), ziprasidone, lurasidone (Latuda), cariprazine.

Uses in bipolar

  • Acute mania (most atypicals)
  • Acute bipolar depression (quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine, olanzapine + fluoxetine)
  • Maintenance therapy

Common adverse effects

  • Metabolic syndrome: Weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia (olanzapine and clozapine worst)
  • Sedation (quetiapine, olanzapine)
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • EPS — less than typical antipsychotics but possible (risperidone has more)
  • Tardive dyskinesia with long-term use
  • Increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis (BBW)

Nursing actions

  • Baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids — monitor regularly
  • AIMS exam for tardive dyskinesia
  • Educate about long-term metabolic risk
  • Quetiapine has dose-dependent effects (low dose for sleep/depression, higher for mania)

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client with bipolar I disorder who has been taking lithium for 6 months. The client reports the past 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea due to gastroenteritis. The client's current lithium level is 1.8 mEq/L. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Show key

Recognition of Toxicity

  • Lithium level of 1.8 mEq/L is in the toxic range (therapeutic: 0.6–1.2 maintenance, 0.8–1.4 acute mania)
  • Toxicity precipitated by dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea
  • Decreased fluid → ↑ lithium concentration → toxicity

Toxicity Manifestations to Assess

  • Coarse tremor, slurred speech
  • Confusion, lethargy, ataxia
  • Hyperreflexia, muscle twitching
  • Severe N/V, diarrhea (worsened by GI illness)
  • Severe (> 2.0): seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse

Nursing Actions

  • HOLD next lithium dose
  • Notify provider immediately
  • IV fluid replacement (NS) for hydration
  • Monitor lithium level every 6–12 hours
  • Severe toxicity (> 2.0): prepare for hemodialysis (most effective treatment)
  • Monitor vital signs, neurologic status, intake/output

Client Education for Preventing Recurrence

  • Maintain 2–3 L fluid intake daily
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake
  • When vomiting/diarrhea/fever/heavy sweating: hold lithium and notify provider
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors
  • Carry a medical alert
  • Schedule routine lithium levels and follow up

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 9 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is reviewing the medication record of a client taking lithium. Which of the following should the nurse identify as a concerning interaction?

  1. A. Acetaminophen 500 mg PRN for pain
  2. B. Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for arthritis
  3. C. Multivitamin once daily
  4. D. Loratadine 10 mg daily for allergies
Show rationale ▾

A. Acetaminophen is safe to use with lithium.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) decrease renal clearance of lithium, leading to elevated levels and toxicity. Avoid NSAIDs or use cautiously with monitoring.

C. A standard multivitamin is not contraindicated.

D. Loratadine is safe with lithium.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q2

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed lithium. Which of the following statements indicate understanding? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. "I will drink 2–3 liters of fluid each day."
  2. B. "I will take this medication with food."
  3. C. "I will use a low-sodium diet to prevent weight gain."
  4. D. "I will get my blood drawn periodically to check levels."
  5. E. "I will stop taking lithium if I feel better."
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Adequate hydration is essential to prevent lithium toxicity. Dehydration concentrates lithium and increases risk.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Taking lithium with food reduces GI upset.

C. INCORRECT — Sodium restriction increases lithium retention and toxicity risk. Maintain a CONSISTENT sodium intake.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and requires routine level monitoring (q3–6 months once stable; more often during titration).

E. INCORRECT — Discontinuing mood stabilizers without medical guidance increases relapse risk and worsens outcomes.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Medication Administration
Q3

A client taking valproic acid for bipolar disorder reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. Which of the following should the nurse suspect?

  1. A. Constipation
  2. B. Pancreatitis
  3. C. Hepatotoxicity
  4. D. Thrombocytopenia
Show rationale ▾

A. Constipation does not typically cause severe pain radiating to the back.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Valproate can cause acute pancreatitis, which presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. This is a serious adverse effect requiring immediate evaluation.

C. Hepatotoxicity typically presents with jaundice, fatigue, and elevated LFTs — not severe back pain.

D. Thrombocytopenia presents with easy bruising and bleeding, not abdominal pain.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q4

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed lamotrigine for bipolar maintenance. Which of the following teaching points is most important?

  1. A. "Take this medication on an empty stomach."
  2. B. "Report any rash to the provider immediately."
  3. C. "Lamotrigine will work within 24 hours."
  4. D. "You can discontinue this medication when you feel stable."
Show rationale ▾

A. Lamotrigine can be taken with or without food. This is not the priority teaching.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Lamotrigine can cause Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, a life-threatening rash. ANY rash warrants immediate evaluation. Slow titration (6+ weeks) is used to reduce this risk.

C. Mood stabilizers take weeks to reach therapeutic effect.

D. Mood stabilizers should be continued long-term to prevent relapse.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q5

A client taking carbamazepine for bipolar disorder reports a sore throat and fever. Which of the following should the nurse do first?

  1. A. Administer acetaminophen for the fever
  2. B. Obtain a CBC
  3. C. Increase fluid intake
  4. D. Continue the current dose and recheck in 1 week
Show rationale ▾

A. Symptomatic treatment is important but does not address the priority concern.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia. A sore throat and fever can be early signs of infection due to neutropenia. The priority is to check the CBC to assess for blood dyscrasias.

C. Hydration is supportive but not the priority assessment.

D. These symptoms require immediate evaluation, not delayed monitoring.

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 10

Psychotic Disorders

Psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, schizoaffective) are treated with first-generation (conventional) antipsychotics like haloperidol and second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics like risperidone, olanzapine, and clozapine. First-gen agents cause more EPS; second-gen cause more metabolic effects.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

1st-gen (conventional) antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) → high EPS risk. 2nd-gen (atypical) (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, clozapine) → metabolic syndrome risk. EPS: acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia. NMS (rare, fatal): fever + rigidity + autonomic instability → stop drug + dantrolene. Clozapine: agranulocytosis — weekly CBC.

First-generation (conventional)

  • Examples: Haloperidol (high-potency), chlorpromazine (low-potency), fluphenazine
  • Block dopamine D2: Treats positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions); minimal effect on negative symptoms
  • EPS effects: Acute dystonia (early), akathisia (early), parkinsonism (weeks), tardive dyskinesia (late, often irreversible)
  • EPS treatment: Anticholinergics (benztropine, diphenhydramine, trihexyphenidyl)
  • Other AE: Anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention), orthostatic hypotension, photosensitivity

Second-generation (atypical)

  • Examples: Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, clozapine
  • Treat positive AND negative symptoms; less EPS than 1st-gen
  • Metabolic syndrome: Weight gain, hyperglycemia (new-onset diabetes), dyslipidemia — monitor lipids, glucose, weight
  • Clozapine: Reserved for treatment-resistant; agranulocytosis (weekly CBC × 6 mo, then biweekly); myocarditis; lowers seizure threshold

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)

  • Triad: Hyperthermia + muscle rigidity + autonomic instability (BP/HR fluctuations)
  • Labs: ↑ CK (rhabdomyolysis), ↑ WBC, AKI
  • Treatment: STOP antipsychotic, cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene + bromocriptine
  • Mortality: 10–20% if untreated — true emergency
Place these extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) on a timeline after starting haloperidol: acute dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia.
Hours–days: acute dystonia (sustained muscle contractions, oculogyric crisis, torticollis) — treat with IM benztropine or diphenhydramine. Days–weeks: akathisia (motor restlessness, can't sit still) — propranolol/benzo. Weeks: parkinsonism (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia) — anticholinergics. Months–years: tardive dyskinesia (lip-smacking, choreoathetoid movements) — often irreversible; switch to atypical or use VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine).
A client on haloperidol presents with temperature 104°F, severe muscle rigidity, and fluctuating BP/HR. What is the diagnosis, and what are the first actions?
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS). Triad: hyperthermia + muscle rigidity + autonomic instability. Labs: ↑ CK (rhabdomyolysis), ↑ WBC, AKI. STOP the antipsychotic immediately. Treatment: cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene + bromocriptine. Mortality is 10–20% if untreated. Differentiate from serotonin syndrome (more clonus/hyperreflexia, less rigidity).
Why is clozapine reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and what is the monitoring schedule?
Clozapine causes agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia, life-threatening infection risk) and is therefore reserved for clients who have failed at least two other antipsychotics. Monitoring: CBC with ANC weekly × 6 months, then every 2 weeks × 6 months, then monthly. Other key risks: myocarditis, lowered seizure threshold, severe metabolic effects.
What metabolic monitoring is required for clients on atypical antipsychotics like olanzapine or risperidone?
Atypicals cause metabolic syndrome: weight gain, new-onset diabetes (hyperglycemia), dyslipidemia. Monitor at baseline and at intervals: weight + BMI (q3 mo first year), fasting glucose (3 mo, then annually), HbA1c, fasting lipid panel (3 mo, then annually), BP, waist circumference. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole and ziprasidone the lowest.

Typical (First-Generation) Antipsychotics

D2 dopamine receptor blockers — effective for positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) but with significant extrapyramidal side effects. Now largely replaced by atypicals for first-line use.

Typical antipsychotics

High EPS

Examples: haloperidol (Haldol) — high potency, chlorpromazine (Thorazine) — low potency, fluphenazine, perphenazine, thioridazine.

Uses

  • Acute psychosis, schizophrenia (positive symptoms)
  • Acute agitation (haloperidol IM)
  • Tourette syndrome
  • Severe nausea (some)

Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)

  • Acute dystonia (hours-days): Sudden severe muscle spasms, torticollis, oculogyric crisis — emergency; give IM benztropine or diphenhydramine
  • Akathisia (days): Inner restlessness, inability to sit still — beta blockers or benzodiazepines
  • Parkinsonism (weeks): Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked face — benztropine, trihexyphenidyl
  • Tardive dyskinesia (months-years): Involuntary movements of face, tongue, extremities — often irreversible; AIMS screening; discontinue offending med

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)

  • Life-threatening reaction
  • Symptoms: hyperthermia (> 103°F), severe muscle rigidity ("lead pipe"), altered mental status, autonomic instability (BP swings, tachycardia, diaphoresis)
  • Labs: ↑ CK, ↑ WBC
  • Treatment: DISCONTINUE antipsychotic immediately, cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene, bromocriptine

Other adverse effects

  • Anticholinergic (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention)
  • Sedation
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Photosensitivity
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia)
  • QT prolongation (especially thioridazine, haloperidol — torsades de pointes)

Nursing actions

  • Baseline AIMS exam; repeat every 3–6 months
  • Monitor for EPS at every encounter
  • Sun protection education
  • Increased mortality in elderly with dementia — BLACK BOX

Atypical (Second-Generation) Antipsychotics

D2 and 5HT2A blockers — first-line for psychotic disorders. Better tolerated than typicals (less EPS) but with significant metabolic side effects.

Atypical antipsychotics

First-line

Examples: olanzapine (Zyprexa), risperidone (Risperdal), quetiapine (Seroquel), aripiprazole (Abilify), ziprasidone (Geodon), paliperidone, lurasidone (Latuda), brexpiprazole, cariprazine.

Uses

  • Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder
  • Bipolar disorder (acute mania and maintenance)
  • Bipolar depression (quetiapine, lurasidone)
  • Major depression (adjunctive — aripiprazole, brexpiprazole)
  • Autism-associated irritability (risperidone, aripiprazole)

Metabolic syndrome

  • Significant weight gain (worst: olanzapine, clozapine)
  • Hyperglycemia/new-onset diabetes (BBW)
  • Dyslipidemia
  • Monitor baseline and ongoing: weight, BMI, waist, fasting glucose, lipids, BP

Other AE

  • Less EPS than typicals — but risperidone has highest EPS of atypicals
  • Tardive dyskinesia (less than typicals but still possible)
  • NMS (less common than typicals)
  • Orthostatic hypotension, sedation
  • Hyperprolactinemia (risperidone, paliperidone especially)
  • QT prolongation (ziprasidone — take with 500-calorie meal for absorption)

Nursing actions

  • Baseline metabolic screening; every 3 months × 1 year then yearly
  • Monitor for early signs of diabetes
  • Educate on diet, exercise
  • BLACK BOX: ↑ mortality in elderly with dementia

Clozapine (Clozaril)

Last-line — risks

Most effective antipsychotic — used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

Critical risks

  • Agranulocytosis — life-threatening; weekly CBC for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly; cannot dispense without ANC check (REMS program)
  • Myocarditis
  • Seizures (dose-dependent)
  • Hypersalivation
  • Severe weight gain, metabolic syndrome
  • Constipation (severe — bowel obstruction possible)

Use criteria

  • Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2+ other antipsychotics)
  • Suicide risk reduction in schizophrenia/schizoaffective

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client with schizophrenia who has been taking haloperidol for 2 weeks. The client now exhibits severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia (104°F), altered mental status, and diaphoresis. The blood pressure is fluctuating. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Show key

Recognition — Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

  • Tetrad: hyperthermia, severe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability
  • Life-threatening neurologic emergency
  • Most often within 2 weeks of starting a typical antipsychotic; can occur with atypicals and abrupt discontinuation of dopamine agonists
  • Mortality 10–20% if untreated

Differential — Distinguish from Serotonin Syndrome

  • NMS: "lead pipe" rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability
  • Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, neuromuscular hyperactivity, plus autonomic and mental status changes
  • Both: hyperthermia and altered mental status — clinical context matters

Immediate Nursing Actions

  • DISCONTINUE the antipsychotic immediately
  • Notify the provider STAT — transfer to ICU
  • Cooling measures (cool blankets, IV fluids, ice packs)
  • IV fluid resuscitation
  • Continuous monitoring of vital signs, cardiac rhythm, mental status
  • Anticipate: dantrolene (muscle relaxation), bromocriptine (dopamine agonist)
  • Monitor CK (rhabdomyolysis); BUN/Cr (renal function); electrolytes

Follow-up After Recovery

  • Switch to a different (preferably atypical) antipsychotic
  • Avoid the offending agent for life
  • Educate client and family about NMS warning signs

Practice · Application Exercises

5 NCLEX-style questions covering Ch 10 core content. Click each exercise to reveal rationales and NCLEX category.

Q1

A nurse is caring for a client receiving haloperidol who develops sudden severe neck spasm and tongue protrusion. The nurse should anticipate administering which of the following medications?

  1. A. Benztropine IM
  2. B. Haloperidol IM
  3. C. Lithium PO
  4. D. Naloxone IM
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — These are acute dystonic reactions, which respond to anticholinergic medications. IM benztropine (or diphenhydramine) is administered for rapid relief.

B. Haloperidol is the cause of the reaction. Giving more would worsen the symptoms.

C. Lithium is a mood stabilizer, not appropriate for acute dystonia.

D. Naloxone reverses opioids, not antipsychotic side effects.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q2

A nurse is caring for a client receiving clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Which of the following is the priority assessment?

  1. A. Daily weight
  2. B. Fasting glucose
  3. C. WBC and ANC
  4. D. Liver function tests
Show rationale ▾

A. Weight monitoring is important but not the priority for clozapine.

B. Glucose monitoring is important due to metabolic effects but not the priority.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Clozapine causes agranulocytosis (life-threatening). Weekly WBC/ANC for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly is required (REMS program). The medication cannot be dispensed without a current count.

D. LFTs are monitored but not the priority for clozapine.

NCLEX · Pharmacological & Parenteral Therapies · Adverse Effects/Contraindications
Q3

A nurse is monitoring a client on long-term antipsychotic therapy. Which of the following findings indicate tardive dyskinesia? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Lip smacking
  2. B. Tongue protrusion
  3. C. Choreoathetoid movements of the extremities
  4. D. Severe muscle rigidity and hyperthermia
  5. E. Acute torticollis
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Repetitive involuntary movements of the face, especially lip smacking and tongue protrusion, are hallmarks of TD.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — TD commonly involves the tongue and face.

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Slow, twisting movements of arms, fingers, and toes are part of TD.

D. These describe NMS, not TD. TD is a movement disorder without autonomic instability.

E. Acute torticollis is acute dystonia, not TD. TD develops over months/years.

Q4

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed risperidone. Which of the following statements indicates the need for further teaching?

  1. A. "I will have my weight and blood sugar monitored regularly."
  2. B. "I can stop taking this medication when I no longer hear voices."
  3. C. "I will avoid alcohol while taking this medication."
  4. D. "I will report any uncontrolled muscle movements."
Show rationale ▾

A. Correct understanding — atypicals require metabolic monitoring.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT (indicates further teaching needed) — Antipsychotics must be continued long-term to prevent relapse. Abrupt discontinuation often leads to symptom return.

C. Correct understanding — alcohol increases sedation and risk.

D. Correct understanding — risperidone has the highest EPS risk among atypicals.

Q5

A nurse is assessing a client newly prescribed an atypical antipsychotic. Which of the following baseline assessments are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

  1. A. Weight, BMI, waist circumference
  2. B. Fasting glucose
  3. C. Fasting lipid panel
  4. D. AIMS exam
  5. E. Pulmonary function tests
Show rationale ▾

A. CORRECT. CORRECT — Baseline anthropometrics are essential for monitoring metabolic side effects.

B. CORRECT. CORRECT — Baseline glucose is needed; atypicals can cause new-onset diabetes (BBW).

C. CORRECT. CORRECT — Dyslipidemia is a known effect of atypical antipsychotics.

D. CORRECT. CORRECT — Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale screens for tardive dyskinesia; reassess every 3–6 months.

E. Not routinely indicated for antipsychotic monitoring.

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 11

Medications for Children and Adolescents Who Have Mental Health Issues

Mental health medications in children and adolescents focus on ADHD (CNS stimulants like methylphenidate and amphetamines; non-stimulant atomoxetine), anxiety and depression (select SSRIs), and conduct/aggression. All psychotropics in pediatrics carry heightened black-box warnings.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

ADHD stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) — Schedule II, monitor weight/height/sleep, take in AM. Atomoxetine — non-stimulant alternative, no abuse potential. SSRIs in pediatrics: fluoxetine and escitalopram FDA-approved; black box for suicidal ideation. Atypicals for severe behavioral issues.

ADHD stimulants

  • Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta, Daytrana patch): Schedule II
  • Amphetamines (Adderall, Vyvanse, dextroamphetamine): Schedule II
  • AE: Appetite suppression (weight loss/growth delay), insomnia, tachycardia, hypertension, irritability
  • Teaching: Give in AM (avoid evening dose); take with food; monitor weight/height; "drug holidays" sometimes used
  • Contraindicated: Cardiac structural abnormalities; severe anxiety

Non-stimulants & antidepressants

  • Atomoxetine (Strattera): SNRI; non-controlled; 1–3 weeks for onset; black box for suicidal ideation
  • Clonidine, guanfacine: Alpha-2 agonists; help with ADHD + tics; sedating
  • SSRIs for pediatric depression/anxiety: Fluoxetine (8+ yo), escitalopram (12+ yo) — FDA approved
  • Black box warning: Heightened suicide risk in children — close monitoring required

Other pediatric psychotropics

  • Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) for autism-related irritability, Tourette
  • Lithium and anticonvulsants used cautiously
  • Always consider non-pharm interventions first (behavioral therapy)

Pediatric MH — additional

  • Desipramine, nortriptyline (TCAs): Sometimes used cautiously for ADHD or depression in adolescents; baseline ECG (cardiac monitoring); narrow TI in overdose
  • Lithium use in children: Approved > 7 yo for bipolar; close monitoring of levels
  • Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine): Prodrug — must be metabolized to be active; less abuse potential than other amphetamines
  • Strattera (atomoxetine): Non-stimulant; 1–3 weeks to onset; black box for suicidal ideation; hepatotoxicity risk
  • Guanfacine (Intuniv), clonidine (Kapvay): Alpha-2 agonists; help with ADHD impulsivity, sleep, Tourette's; sedating; rebound HTN if stopped
  • Eating disorders: Fluoxetine FDA-approved for bulimia; do not initiate antidepressants if active anorexia (risk of seizures with electrolyte imbalances)
A child started on methylphenidate (Concerta) for ADHD. What are the four key monitoring/teaching points?
(1) Give in the morning — late dosing causes insomnia. (2) Monitor weight and height — appetite suppression can cause growth delay; consider "drug holidays" on weekends/summers. (3) Monitor cardiac status (HR, BP) — contraindicated in structural heart abnormalities. (4) Schedule II controlled substance — written Rx, no refills, secure storage. Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) is a prodrug → less abuse potential than other amphetamines.
When would atomoxetine (Strattera) be chosen over a stimulant for ADHD — and what are its key downsides?
Chosen when: stimulants contraindicated (cardiac issues, severe anxiety), history of substance abuse, or tics/Tourette syndrome. Mechanism: SNRI; not a controlled substance. Downsides: takes 1–3 weeks for onset (vs. stimulants in 30 min), black box warning for suicidal ideation, and risk of hepatotoxicity (teach client to report jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain).
Which two SSRIs are FDA-approved for pediatric depression — and what is the critical safety counseling?
Fluoxetine (Prozac): approved age 8+. Escitalopram (Lexapro): approved age 12+. Black box warning: heightened risk of suicidal ideation in children/adolescents, especially in first 4 weeks. Counsel parents to watch for worsening mood, agitation, new suicidal thoughts. Schedule weekly follow-up initially. Therapy is most effective combined with psychotherapy.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse working in a pediatric mental health clinic is caring for a client who has a new prescription for risperidone for the treatment of conduct disorder. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify at least four adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Identify at least four nursing interventions to prevent or minimize the adverse effects of this medication.
Show key

Complications

  • New onset of diabetes mellitus or loss of glucose control in clients who have diabetes
  • Weight gain
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Anticholinergic effects (urinary hesitancy or retention, dry mouth)
  • Agitation
  • Dizziness
  • Sedation
  • Sleep disruption
  • Tremors
  • Agranulocytosis, neutropenia
  • Hyperprolactinemia

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain the client's fasting blood glucose prior to and periodically throughout treatment.
  • Instruct the client to report indications of diabetes mellitus including increased thirst, urination, and appetite.
  • Advise clients to follow a healthy, low-caloric diet.
  • Recommend regular exercise.
  • Monitor weight throughout treatment.
  • Monitor cholesterol and triglycerides, especially if weight gain is more than 30 lb.
  • Monitor blood pressure with first dose and instruct client to change positions slowly.
  • Encourage the client to sip fluids throughout the day.
  • Monitor and report manifestations of an infection (a sore throat).
  • Monitor and report gyneocomastia and amenorrhea.
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 12

Substance Use Disorders

Substance use disorders are treated with deterrents, replacement therapies, and withdrawal management. Alcohol: disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate. Opioids: methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone, naloxone (overdose reversal). Tobacco: nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Alcohol: Disulfiram (deterrent — avoid all alcohol/mouthwash), naltrexone, acamprosate. Opioids: Methadone (long-acting agonist replacement), buprenorphine (partial agonist), naltrexone (antagonist), naloxone (overdose reversal). Tobacco: Nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion. Acute withdrawal: benzos for alcohol; clonidine for opioids.

Alcohol use disorder

  • Disulfiram (Antabuse): Aversion therapy — inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase → severe reaction (flushing, vomiting, hypotension) if alcohol consumed
  • AVOID: All alcohol-containing products (cough syrup, mouthwash, vanilla extract, aftershave) for 2 weeks after stopping
  • Naltrexone: Opioid antagonist — reduces alcohol craving and pleasure response
  • Acamprosate: Reduces craving; OK with active drinking
  • Withdrawal: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) prevent seizures and DTs

Opioid use disorder

  • Methadone: Full agonist, long half-life — replacement therapy; only at certified clinics
  • Buprenorphine (Subutex, Suboxone): Partial agonist; ceiling effect on respiratory depression; office-based
  • Naltrexone: Antagonist — must be opioid-free 7–10 days before starting
  • Naloxone (Narcan): EMERGENCY OVERDOSE REVERSAL — IM, IV, intranasal; short duration (may need repeat dosing)
  • Withdrawal: Clonidine (alpha-2 agonist) reduces autonomic symptoms

Tobacco & other

  • Nicotine replacement (gum, patch, lozenge, inhaler, spray)
  • Varenicline (Chantix): Partial nicotinic agonist — black box for neuropsychiatric symptoms
  • Bupropion (Zyban): Atypical antidepressant for smoking cessation
A client is taking disulfiram (Antabuse). Which everyday products must they avoid — and for how long after stopping the medication?
Avoid all alcohol-containing products for 2 weeks after stopping: mouthwash, cough syrup, aftershave/cologne, vanilla extract, hand sanitizer, certain OTC liquid meds. Even small dermal/oral exposure can trigger the disulfiram reaction — flushing, severe vomiting, hypotension, tachycardia, headache, dyspnea.
An adult is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and respirations of 4/min. What is the priority medication — and what is the critical catch about its duration of action?
Naloxone (Narcan) — IM, IV, or intranasal. Critical catch: naloxone's half-life (~30–90 min) is shorter than most opioids (especially long-acting ones like methadone or fentanyl). The client can re-sedate after the dose wears off. Monitor closely for return of respiratory depression and repeat dose PRN.
Differentiate methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone as medication-assisted treatment for opioid use disorder.
Methadone: full agonist; long half-life; replacement therapy; only at certified opioid treatment clinics. Buprenorphine (Subutex/Suboxone): partial agonist; ceiling effect on respiratory depression; office-based prescribing. Naltrexone: opioid antagonist; client must be opioid-free 7–10 days before starting or precipitated withdrawal occurs.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has tobacco use disorder about a new prescription for varenicline to promote smoking cessation. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify at least three adverse effects.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify at least two teaching points.
  • EVALUATION OF MEDICATION EFFECTIVENESS: Identify a client outcome to indicate medication effectiveness.
Show key

Expected Pharmacological Action

Varenicline is a nicotinic receptor agonist that promotes the release of dopamine to simulate the pleasurable effects of nicotine.

Therapeutic Uses

Varenicline is indicated to reduce nicotine cravings and block the desired effects of nicotine in clients who have tobacco use disorder.

Complications

  • New-onset hypertension
  • Loss of glycemic control in clients who have diabetes mellitus
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Insomnia
  • New-onset depression
  • Suicidal thoughts

Client Education

  • Clients who are commercial truck or bus drivers, airplane pilots, or air traffic controllers should not take varenicline.
  • Take medication after a meal.
  • Titrate as prescribed to minimize adverse effects.
  • Notify the provider if adverse effects occur.

Evaluation Of Medication Effectiveness

  • The client will maintain smoking cessation.
  • The client will report reduced cravings for nicotine.
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 13

Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Chronic neurologic disorders include Parkinson disease (levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists), Alzheimer disease (donepezil, memantine), multiple sclerosis (interferon beta, glatiramer), myasthenia gravis (neostigmine, pyridostigmine), epilepsy (phenytoin, valproate, gabapentin), and migraine (triptans, ergot alkaloids).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Parkinson: Levodopa/carbidopa (prototype) — wearing-off, on-off; avoid high-protein meals. Alzheimer: Donepezil (cholinesterase inhibitor) for mild-moderate; memantine for moderate-severe. Seizures: Phenytoin therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL; gingival hyperplasia. Myasthenia gravis: Neostigmine. Migraine: Sumatriptan (acute), propranolol (prevention).

Parkinson disease

  • Levodopa/carbidopa (Sinemet): Prototype; carbidopa prevents peripheral conversion
  • Wearing-off effect (end-of-dose return of symptoms); on-off phenomenon (sudden loss of function)
  • Avoid high-protein meals with levodopa (amino acids compete for absorption)
  • Other: Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole), COMT inhibitors (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline)
  • AVOID conventional antipsychotics — worsen symptoms

Alzheimer disease & dementia

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine — mild-moderate
  • Memantine (Namenda): NMDA antagonist — moderate-severe
  • Cholinergic AE: Bradycardia, GI distress, dizziness
  • These medications slow progression — they do not cure

Seizures, MS, ALS, MG

  • Phenytoin: Therapeutic 10–20 mcg/mL; gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, ataxia, narrow TI
  • Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, levetiracetam: Various seizure types
  • Multiple sclerosis: Interferon beta, glatiramer (immunomodulators)
  • ALS: Riluzole (slows progression)
  • Myasthenia gravis: Neostigmine, pyridostigmine (cholinesterase inhibitors) — atropine reverses cholinergic crisis

Migraine

  • Acute: Triptans (sumatriptan) — contraindicated in CAD, uncontrolled HTN, recent MI; ergot alkaloids (ergotamine)
  • Prevention: Propranolol, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline; new CGRP inhibitors
  • NEVER combine triptans + MAOIs or 2 triptans within 24 hr (serotonin syndrome)
Why is a high-protein meal a problem for a client taking levodopa/carbidopa?
Levodopa is an amino acid. High-protein meals release competing amino acids that compete for absorption across the GI tract and at the blood-brain barrier → reduced drug effect and worse Parkinson symptoms. Teach: take levodopa 30 min before meals if tolerated, distribute protein across the day, avoid high-protein loads. Also be aware of wearing-off (end-of-dose return of symptoms) and on-off (sudden loss of function).
What is the therapeutic range for phenytoin, what are the classic toxicity signs, and what oral side effect should every nurse teach about?
Therapeutic range: 10–20 mcg/mL (narrow TI). Toxicity signs by level: >20 nystagmus + ataxia; >30 confusion, dysarthria; >40 coma, cardiac arrhythmias. Classic chronic effect: gingival hyperplasia — teach meticulous oral hygiene (brushing twice daily, flossing, regular dental visits). Also: hirsutism, rash, drug-induced lupus, fetal hydantoin syndrome (Category D).
Differentiate donepezil and memantine for Alzheimer disease — when each is used and the realistic expectation.
Donepezil (Aricept) — cholinesterase inhibitor: mild-to-moderate AD; also rivastigmine, galantamine. AE: bradycardia, syncope, GI distress. Memantine (Namenda) — NMDA antagonist: moderate-to-severe AD; well-tolerated. Both slow progression but do NOT cure. Family teaching: realistic expectation is delay of decline by ~6–12 months — disease still advances.
A client with migraine takes sertraline and asks about sumatriptan. What are the contraindications and the dangerous combination?
Cardiac contraindications: CAD, uncontrolled HTN, recent MI, history of stroke, severe peripheral vascular disease — triptans cause vasoconstriction. Drug interactions: NEVER combine with MAOIs or with another triptan within 24 hr → serotonin syndrome. With SSRIs (sertraline), there is theoretical serotonin-syndrome risk; use with caution and monitor. Also avoid ergot derivatives within 24 hr.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is planning care for a client who has tonic-clonic seizures and a new prescription for phenytoin. Considering the adverse effects and nursing interventions, what should the nurse include in the plan of care? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item to include the following:

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects and two medication interactions.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Include two interventions that relate to the two adverse effects, and two interventions that relate to the two medication interactions.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Phenytoin is a hydantoin medication that suppresses partial seizure and primary generalized seizure activity in the affected neurons.

Complications

  • CNS effects
  • Gingival hyperplasia
  • Teratogenic birth defects
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and glucocorticoids
  • Causes stimulation of hepatic medication-metabolizing enzymes
  • Alcohol (acute use), diazepam, cimetidine, and valproic acid increase phenytoin levels.
  • Carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and chronic alcohol use decrease phenytoin levels.
  • Additive CNS depressant effects can occur with concurrent use of CNS depressants.

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client to refrain from alcohol and other medications that cause CNS depression, such as barbiturates.
  • Encourage the client to use dental floss and massage gums daily.
  • Instruct the client to avoid pregnancy and use an alternate form of contraception.
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin and blood glucose levels if taking a glucocorticoid.
  • Monitor therapeutic effects of warfarin and glucocorticoids.
  • Never abruptly discontinue antiepileptic medications.
  • Advise clients to avoid use of alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Monitor blood phenytoin levels
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 14

Eye and Ear Disorders

Eye disorders include glaucoma (treated with beta blockers, prostaglandin analogs, cholinergics, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), allergic conjunctivitis, and infections. Ear disorders are primarily otitis externa (topical antibiotic-steroid drops) and otitis media (oral antibiotics).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Glaucoma medications lower IOP. Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost) = first-line, once-daily. Beta blockers (timolol) = systemic AE possible (bradycardia, bronchospasm). Cholinergics (pilocarpine) = miosis, blurred vision. Eye drop technique: press inner canthus 1 min to prevent systemic absorption. Ear drops: warm to body temp, pull pinna up/back (adult) or down/back (child).

Glaucoma medications

  • Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost): First-line; iris color change, lash growth
  • Beta-adrenergic blockers (timolol, betaxolol): Avoid in asthma/COPD/heart block — can cause systemic effects
  • Alpha-adrenergic agonists (brimonidine): Drowsiness, dry mouth
  • Cholinergics (pilocarpine): Miosis, blurred vision, headache
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide PO, dorzolamide drops): Sulfa allergy caution

Eye drop administration

  • Wash hands; tilt head back; pull lower lid down to form cul-de-sac
  • Instill drop without touching eye
  • Apply pressure to nasolacrimal duct (inner canthus) for 1 minute — prevents systemic absorption
  • Wait 5–10 minutes between different drops
  • Suspensions: shake well; ointments: applied last

Ear & other ophthalmic

  • Otic drops: Warm to body temp (prevent dizziness); adult: pinna up & back; child < 3: down & back
  • Have client lie on opposite side for 5 min after instilling
  • Otitis media: Oral antibiotics (amoxicillin first-line)
  • Otitis externa: Topical antibiotic + corticosteroid drops
  • Allergic conjunctivitis: Antihistamine drops, mast cell stabilizers

Glaucoma — additional medications

  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — Acetazolamide (PO), dorzolamide (drops): Reduce aqueous humor production
  • Acetazolamide also treats: Acute glaucoma, altitude sickness, seizures
  • Sulfonamide-derived — caution with sulfa allergy
  • Mannitol (IV): Osmotic agent — acute angle-closure glaucoma emergency
  • Brimonidine (alpha-2 agonist): First-line; can cross BBB; monitor BP
  • Allergic conjunctivitis: Olopatadine, cromolyn (mast cell stabilizer); avoid in active eye infection
  • Cerumenolytics (carbamide peroxide): Soften ear wax; never if perforated eardrum
A client uses timolol eye drops for glaucoma. What technique reduces systemic absorption and prevents bradycardia/bronchospasm?
After instilling the drop, apply pressure to the inner canthus (nasolacrimal duct) for 1 full minute. This blocks systemic absorption through the lacrimal duct/nasal mucosa — critical for beta-blocker drops which can cause bradycardia and bronchospasm systemically. Other key steps: tilt head back, pull lower lid down to form a "cul-de-sac", don't touch the dropper to the eye, wait 5–10 min between different drops. Avoid timolol in asthma/COPD/heart block.
Latanoprost is first-line for glaucoma. What is the mechanism, and what cosmetic side effects must clients be informed about?
Mechanism: prostaglandin analog → ↑ uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor → lowers IOP. Cosmetic AE (important to disclose): permanent iris darkening (especially in mixed-color irises), eyelash lengthening/darkening/thickening, and periorbital skin pigmentation. Most are unilateral if the drop is only used in one eye. Dosed once daily, usually evening. Other glaucoma classes: beta blockers, alpha-2 agonists, cholinergics, CAIs.
Which direction is the pinna pulled for ear-drop instillation — and how does it differ between adults and young children?
Adult or child > 3 yo: pull pinna UP and BACK (the ear canal slopes anteriorly and inferiorly). Child < 3 yo: pull pinna DOWN and BACK (the immature canal slopes differently). Also: warm drops to body temperature first (cold drops cause dizziness and nausea), have client lie on the opposite side for at least 5 minutes after, never instill drops if eardrum perforation is suspected.
A nurse is about to give acetazolamide to a client with allergies. Which allergy is the major concern, and what are this drug's other notable uses?
Sulfa allergy — acetazolamide is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor; cross-reactivity possible. Other uses besides glaucoma: acute high-altitude sickness (prevention and treatment), some seizure types, metabolic alkalosis. Mannitol (IV osmotic) is reserved for acute angle-closure glaucoma emergencies. Dorzolamide (drops) is also a CAI; same sulfa caution applies.

A nurse in a provider's office is teaching a client who has a prescription for ciprofloxacin/hydrocortisone about the medication and how to prevent otitis externa. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two potential adverse effects.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify two actions to prevent otitis externa.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

The bactericidal effects of ciprofloxacin and the anti-inflammatory effect of hydrocortisone decreases pain, edema, and erythema in the ear.

Complications

  • Rash
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, tremors, restlessness, and convulsions

Client Education

  • Keep foreign bodies out of ear canal.
  • Avoid manual measures to remove cerumen.
  • Dry ear canal after bathing or swimming using a towel.
  • Avoid use of ear plugs except for swimming.
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 15

Miscellaneous Central Nervous System Medications

Miscellaneous CNS medications include centrally-acting skeletal muscle relaxants for muscle spasm (cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, baclofen, dantrolene) and migraine therapies. Most cause significant CNS depression.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Centrally-acting muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, baclofen, tizanidine) — all cause CNS depression and drowsiness. Cyclobenzaprine: most prescribed; anticholinergic; not with MAOIs. Dantrolene (direct-acting): treats malignant hyperthermia and NMS. Baclofen: spasticity from MS/spinal cord injury; do not abruptly stop (withdrawal seizures).

Centrally-acting muscle relaxants

  • Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril): Most common; anticholinergic effects; max 2–3 weeks; contraindicated with MAOIs
  • Methocarbamol, carisoprodol, metaxalone, chlorzoxazone: Short-term muscle spasm
  • Baclofen (Lioresal): Spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury); abrupt discontinuation = seizures, hallucinations
  • Tizanidine: Hypotension, hepatotoxicity
  • All cause: Drowsiness, dizziness — avoid alcohol, hazardous activities

Direct-acting & key uses

  • Dantrolene (Dantrium): Direct skeletal muscle relaxant
  • Critical uses: Malignant hyperthermia (anesthesia complication) and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
  • Hepatotoxic — monitor LFTs with chronic use

General anesthesia adjuncts & cholinergics

  • Bethanechol: Cholinergic (muscarinic agonist) — treats urinary retention, post-op ileus
  • Bethanechol AE: Bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, sweating, abdominal cramps
  • Contraindicated in asthma, peptic ulcer, hyperthyroidism, urinary tract obstruction
  • Antidote for bethanechol toxicity: Atropine
  • Centrally-acting muscle relaxants (also covered in Ch 16 sedatives) for spasticity
In what two emergency situations is dantrolene the critical medication, and what is its mechanism?
(1) Malignant hyperthermia (anesthesia complication — typically with halothane or succinylcholine) and (2) Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS). Mechanism: direct skeletal muscle relaxant — blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, halting the runaway muscle hypermetabolism. Hepatotoxic with chronic use — monitor LFTs. Have dantrolene immediately accessible in any OR.
Why must baclofen never be abruptly discontinued in a client with spinal cord injury or MS?
Abrupt discontinuation can cause seizures, hallucinations, hyperthermia, rebound spasticity, and rhabdomyolysis — potentially fatal, particularly with intrathecal baclofen pumps. Always taper slowly over 1–2 weeks for oral; pump failure is a medical emergency requiring oral substitution and admission. Teach clients to keep a backup oral supply, never run out, and recognize early withdrawal signs (itching, increased spasticity, tachycardia).
A post-op client is given bethanechol for urinary retention and develops bradycardia, severe abdominal cramps, and bronchospasm. What is happening — and what is the antidote?
Muscarinic toxicity from bethanechol (a direct cholinergic/muscarinic agonist). Classic effects (SLUDGE-BBB): salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea. Antidote: atropine (muscarinic antagonist). Contraindications for bethanechol: asthma, peptic ulcer disease, hyperthyroidism, urinary tract obstruction.

Therapeutic Uses

  • Endotracheal intubation
  • Electroconvulsive therapy
  • Endoscopy
  • Adjunct to mechanical ventilation
  • Muscle relaxation during surgery

Medication Administration

  • Clients must receive continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring during therapy.
  • Monitor clients following administration of a neuromuscular blocker for respiratory depression and have life support equipment available.
  • Continue to carefully monitor for return of respiratory function.
  • Succinylcholine is contraindicated for clients at risk for hyperkalemia (trauma, severe burns).
Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 16

Sedative-Hypnotics

Sedative-hypnotics treat insomnia and induce sedation. Three classes dominate: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, temazepam), non-benzodiazepine "Z-drugs" (zolpidem, eszopiclone), and newer agents (ramelteon, suvorexant). All risk dependence; benzos reversed with flumazenil.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Benzodiazepines (diazepam prototype, lorazepam, temazepam, midazolam) — risk dependence, anterograde amnesia, paradoxical reactions in older adults; reverse with flumazenil. Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon) — less dependence; complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving). Ramelteon — melatonin agonist, no dependence. All: avoid alcohol, evening dosing only.

Benzodiazepines

  • Diazepam (Valium): Long-acting prototype; metabolites prolong effect
  • Lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam: No active metabolites — safer in elderly and liver disease
  • Midazolam: Short-acting; pre-procedural sedation
  • AE: CNS depression, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, tolerance, dependence
  • Paradoxical reactions (excitation) in children and older adults
  • Overdose: Reverse with flumazenil (may precipitate seizures in dependent clients)
  • Pregnancy: Category D — avoid; teratogenic (cleft palate)

Z-drugs (non-benzodiazepine hypnotics)

  • Zolpidem (Ambien): Most prescribed; rapid onset
  • Eszopiclone (Lunesta), zaleplon (Sonata): Similar mechanism
  • Complex sleep behaviors: Sleep-driving, sleep-eating, sleep-walking — discontinue if occurs
  • Take only when 7–8 hours of sleep available
  • Less dependence risk than benzos but still controlled (Schedule IV)

Newer agents & general teaching

  • Ramelteon (Rozerem): Melatonin receptor agonist; no dependence; no Schedule classification
  • Suvorexant (Belsomra): Orexin antagonist
  • Doxepin (low-dose): Antihistamine action for sleep
  • Diphenhydramine: OTC; anticholinergic — avoid in older adults (Beers Criteria)
  • NEVER combine with alcohol or opioids

General anesthesia adjuncts

  • Propofol (Diprivan): IV induction & maintenance of anesthesia; rapid onset/offset; propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) with prolonged use (acidosis, rhabdomyolysis); supports bacterial growth — change tubing q12h; egg/soy allergy caution
  • Ketamine (Schedule III): Dissociative anesthetic; bronchodilator (good in asthma); causes emergence reactions (hallucinations, vivid dreams) — pretreat with benzodiazepine; ↑ BP/HR (avoid in CAD); also low-dose for treatment-resistant depression
  • Fentanyl (anesthesia adjunct): Potent opioid; balanced anesthesia; respiratory depression
  • Etomidate: IV induction; minimal CV depression; adrenal suppression (avoid in sepsis)
  • Barbiturates — Pentobarbital: Older sedative; Schedule II–IV; respiratory depression; no antidote (unlike benzos); rarely used due to safety profile
A client on zolpidem reports waking up to find evidence of eating or driving with no memory of it. What is happening, and what is the nursing action?
Complex sleep-related behaviors — sleep-driving, sleep-eating, sleep-walking, sleep-sex — a class effect of Z-drugs (zolpidem, eszopiclone, zaleplon). FDA black box warning since 2019. Action: discontinue the medication and notify provider. Other teaching: only take when 7–8 hours of sleep are available before next activity, never combine with alcohol or other CNS depressants, swallow whole (don't crush extended-release).
A nurse gives lorazepam to an agitated older adult and the client becomes MORE agitated and combative. What is this called and what should the nurse do?
Paradoxical reaction to benzodiazepines — increased agitation, excitation, hostility, or rage instead of the expected sedation. More common in older adults and children. Action: stop further benzo doses, notify provider, use non-pharm de-escalation or alternative agents (haloperidol for delirium-related agitation). Also avoid long-acting benzos (diazepam) in older adults — use lorazepam/oxazepam/temazepam (no active metabolites).
What allergy must be screened before propofol administration, why must tubing be changed every 12 hours, and what is PRIS?
Egg and soy allergy — propofol is formulated in a lipid emulsion containing egg lecithin and soybean oil. Tubing change q12h: the lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth — strict sterile technique and frequent tubing changes prevent infection. Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS): rare but life-threatening complication of prolonged high-dose infusion (>48 hr, >4 mg/kg/hr) — metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, cardiac failure.

  • Seizure disorders
  • Insomnia
  • Muscle spasms
  • Alcohol withdrawal
  • Panic disorder
  • Induction of anesthesia

Contraindications / Precautions

Unit 3 · Respiratory · Chapter 17

Airflow Disorders

Airflow disorders (asthma, COPD) are managed with bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-2 agonists, anticholinergics, methylxanthines), anti-inflammatory medications (inhaled glucocorticoids, leukotriene modifiers, mast cell stabilizers), and biologics (omalizumab). Quick-relief vs. long-term controller distinction guides therapy.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Quick-relief: SABA (albuterol — prototype) for acute attacks. Long-term controllers: ICS (fluticasone), LABA (salmeterol — never solo, always with ICS), leukotriene modifiers (montelukast), anticholinergics (ipratropium short, tiotropium long). Status asthmaticus: IV magnesium, IV corticosteroids. Teach: rinse mouth after ICS (prevents thrush).

Bronchodilators

  • SABA — Albuterol (prototype): Quick relief for acute bronchospasm; onset 5–15 min; AE: tachycardia, tremor, nervousness
  • LABA — Salmeterol, formoterol: Long-term control; BLACK BOX warning — never use alone in asthma (↑ death risk); always combine with ICS
  • Anticholinergics — Ipratropium (short), tiotropium (long): COPD first-line; dry mouth, urinary retention
  • Methylxanthines — Theophylline: Narrow TI (10–20 mcg/mL); monitor levels; avoid caffeine; toxicity = N/V, tremor, seizures

Anti-inflammatory & biologics

  • Inhaled glucocorticoids — Fluticasone, budesonide: First-line controller for asthma
  • Rinse mouth after each use — prevents oral candidiasis (thrush) and hoarseness
  • Leukotriene modifiers — Montelukast: PO; daily; AE: mood/behavior changes (black box for neuropsych)
  • Mast cell stabilizers — Cromolyn: Preventive only — NOT for acute attacks
  • Biologics — Omalizumab (anti-IgE): Severe persistent asthma; SC injection; risk anaphylaxis

Critical teaching

  • Order with combo: SABA first, wait 5 min, then ICS — opens airway before steroid
  • Always carry rescue inhaler; track frequency of SABA use (>2 days/week = poor control)
  • Use spacer to improve delivery and reduce thrush
  • Peak flow monitoring: green (>80%), yellow (50–79%), red (<50% = ER)

Inhaler technique & asthma severity

  • MDI technique: Shake well, exhale, seal lips around mouthpiece (or use spacer), press canister while inhaling slowly over 3–5 sec, hold breath 10 sec; wait 1 min between puffs
  • Spacer benefits: Better drug delivery to lungs, reduces oropharyngeal deposition (less thrush with ICS), critical for children/older adults
  • DPI (dry powder inhaler): Don't exhale into the device (moisture clumps powder); inhale fast and deep; no spacer
  • Asthma severity classification guides therapy: Intermittent → Mild persistent → Moderate persistent → Severe persistent
  • Asthma action plan (color zones): Green = good control, Yellow = caution (use SABA, contact provider), Red = medical alert (severe, ER)
  • Status asthmaticus: Life-threatening; IV magnesium sulfate, IV corticosteroids, IV epinephrine, intubation if respiratory failure
  • COPD GOLD stages: Stage 1 mild (FEV1 ≥ 80%), 2 moderate (50–79%), 3 severe (30–49%), 4 very severe (< 30%)
  • COPD treatment progression: SABA PRN → add LABA + LAMA → add ICS if frequent exacerbations
  • Roflumilast: PDE-4 inhibitor for severe COPD with chronic bronchitis; reduces exacerbations
A client uses fluticasone (ICS) for asthma. What two interventions reduce the risk of oral candidiasis (thrush)?
(1) Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use — washes residual steroid off oral mucosa. (2) Use a spacer device — reduces oropharyngeal deposition, improves lung delivery. Also: gargling helps. Inspect mouth at every visit. If thrush develops: treat with nystatin oral suspension, continue ICS (the asthma controller is essential). Order matters in combo therapy: SABA first, wait 5 min, then ICS — bronchodilator opens airways so steroid reaches deeper.
Why does salmeterol carry a black-box warning, and what is the rule for its use in asthma?
LABA monotherapy in asthma → increased risk of asthma-related death (FDA black-box warning). Rule: LABA must ALWAYS be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) in asthma — typically a combination inhaler like fluticasone/salmeterol (Advair). LABAs do not treat the underlying inflammation; they mask worsening control while bronchodilating. Step up the ICS, don't add solo LABA. (LABA monotherapy is acceptable in COPD.)

Scenario

A nurse is instructing a client who has a new prescription for albuterol PO. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Beta2-adrenergic agonists act by selectively activating the beta2-receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle, resulting in bronchodilation. They also suppress histamine release and promote ciliary motility.

Complications

  • Oral agents can cause tachycardia and angina due to activation of alpha1 receptors in the heart.
  • Activation of beta2 receptors in skeletal muscle causes tremors.
Unit 3 · Respiratory · Chapter 18

Upper Respiratory Disorders

Upper respiratory medications target cough (antitussives — codeine, dextromethorphan), mucus production (expectorants — guaifenesin), thick secretions (mucolytics — acetylcysteine), nasal congestion (decongestants — phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine), and allergy symptoms (antihistamines — diphenhydramine, loratadine, cetirizine).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Antitussives: Codeine (opioid — controlled), dextromethorphan (OTC). Expectorant: guaifenesin (thins secretions). Mucolytic: acetylcysteine (also acetaminophen overdose antidote). Decongestants (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine) — caution in HTN. Antihistamines: 1st-gen (diphenhydramine) = sedating, anticholinergic; 2nd-gen (loratadine, cetirizine) = non-sedating.

Cough & secretion management

  • Codeine: Opioid antitussive; Schedule II/III; AE: respiratory depression, constipation, dependence
  • Dextromethorphan: Non-opioid; common in OTC products; abuse potential at high doses
  • Guaifenesin: Expectorant — thins respiratory secretions; encourage fluids
  • Acetylcysteine: Mucolytic (inhaled, smells like rotten eggs); also antidote for acetaminophen overdose (PO/IV)

Nasal congestion & allergies

  • Phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine (PO): Sympathomimetic decongestants; AE: HTN, tachycardia, insomnia, restlessness
  • Avoid in HTN, CAD, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism, BPH
  • Oxymetazoline (intranasal): Limit to 3–5 days — rebound congestion if longer
  • Intranasal glucocorticoids (fluticasone, mometasone): First-line for allergic rhinitis

Antihistamines (H1 blockers)

  • First-generation — Diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, hydroxyzine: Sedating; strong anticholinergic effects
  • Beers Criteria: AVOID 1st-gen antihistamines in older adults (confusion, falls)
  • Second-generation — Loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine, desloratadine: Non-sedating; less anticholinergic
  • Diphenhydramine also used for anaphylaxis (after epinephrine), motion sickness, EPS reactions

Decision-making & age-specific cautions

  • Productive cough: Use expectorant (guaifenesin) + ↑ fluids; avoid suppressants — they keep mucus in lungs
  • Non-productive (dry) cough: Antitussive (dextromethorphan, codeine) appropriate; sleep-disrupting cough
  • Children < 4 yo: AVOID OTC cough/cold medications (FDA warning) — risk outweighs benefit
  • Children < 12 yo: AVOID codeine and tramadol (variable metabolism, deaths reported)
  • Methamphetamine precursor: Pseudoephedrine sale tracked (BTC — behind-the-counter); ID required; limited monthly
  • Nasal saline irrigation/neti pot: Use distilled or sterile water only (tap water → fatal amebic meningoencephalitis from Naegleria fowleri)
  • Intranasal glucocorticoids (fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone, budesonide): First-line for allergic rhinitis; takes days to work; AE: epistaxis, nasal dryness; teach proper technique (point away from septum)
  • Combination products (Theraflu, NyQuil, etc.) — multiple ingredients risk duplicate/overdose; check for hidden acetaminophen and pseudoephedrine
  • Cetirizine vs loratadine vs fexofenadine: All 2nd-gen, similar efficacy; cetirizine slightly more sedating than the others
Acetylcysteine has two major clinical uses. What are they — and what is the route for each?
(1) Mucolytic — inhaled/nebulized for thick respiratory secretions (cystic fibrosis, COPD exacerbations). Smells like rotten eggs (sulfur), often given with a bronchodilator first. (2) Antidote for acetaminophen overdose — PO or IV within 8–10 hours of ingestion (ideal); replenishes hepatic glutathione, neutralizing the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to guide need for treatment based on serum APAP level.
A client has been using oxymetazoline (Afrin) nasal spray daily for 2 weeks for cold congestion. What is the problem, and what is the recovery plan?
Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion) — topical decongestants used >3–5 days cause worsening congestion when the dose wears off, creating a use-cycle. Recovery: taper to one nostril at a time over a week, expect significant rebound congestion during withdrawal (5–7 days). Substitute intranasal saline for comfort and an intranasal glucocorticoid (fluticasone, mometasone) for sustained relief. Teach the <3–5 day rule going forward.
What is the FDA recommendation about OTC cough and cold medications in young children, and what age groups must avoid codeine/tramadol?
OTC cough/cold medications: AVOID in children < 4 years old (FDA warning) — risk of cardiac events, seizures, decreased consciousness, death; benefit is minimal. Codeine and tramadol: contraindicated < 12 years old (variable CYP2D6 metabolism → unpredictable opioid effect; deaths reported), and also in adolescents 12–18 who are post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy or are breastfeeding mothers. Non-pharm care for pediatric colds: humidified air, fluids, saline drops, honey (only > 1 year old).

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 19

Medications Affecting Urinary Output

Diuretics remove excess fluid by inhibiting sodium and water reabsorption in different parts of the nephron. Four classes: loop diuretics (furosemide), thiazide (hydrochlorothiazide), potassium-sparing (spironolactone), and osmotic (mannitol). Used for HTN, heart failure, edema, and cerebral edema.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Loop (furosemide — prototype): Most powerful; HF, edema, HTN; ↓K, ↓Mg, ↓Ca; ototoxic (slow IV push). Thiazide (HCTZ): First-line HTN; ↓K; ↑Ca, ↑uric acid, ↑glucose. K-sparing (spironolactone): ↑K (hyperkalemia risk); gynecomastia. Osmotic (mannitol): IV only; ↑ICP, glaucoma; crystals — use filter needle.

Loop diuretics

  • Furosemide (prototype), bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid
  • Mechanism: Block Na/K/2Cl reabsorption in ascending loop of Henle
  • Uses: Heart failure, pulmonary edema, severe HTN, edema
  • Major AE: ↓K (hypokalemia), ↓Mg, ↓Ca, ↓Na; dehydration; hypotension
  • Ototoxicity: Especially with rapid IV push or concurrent aminoglycoside — administer IV slowly
  • Encourage K-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes); monitor BUN/Cr

Thiazide & K-sparing

  • Thiazide — Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), chlorthalidone, metolazone
  • HCTZ first-line for HTN; works on distal tubule
  • HCTZ AE: ↓K, ↓Na; ↑Ca, ↑glucose, ↑uric acid (gout), ↑lipids; sulfa allergy caution
  • K-sparing — Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist), eplerenone, triamterene, amiloride
  • Spironolactone AE: Hyperkalemia (avoid salt substitutes, K supplements, ACE/ARB combo without monitoring); gynecomastia, menstrual irregularity

Osmotic & critical teaching

  • Mannitol: IV only — reduces ICP (TBI), intraocular pressure; treats acute renal failure
  • Filter needle required — solution may have crystals
  • NEVER add electrolytes to mannitol — precipitation
  • All diuretics: Monitor I&O, daily weights (2 lb/day = fluid retention/loss), BP, electrolytes
A client on furosemide for heart failure reports muscle cramps and weakness. What electrolyte derangements are likely, and what are the key teaching points?
Likely hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia, and dehydration. Loop diuretics block Na/K/2Cl reabsorption in the ascending loop of Henle, wasting these electrolytes. Teaching: eat K-rich foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes, leafy greens, tomatoes), report cramping/weakness/palpitations, weigh daily at same time (2 lb/day = significant). Often paired with K supplement or spironolactone. Monitor BUN/Cr, electrolytes, BP, daily weight.
A nurse administers IV furosemide. What is the maximum rate of administration, and why?
Maximum 20 mg/min IV push (or 4 mg/min for doses >120 mg). Reason: ototoxicity — rapid IV push can cause transient or even permanent hearing loss and tinnitus. Risk is higher when combined with aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) or other ototoxic drugs. Always check the bag for crystals and use slow IV push. Same caution applies to ethacrynic acid (highest ototoxicity risk among loops).
A client on spironolactone for heart failure also takes lisinopril. The serum K is 5.8 mEq/L. What is happening, and what foods/products should the client avoid?
Hyperkalemia — both spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist, K-sparing) and ACE inhibitors raise K; combining them compounds the risk. K >5.5 needs intervention; K >6.0 with ECG changes is an emergency (peaked T waves → wide QRS → sine wave). Avoid: salt substitutes (most contain KCl), K supplements, K-rich foods in excess (bananas, oranges, melons, potatoes, tomatoes, leafy greens). Other AE of spironolactone: gynecomastia and menstrual irregularity (anti-androgenic).
A nurse is preparing mannitol IV for elevated intracranial pressure. What two equipment/administration cautions are critical?
(1) Use a filter needle / in-line filter — mannitol solutions readily form crystals, especially when stored or chilled; warm the bag (under hot water or in a warmer) to redissolve before use. (2) NEVER add other medications or electrolytes to mannitol — causes precipitation. Mannitol is IV only, used for ↑ICP (TBI), acute glaucoma, and oliguric acute renal failure. Monitor strict I&O, electrolytes, neuro status. Effect typically within 15–30 min, peaks at 1 hr.

Active Learning Scenario

Scenario

A charge nurse is reviewing the use of loop diuretics with a group of nurses. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify two.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe three adverse effects.
