Therapeutic Uses

  • Used when there is an emergent need for rapid mobilization of fluid
  • Pulmonary edema caused by heart failure
  • Liver, cardiac, or kidney disease
  • Hypertension
  • Unlabeled use: hypercalcemia

Complications

  • Dehydration
  • Hypotension
  • Ototoxicity
  • Hypokalemia

Nursing Interventions

  • Dehydration: Assess for dry mouth, increased thirst, low urine output, weight loss.
  • Hypotension: monitor orthostatic blood pressure and pulse; monitor for manifestations of postural hypotension.
  • Ototoxicity: Assess for tinnitus; avoid administering ototoxic medications.
  • Hypokalemia: monitor laboratory values; offer potassium-rich foods; assess for general weakness, nausea, and vomiting.
Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 20

Medications Affecting Blood Pressure

Antihypertensive medications work through multiple mechanisms: ACE inhibitors (captopril) and ARBs (losartan), aldosterone antagonists, direct renin inhibitors, alpha blockers, central alpha-2 agonists (clonidine), beta blockers, calcium channel blockers (covered in Ch 22-23), vasodilators (hydralazine), and emergency IV agents (nitroprusside).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril, enalapril) — "-pril"; dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia; Category D — teratogenic. ARBs (losartan, valsartan) — "-sartan"; switch from ACEi for cough; same risks otherwise. Clonidine — central α2; rebound HTN if abruptly stopped. Hydralazine, nitroprusside — direct vasodilators (IV for emergency).

ACE inhibitors & ARBs

  • ACE inhibitors — Captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril ("-pril")
  • Mechanism: Block conversion of angiotensin I → II; ↓ aldosterone; vasodilation
  • Uses: HTN, HF, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy (renoprotective)
  • Key AE: Persistent dry cough (10–20%), angioedema (life-threatening), hyperkalemia, hypotension (especially first dose)
  • ARBs — Losartan, valsartan, irbesartan ("-sartan") — no cough, less angioedema
  • BOTH contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D — fetal renal damage)
  • Monitor BUN/Cr (renal function) and K+
  • AVOID combining ACE + ARB (no benefit, more harm)

Aldosterone antagonists & DRI

  • Eplerenone, spironolactone: Block aldosterone; hyperkalemia risk
  • Aliskiren (direct renin inhibitor): Less commonly used; same Category D pregnancy restriction

Alpha blockers, central agonists, vasodilators

  • Alpha-1 blockers — Prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin: First-dose orthostatic hypotension — take at bedtime; rise slowly
  • Central alpha-2 — Clonidine, methyldopa: NEVER abruptly stop — rebound HTN crisis; sedation, dry mouth
  • Methyldopa = safe in pregnancy
  • Hydralazine (PO/IV): Direct vasodilator; reflex tachycardia; lupus-like syndrome at high dose
  • Nitroprusside (IV only): Hypertensive emergency; cyanide toxicity (max 72 hr); protect from light
A client started on lisinopril 4 weeks ago calls reporting a persistent dry cough that won't resolve. What is the cause, and what is the nursing action?
ACE-inhibitor cough — a class effect from bradykinin accumulation (ACE normally inactivates bradykinin). Occurs in 10–20% of clients, often after weeks. Not dose-dependent, doesn't resolve over time. Action: notify provider — switch to an ARB ("-sartan") which preserves the BP/renal benefits without the bradykinin effect. Worse than cough: angioedema (swelling of lips/tongue/airway) — life-threatening, requires immediate discontinuation and emergency care. Both ACE and ARB are Category D — teratogenic.
Why is clonidine particularly dangerous to abruptly discontinue, and what is the safe approach?
Rebound hypertension crisis — abruptly stopping clonidine (central α2 agonist) causes sympathetic surge with severe HTN, tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, headache — can precipitate stroke or MI. Safe approach: taper over 2–4 days. Critical patient teaching: never miss doses, fill prescriptions on time, keep a backup supply when traveling, NEVER stop on your own. Same precaution applies to methyldopa (the safer-in-pregnancy alternative).
A client is starting prazosin for HTN. What is the "first-dose phenomenon," and what teaching prevents injury?
First-dose orthostatic hypotension — alpha-1 blockers (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin) cause profound BP drop on initial dose, with risk of syncope and falls. Teaching: take first dose at bedtime, while in bed, and don't plan activities afterward. Going forward: rise slowly (sit on edge of bed before standing), avoid hot showers/alcohol/dehydration, take consistently with food. Prazosin also has off-label use for PTSD-related nightmares.
A client is on IV nitroprusside for hypertensive emergency. What is the major toxicity risk, the time limit, and the storage requirement?
Cyanide / thiocyanate toxicity — nitroprusside breaks down to release cyanide ions; the body detoxifies them to thiocyanate (renally cleared). Time limit: max 72 hours; shorter in renal impairment. Signs: metabolic acidosis, tachycardia, altered mental status, almond-scented breath (cyanide). Storage: protect from light — wrap bag in foil; solution turns from clear to brown/blue/green if degraded → discard. Always have an arterial line for tight BP monitoring; titrate continuously.

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse in an outpatient facility is teaching a client who has a new prescription for aliskiren to treat hypertension. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for aliskiren.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one test to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify two teaching points.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Aliskiren binds with renin to inhibit production of angiotensin I, thus decreasing production of both angiotensin II and aldosterone. Aliskiren is used solely for treating hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensives.

Complications

  • Diarrhea: dose-related, occurs most frequently in females and older adult clients
  • Risk for angioedema and rash caused by allergy to the medication
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hypotension

Nursing Interventions

Monitor blood electrolytes, paying close attention to potassium levels, because the client is at risk for hyperkalemia. This is especially important when the client takes ACE inhibitors concurrently, because these medications also raise potassium levels.

Client Education

  • Do not take aliskiren with foods high in fat, which decreases absorption of the medication.
  • Do not take potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium.
  • Clients should not take aliskiren during pregnancy.
  • If a rash or angioedema occurs, discontinue aliskiren and notify the provider.
  • Call 911 if severe manifestations of allergy are present.
Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 21

Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure

Heart failure management uses cardiac glycosides (digoxin) for inotropic support and rate control in atrial fibrillation. Other key agents: catecholamines (dopamine, dobutamine), human B-type natriuretic peptide (nesiritide), and combination ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Digoxin: positive inotrope (↑ contractility), negative chronotrope (↓ HR). Therapeutic 0.5–2.0 ng/mL. Apical pulse 1 min before dose — hold if <60 (adult) or <90–110 (infants/kids). Toxicity: N/V, anorexia, visual halos (yellow-green), dysrhythmias. Hypokalemia ↑ toxicity. Antidote: digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).

Digoxin

  • Mechanism: Inhibits Na/K ATPase → ↑ intracellular Ca → ↑ contractility (positive inotrope); slows AV conduction (negative chronotrope/dromotrope)
  • Uses: HF with reduced EF, atrial fibrillation (rate control)
  • Therapeutic level: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL
  • Before each dose: Check apical pulse for 1 full minute
  • HOLD and call provider: Adult HR <60; child <90; infant <110

Digoxin toxicity

  • Early signs: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
  • Cardiac: Bradycardia, AV blocks, ventricular dysrhythmias
  • Visual: Yellow-green halos around lights, blurred vision
  • Neurological: Fatigue, weakness, confusion
  • Risk factors: Hypokalemia (most common), hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, advanced age
  • Antidote: Digoxin immune Fab (Digibind) for life-threatening toxicity

Other inotropic & HF agents

  • Catecholamines — Dopamine, dobutamine: IV infusion; short-term inotropic support (cardiogenic shock)
  • Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto): ARNI for HF; replaces ACE/ARB (don't combine — angioedema)
  • Nesiritide: Recombinant BNP for acute decompensated HF
  • Ivabradine: Slows HR; for HF with elevated HR despite beta blockade
A client on digoxin reports yellow-green halos around lights and lost appetite. What is the therapeutic range, what does this presentation suggest, and what are the next steps?
Therapeutic range: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL. Yellow-green halos and anorexia are classic digoxin toxicity. Other early signs: N/V, fatigue, confusion. Cardiac: bradycardia, AV blocks, ventricular dysrhythmias. Steps: hold the next dose, obtain stat digoxin level + serum K, Mg, Ca, BUN/Cr, ECG. Severe toxicity → digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).
What is the pre-administration assessment for every digoxin dose, and the hold parameters by age?
Check apical pulse for a full minute before every dose. HOLD and call provider: Adult HR < 60, child < 90, infant < 110. Document rhythm regularity. Also assess for digoxin toxicity signs (vision changes, anorexia, N/V). Digoxin acts as a positive inotrope (↑ contractility) and negative chronotrope (↓ HR, slows AV conduction) — that's why bradycardia is the hold trigger.
A client on digoxin and furosemide has a serum K of 3.0 mEq/L. Why is this particularly dangerous?
Hypokalemia dramatically increases digoxin toxicity risk, even at therapeutic digoxin levels. Mechanism: digoxin competes with K⁺ for Na/K-ATPase binding; when K⁺ is low, more digoxin binds → toxicity. Furosemide commonly causes hypokalemia → classic dangerous combo. Actions: replace K⁺ before next digoxin dose, monitor ECG, consider adding K-sparing diuretic or K supplement. Hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia also potentiate toxicity.
Why must sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) never be combined with an ACE inhibitor — and what is the washout requirement?
Severe angioedema risk — sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (which degrades bradykinin and ANP); ACE inhibitors also raise bradykinin. Combination → markedly elevated bradykinin → potentially fatal angioedema. Washout: at least 36 hours after stopping ACE inhibitor before starting Entresto (and vice versa). Entresto replaces ACE/ARB in HFrEF (it contains valsartan, an ARB). Same Category D pregnancy restriction.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who has heart failure and a new prescription for digoxin 0.125 mg PO daily. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include three teaching points.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Digoxin improves the heart's pumping effectiveness and increases cardiac output and stroke volume. It decreases heart rate by slowing depolarization through the SA node, thus allowing more time for the ventricles to fill with blood. Due to these effects, digoxin is used to treat heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and some other tachydysrhythmias.

Complications

The client should monitor for manifestations of digoxin toxicity, which include GI effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), CNS effects (fatigue, weakness), visual effects (yellow-tinged vision, halos around lights, diplopia), heart rate less than 60/ min in adults, or skipped beats when checking the pulse.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor digoxin blood levels periodically during treatment. The expected reference range is 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL.
  • Monitor blood potassium levels because hypokalemia can cause cardiac dysrhythmias, especially in older adult clients. monitoring ECG is also important to check for dysrhythmias.

Client Education

  • Take oral digoxin at the same time each day. Do not skip a dose or take more than the prescribed dose each day.
  • Monitor for manifestations of toxicity.
  • Report any new prescriptions and to contact provider before taking OTC medications, because digoxin interacts with many other substances.
Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 22

Angina

Angina (chest pain from coronary ischemia) is treated with organic nitrates (nitroglycerin — prototype), beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and ranolazine. Goal: decrease myocardial oxygen demand and increase supply. Nitroglycerin remains the cornerstone for acute attacks.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Nitroglycerin (prototype): SL tab/spray for acute attack — take 1 dose, wait 5 min, repeat; if no relief after 3 doses or 15 min → 911. Patch: 10–12 hr on, 12–14 hr off to prevent tolerance. Side effects: headache (common), orthostatic hypotension. AVOID with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) — severe hypotension. Beta blockers + CCBs for chronic angina.

Nitrates

  • Nitroglycerin (NTG): Vasodilation → ↓ preload (mainly) and afterload → ↓ myocardial O2 demand
  • Sublingual: Acute angina — take 1 tab, wait 5 min, take another; max 3 doses; call 911 if no relief
  • SL storage: Original dark glass bottle; replace q6mo (loses potency); should cause slight burning/tingling
  • Patch: Apply hairless skin; remove 12–14 hr/day to prevent tolerance
  • Ointment: Apply paper applicator; do not rub in; wear gloves
  • IV NTG: Glass bottle and tubing (absorbs into PVC); for unstable angina/HF
  • AE: Headache (common — pretreat with acetaminophen), orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia

Drug interactions

  • NEVER combine with PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil/Viagra, tadalafil/Cialis, vardenafil) — severe, prolonged hypotension
  • Caution with alcohol, other antihypertensives

Other anti-anginal agents

  • Beta blockers (metoprolol, atenolol): Reduce HR, contractility — long-term prevention; do not abruptly stop (rebound angina, MI)
  • Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem, amlodipine): For variant (Prinzmetal) angina; vasodilate coronary arteries
  • Ranolazine: For chronic angina unresponsive to standard tx; doesn't affect HR/BP; can prolong QT

Angina types & post-MI medications

  • Stable angina: Predictable pain with exertion, relieved by rest or NTG; chronic CAD
  • Unstable angina: New, worsening, or at rest pain → potential STEMI/NSTEMI; ER, ECG, troponin, aspirin, nitroglycerin, possible heparin, urgent cath
  • Variant (Prinzmetal/vasospastic) angina: Caused by coronary artery spasm (not occlusion); often at rest, sometimes triggered by cold/stress; CCBs are first-line (not beta blockers)
  • NTG sublingual sequence: Sit/lie down (orthostatic hypotension), take 1 SL → wait 5 min → if no relief, call 911 → take 2nd → wait 5 → take 3rd; do not delay 911
  • Post-MI medications (MONA-BASH then home regimen):
  • • Acute: Morphine, Oxygen if hypoxic, Nitroglycerin, Aspirin, Beta blocker, ACE inhibitor, Statin, Heparin/thrombolytic
  • • Discharge regimen: Aspirin (often + P2Y12 inhibitor for 12 months), beta blocker, ACE/ARB, statin, NTG SL PRN
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor/prasugrel after PCI/stent — typically 12 months
  • Ranolazine specifics: Late sodium channel modulator; doesn't change HR or BP (useful when patient can't tolerate beta blocker or CCB); CYP3A4 substrate; QT prolongation
  • Cardiac rehab: Recommended for all MI/CABG patients — exercise prescription, diet, smoking cessation, stress management
A client with angina has chest pain at home. Walk through the correct SL nitroglycerin sequence and the 911 trigger.
(1) Sit or lie down first (orthostatic hypotension risk). (2) Place 1 SL tablet under tongue (let dissolve, do NOT swallow); should feel slight burning/tingling (confirms potency). (3) Wait 5 minutes. If no relief → CALL 911. (4) While waiting: may take a 2nd SL dose, wait 5 min, then a 3rd. Max 3 doses. Older guidance was "3 doses then call 911"; current AHA recommends calling at 5 min/1st-dose failure to avoid delay.
A man with chest pain reports taking sildenafil (Viagra) 12 hours ago. Why is sublingual nitroglycerin contraindicated, and what timing rule applies?
Severe, prolonged hypotension and possible death from synergistic vasodilation — nitrates + PDE-5 inhibitors both potentiate cGMP signaling. Timing rules: avoid nitrates for 24 hours after sildenafil/vardenafil; 48 hours after tadalafil (longer half-life). Always ask men with chest pain about PDE-5 use before giving NTG. Use IV alternatives (non-nitrate vasodilators) or supportive care if NTG is contraindicated.
Why is the nitroglycerin patch removed for 12–14 hours each day, and what storage rules apply to SL tablets?
Patch dosing: apply 10–12 hr on, remove 12–14 hr off (typically overnight) — prevents tolerance, which would render the drug ineffective. SL tablet storage: keep in the original dark glass bottle (light degrades the drug), replace every 6 months after opening, do not mix with other meds in a pill organizer. Slight burning/tingling on the tongue confirms potency. Apply patches to hairless skin; rotate sites.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who has angina pectoris and a new prescription for oral nitroglycerin capsules. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify similarities and differences for the forms of nitroglycerin: oral, sublingual, and transdermal.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects of the medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three nursing actions for clients taking nitroglycerin oral capsules.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Sublingual tablets or spray are used to treat an angina attack after it begins, while the oral tablets, transdermal patch, and transdermal ointment are used for prevention of angina. The capsules and transdermal forms have a slower onset and longer duration of action than the sublingual forms. Sublingual nitroglycerin begins working within 2 min, but the duration of action is only 30 min. Oral forms are taken several times daily, but duration of action is several hours.

Complications

Major adverse effects include headache, dizziness caused by hypotension, and rebound tachycardia.

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach the client that the oral sustained-release form of nitroglycerin should not be used to abort an angina attack. In addition, it should be taken on an empty stomach with at least 8 oz of water and must be swallowed whole.
  • Teach the client not to perform activities that require alertness if dizziness is experienced while taking oral nitroglycerin.
  • The client should inform the provider if headaches are persistent because the dose of nitroglycerin might need to be decreased.
  • The client should inform the provider if tachycardia occurs, because a beta-adrenergic blocker or other medication can be prescribed to slow the pulse rate.
Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 23

Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm

Antidysrhythmics are organized by Vaughan Williams classification: Class I (sodium channel blockers — procainamide, lidocaine, propafenone), Class II (beta blockers — propranolol), Class III (potassium channel blockers — amiodarone), Class IV (calcium channel blockers — verapamil). Plus adenosine and digoxin.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Vaughan Williams classes: I (Na+ block — procainamide, lidocaine), II (β-block — propranolol), III (K+ block — amiodarone), IV (Ca++ block — verapamil). Amiodarone: pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, thyroid (hypo/hyper), corneal deposits, blue-gray skin, photosensitivity, very long half-life (40–60 days). Adenosine: rapid IV push (1–2 sec); brief asystole.

Classes I & II

  • Class I — Sodium channel blockers (slow conduction)
  • Class IA — Procainamide, quinidine, disopyramide: Risk of torsades de pointes; lupus-like syndrome (procainamide)
  • Class IB — Lidocaine (IV only): Ventricular arrhythmias; CNS toxicity (confusion, seizures); narrow TI
  • Class IC — Propafenone, flecainide: Proarrhythmic; avoid in structural heart disease
  • Class II — Beta blockers (propranolol, esmolol, metoprolol): Slow AV conduction; treat SVT, afib rate control; bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypoglycemia masking

Class III & IV

  • Amiodarone (Class III): Most effective antiarrhythmic; treats VT, VF, afib
  • Amiodarone toxicities (MANY): Pulmonary fibrosis (most serious — baseline CXR, PFTs), hepatotoxicity, thyroid dysfunction, corneal microdeposits, photosensitivity, blue-gray skin (slate), bradycardia/heart block
  • Amiodarone half-life: 40–60 days — effects persist long after stopping
  • Sotalol, dofetilide (Class III): QT prolongation; torsades risk
  • Class IV — Verapamil, diltiazem (CCB): SVT, afib rate control; constipation (verapamil), bradycardia, heart block

Other key agents

  • Adenosine: Terminates SVT; very short half-life (10 sec); rapid IV push (1–2 sec) followed by 20 mL saline flush; expect brief asystole; flushing, chest pain
  • Digoxin: Rate control in afib
  • Magnesium sulfate: Torsades de pointes — IV
  • Atropine: Symptomatic bradycardia
List the major long-term toxicities of amiodarone and the recommended monitoring.
(1) Pulmonary fibrosis (most serious — baseline CXR and PFTs, repeat annually; cough/dyspnea is a red flag). (2) Hepatotoxicity (baseline LFTs, q6 mo). (3) Thyroid dysfunction — both hypo and hyper (baseline + q6mo TSH; amiodarone is ~37% iodine by weight). (4) Corneal microdeposits (almost universal; usually asymptomatic — annual ophtho). (5) Photosensitivity + blue-gray skin discoloration (sun protection). (6) Bradycardia/heart block. Half-life is 40–60 days — effects persist long after stopping.
How is adenosine administered for SVT, and what should the nurse warn the client to expect?
Rapid IV push over 1–2 seconds through the most proximal IV site (antecubital ideal), immediately followed by a 20 mL saline flush. Half-life is ~10 seconds — anything slower won't reach the heart in time. Warn the client they will likely feel brief chest pressure, flushing, dyspnea, and "a sense of impending doom" for ~10 seconds; the monitor will show brief asystole (intentional — interrupts the reentry circuit). Have defibrillator at bedside. May need repeat dose at 12 mg.
A client on continuous IV lidocaine for ventricular arrhythmia develops confusion, slurred speech, and twitching. What is happening, and what is the action?
Lidocaine CNS toxicity — lidocaine has a narrow therapeutic index. Progression: perioral numbness → tinnitus → confusion/slurred speech → muscle twitching → seizures → respiratory arrest → cardiac arrest. Action: stop the infusion immediately, notify provider, prepare for seizure precautions (benzo) and cardiac/respiratory support, draw a lidocaine level. Therapeutic range 1.5–5 mcg/mL. Higher risk in liver disease (lidocaine is hepatically cleared).
A client on dofetilide develops torsades de pointes. What is the first-line treatment, and which classes of antiarrhythmics are at highest risk for torsades?
First-line: IV magnesium sulfate (1–2 g IV bolus) — even when serum Mg is normal. Adjuncts: correct hypokalemia, overdrive pacing, defibrillation if pulseless. Stop the offending drug. High-risk antiarrhythmic classes: Class IA (procainamide, quinidine, disopyramide) and Class III (amiodarone less so, but sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide significantly) — all prolong QT. Non-antiarrhythmic culprits: methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol, azoles, fluoroquinolones, macrolides.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is preparing to provide teaching to a client who has a new prescription for verapamil for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify three adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three, including diagnostic tests the nurse should monitor.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and a class IV antidysrhythmic medication that decreases heart rate, slows conduction through both the SA and AV nodes, and decreases force of contraction of the heart. It is used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).

Complications

  • Bradycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Heart failure
  • Constipation

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor both kidney and liver function because the medication dosage might need to be lowered if either kidney or liver impairment are present.
  • Monitor blood pressure and pulse.
  • Monitor periodic ECG testing for dysrhythmias and for improvement of SVT.
  • Assess for manifestations of heart failure, such as dyspnea and crackles in the lungs.
  • Question the client about dizziness, which can occur due to hypotension.
  • Teach the client to move slowly from lying to sitting or standing and to avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until effects of verapamil are known.
Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 24

Antilipemic Agents

Antilipemic medications lower LDL and triglycerides, raise HDL. Statins (atorvastatin — prototype) reduce LDL production and are first-line. Other agents: cholesterol absorption inhibitors (ezetimibe), bile acid sequestrants (colesevelam), fibrates (gemfibrozil), niacin, and PCSK9 inhibitors (alirocumab).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Statins (atorvastatin — prototype): First-line; ↓LDL most; AE: myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain + ↑CK — STOP drug), hepatotoxicity (↑LFTs), Category X — teratogenic. Take in evening (cholesterol synthesis peaks at night). Avoid grapefruit juice. Ezetimibe: blocks intestinal absorption. Bile acid sequestrants (colesevelam): constipation; separate from other meds 4 hr. PCSK9 inhibitors (alirocumab): SC injection.

Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors)

  • Atorvastatin (Lipitor — prototype), simvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin, lovastatin
  • Mechanism: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ hepatic cholesterol synthesis → ↑ LDL receptors → ↓ LDL
  • Take in the evening (cholesterol synthesis higher at night) — except atorvastatin and rosuvastatin (long half-life, anytime)
  • Major AE: Myopathy → rhabdomyolysis — myalgia + ↑ CK (CPK) + dark urine; STOP and call provider
  • Hepatotoxicity: Baseline LFTs, then if symptoms; jaundice, malaise
  • Category X — teratogenic; discontinue before pregnancy
  • AVOID grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibitor — ↑ levels → toxicity)
  • Statin myopathy risk ↑ with fibrates (gemfibrozil), azoles, macrolides

Other lipid-lowering agents

  • Ezetimibe (Zetia): Blocks cholesterol absorption in small intestine; often combined with statin (Vytorin)
  • Bile acid sequestrants — Colesevelam, cholestyramine, colestipol: Bind bile acids; constipation, bloating
  • Separate from other meds by 4 hours — bind/decrease absorption of many drugs
  • Fibrates — Gemfibrozil, fenofibrate: ↓ triglycerides most; gallstones; ↑ myopathy with statins
  • Niacin (nicotinic acid): Flushing (pretreat with aspirin); hepatotoxicity at high doses
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — Alirocumab, evolocumab: SC injection q2wk; very effective LDL ↓; expensive
A client on atorvastatin reports new-onset muscle aches and brown urine. What is happening, what lab confirms it, and what is the action?
Rhabdomyolysis — severe statin myopathy with muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin → brown/cola-colored urine, AKI risk. Lab: markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK/CPK), plus ↑ creatinine, hyperkalemia. Action: STOP the statin immediately, IV hydration, monitor renal function and electrolytes. Risk factors for myopathy: combination with fibrates (gemfibrozil), CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, grapefruit juice), hypothyroidism, advanced age, renal impairment.
When should statins be taken — and which substance must be specifically avoided with simvastatin and lovastatin?
Take in the evening (cholesterol synthesis peaks at night). Exceptions: atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives → may be taken any time. AVOID grapefruit juice with simvastatin and lovastatin (strong CYP3A4 substrates) — grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → ↑ drug levels → ↑ myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are less affected. Statins are Category X — teratogenic; discontinue before pregnancy.
A client takes colesevelam plus several other medications. What is the key teaching about timing?
Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) bind to many other medications in the gut and reduce their absorption — including digoxin, warfarin, levothyroxine, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and thiazide diuretics. Teaching: take other medications at least 1 hour BEFORE or 4 hours AFTER the bile acid sequestrant. Mix powders with full glass of water/juice (never dry). Major AE: constipation, bloating; useful for itching of cholestasis. Niacin: pretreat with aspirin 30 min before to reduce flushing.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is providing care for a client who has elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides, and has a new prescription for atorvastatin once daily. The client has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. What should the nurse teach the client about atorvastatin? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for atorvastatin.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three two tests to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include two teaching points.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Atorvastatin decreases LDL and triglycerides, and elevates hDL. It reduces the risk for cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction) and also provides secondary prevention in clients who have had a cardiovascular event. In clients who have diabetes mellitus and hypertension, atorvastatin can reduce mortality by controlling cholesterol levels.

Complications

  • Muscle pain/tenderness (myopathy)
  • Liver toxicity with findings (jaundice, upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea)

Nursing Interventions

Monitor baseline and periodic cholesterol levels (including LDL, hDL, and triglycerides), creatine kinase levels for myopathy, and liver function tests for liver toxicity.

Client Education

  • Perform additional ways to help decrease cholesterol and improve health (exercise, low-fat diet, weight control, and smoking cessation).
  • Take atorvastatin in the evening without regard to meals. (Antilipemic agents are given in the evening because cholesterol is mostly synthesized during the night.)
Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 25

Medications Affecting Coagulation

Coagulation medications prevent and treat thromboembolic events. Three classes: anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs), antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, abciximab), and thrombolytics (alteplase). All carry significant bleeding risk requiring careful monitoring.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Heparin (parenteral): aPTT 1.5–2× normal (60–80 sec); antidote protamine sulfate; HIT — switch to argatroban. Warfarin (PO): INR 2–3 (or 2.5–3.5 mech valve); antidote vitamin K; many interactions; consistent green leafy vegetable intake. DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban): no routine labs. Antiplatelets: aspirin, clopidogrel. Thrombolytics: alteplase — short window post-stroke/MI.

Heparin & LMWH

  • Heparin (unfractionated): IV continuous or SC; immediate onset
  • Monitor aPTT (therapeutic 1.5–2× control = 60–80 sec); platelet count for HIT
  • Antidote: protamine sulfate
  • HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia): Stop heparin, use argatroban or bivalirudin
  • LMWH — Enoxaparin (Lovenox): SC; no routine labs; abdomen "love handle"; don't expel air bubble; do not rub site
  • Fondaparinux: Synthetic factor Xa inhibitor; no HIT risk

Warfarin & DOACs

  • Warfarin (Coumadin): PO; 3–5 days for full effect; vitamin K antagonist
  • Monitor INR: target 2–3 (DVT/PE/afib); 2.5–3.5 (mechanical heart valve)
  • Antidote: Vitamin K (phytonadione); severe bleed = FFP
  • Consistent intake of vitamin K foods (green leafy vegetables) — not avoid, just consistent
  • Many interactions: Many antibiotics, NSAIDs, herbals (ginkgo, garlic) ↑ INR; rifampin, OCPs, foods ↓ INR
  • Category X — teratogenic
  • DOACs — Dabigatran (direct thrombin), rivaroxaban/apixaban (factor Xa): No labs; idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa for Xa

Antiplatelets & thrombolytics

  • Aspirin: Irreversible COX inhibition; ASA 81 mg daily for cardiovascular prevention; bleeding, GI ulcer, Reye syndrome (children)
  • Clopidogrel (Plavix), prasugrel, ticagrelor: P2Y12 inhibitors; post-stent placement
  • Abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors; IV for ACS
  • Thrombolytics — Alteplase (tPA), tenecteplase: Acute MI within 12 hr; ischemic stroke within 3 hr (up to 4.5); PE
  • Thrombolytic contraindications: Active bleeding, recent surgery, recent hemorrhagic stroke, severe HTN

Other antiplatelets & specifics

  • Dipyridamole (Persantine): Antiplatelet + vasodilator; combined with aspirin (Aggrenox) for stroke prevention; caution in angina (steal phenomenon)
  • Cilostazol, pentoxifylline: Intermittent claudication (PAD)
  • Heparin reversal step-by-step: Calculate based on time since heparin dose; protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units heparin remaining (max 50 mg/dose)
  • Warfarin reversal: Low INR no bleed = hold + reduce dose; high INR no bleed = oral vit K; bleeding = IV vit K + FFP or PCC; major bleed = 4-factor PCC (faster than FFP)
A client is on IV heparin. What lab is monitored, what is the therapeutic target, and what is the antidote for major bleeding?
Lab: aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time). Therapeutic target: 1.5–2× the control value, typically 60–80 seconds. Also monitor platelets (HIT risk). Antidote: protamine sulfate — 1 mg per 100 units of heparin still in circulation; max 50 mg per dose. For LMWH (enoxaparin), protamine only partially reverses (~60%). DOACs: dabigatran reversed by idarucizumab; factor Xa inhibitors by andexanet alfa.
A client on day 6 of heparin therapy has a platelet drop from 230,000 to 80,000 with new thrombosis. What is the diagnosis, and what is the management?
Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) — paradoxical: heparin antibodies activate platelets, causing thrombosis (often arterial, limb-threatening) despite low count. Typically occurs day 5–10 with platelet drop ≥50% from baseline. Management: STOP all heparin (including flushes!), do NOT give platelets (worsens thrombosis), start a direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban or bivalirudin), avoid heparin for life. Future surgeries/procedures: alert team and use non-heparin anticoagulation.
A client on warfarin has an INR of 4.2 with no bleeding. What are the standard INR targets, and what is the management here?
Standard targets: INR 2.0–3.0 for atrial fibrillation, DVT/PE prevention/treatment; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical heart valves. INR 4.2 with no bleed: hold the next 1–2 doses, reduce maintenance dose, recheck INR in a few days. If higher (5–10) no bleed: add oral vitamin K. Any major bleed: IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (faster than FFP). Warfarin = Category X. Many interactions: NSAIDs/herbals/antibiotics ↑ INR; rifampin/St. John's wort ↓ INR.
A client newly started on warfarin asks if they should avoid spinach and kale. What is the correct teaching?
Maintain CONSISTENT intake of vitamin-K-rich foods (spinach, kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, collards) — not avoid them. The dose is calibrated to the client's usual diet; sudden binges or eliminations swing INR. Other teaching: avoid alcohol, use a soft toothbrush and electric razor, no aspirin/NSAIDs/herbals without provider OK (ginkgo, garlic, ginger, ginseng — "the 4 G's" — increase bleeding), get regular INR checks, wear medical alert ID, report unusual bruising/bleeding/dark stools/headaches.
A client presents 90 minutes after onset of left-sided weakness. What is the time window for IV alteplase (tPA) in ischemic stroke, and what conditions absolutely contraindicate it?
IV alteplase window for ischemic stroke: 3 hours from onset (up to 4.5 hours for selected patients). Must rule out hemorrhagic stroke with non-contrast CT first. Absolute contraindications: active bleeding, recent intracranial/spinal surgery or trauma (within 3 mo), prior intracranial hemorrhage, intracranial neoplasm/aneurysm/AVM, current severe HTN (>185/110 unresponsive to treatment), suspected aortic dissection. For MI, alteplase window is up to 12 hours (PCI preferred when available).

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for clopidogrel following a myocardial infarction. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the intended effect.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects for this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three, including one test the nurse should monitor periodically.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Clopidogrel inhibits platelet aggregation and prolongs bleeding time. It is used to prevent myocardial infarction (mI) or stroke in clients who have already had an mI or stroke.

Complications

Like other platelet inhibitors, clopidogrel can cause bleeding due to thrombocytopenia. It can also cause GI effects (abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea).

Nursing Interventions

  • The nurse should plan to monitor the platelet count periodically while the client takes clopidogrel.
  • Teach the client to monitor for bleeding. The client should watch for black stools, coffee-ground emesis, blood in the urine, nose bleeds, unusual bruising, or petechiae. The client should inform the provider if these occur and about GI effects.
  • The nurse should be aware of all medications the client is taking, because risk for bleeding increases if the medication is taken with anticoagulants or antiplatelet medications. Clopidogrel is sometimes administered concurrently with aspirin, and that increases the risk for bleeding. The medication should be discontinued 7 days before any elective surgery.
Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 26

Growth Factors

Hematopoietic growth factors stimulate production of specific blood cells: erythropoietin (epoetin alfa) for RBCs, granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (filgrastim, sargramostim) for WBCs, and thrombopoietin agonists (oprelvekin, romiplostim) for platelets. Used in anemia of chronic disease, chemo-induced cytopenias.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Epoetin alfa (Epogen, Procrit): SC/IV for anemia (CKD, chemo, HIV); target Hgb < 11–12 (higher = stroke/MI/death). Filgrastim (Neupogen): SC for chemo-induced neutropenia; bone pain common. Sargramostim (Leukine): bone marrow transplant recovery. Oprelvekin, romiplostim: thrombopoietic agents for thrombocytopenia.

Erythropoietin & RBC growth factors

  • Epoetin alfa, darbepoetin: Stimulate RBC production; treat anemia in CKD, chemo, HIV
  • Target Hgb: 10–11 g/dL — higher levels associated with cardiovascular events
  • Black box warning: ↑ risk of stroke, MI, tumor progression at higher Hgb
  • AE: HTN, headache; ensure adequate iron stores (ferritin) before initiation
  • Subcutaneous typically; do NOT shake vials

WBC growth factors

  • Filgrastim (G-CSF): Stimulates neutrophil production; chemo-induced neutropenia
  • Pegfilgrastim: Long-acting (single dose per chemo cycle)
  • Sargramostim (GM-CSF): Broader effect on multiple WBC lines; post-bone marrow transplant
  • AE: Bone pain (very common — pretreat with acetaminophen), leukocytosis, splenic rupture (rare)
  • Monitor CBC with differential

Platelet growth factors

  • Oprelvekin (IL-11): Stimulates megakaryocytes; for chemo-induced thrombocytopenia
  • Romiplostim, eltrombopag: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists for ITP
  • AE: Fluid retention, edema, thromboembolism risk
A client with CKD is started on epoetin alfa for anemia. What is the target Hgb, and what is the black-box warning if it goes too high?
Target Hgb: 10–11 g/dL (some sources 11–12). Black-box warning: Hgb > 11 g/dL is associated with increased cardiovascular events — stroke, MI, thrombosis, death — and tumor progression in cancer clients. Other key points: check iron stores (ferritin, transferrin saturation) before starting — no point stimulating production without raw material; monitor BP (HTN is common); do NOT shake vials (denatures protein); typically SC or IV.
A client on filgrastim after chemo reports severe bone pain in the sternum, pelvis, and long bones. Is this expected, and what is the management?
Yes — expected and very common. Bone pain occurs because filgrastim (G-CSF) stimulates rapid marrow expansion. Pain is often most felt in highly cellular bones (sternum, ribs, pelvis, femurs). Management: pretreat with acetaminophen 30–60 min before dose; NSAIDs and antihistamines (loratadine) also used; opioids if severe. Monitor CBC with differential — goal ANC > 1,500. Rare AE: splenic rupture (sudden L upper-quadrant or shoulder-tip pain — emergency).
When is romiplostim or eltrombopag used, and what is the major risk?
Thrombopoietin receptor agonists used for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) that has failed steroids/splenectomy/IVIG. Romiplostim is SC weekly; eltrombopag is PO daily. Major risks: thromboembolism (paradoxical — even with low platelets, hyperstimulation can cause clots), bone marrow fibrosis with long-term use, hepatotoxicity (eltrombopag). Monitor platelet count weekly initially. Stop if platelets exceed target (~50,000) to avoid thrombosis.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has chronic kidney disease and a new prescription for subcutaneous epoetin alfa three times weekly. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify why epoetin alfa would benefit this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe four, including two tests the nurse should monitor periodically.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Erythropoietin, a substance that stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells, is produced by the kidney. In clients who have chronic kidney disease, erythropoietin is no longer present and anemia results. Epoetin alfa stimulates production of red blood cells in these clients.

Complications

  • Headaches and myalgia (body aches)
  • Thrombotic events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke
  • Hypertension (common, sometimes serious)
  • A too-rapid increase (hgb greater than 1 g/dL over 2 weeks, or hgb greater than 10 g/dL) can worsen hypertension, increase risk of thrombosis, and cause seizures.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor baseline iron levels, CBC with differential, and platelet count.
  • Monitor hgb and hct twice weekly until blood counts stabilize.
  • Calculate dosages carefully. Both subcutaneous and IV epoetin alfa have dosages based on the client's weight. Do not shake the epoetin alfa vial, and discard vial after one dose is removed.
  • Monitor blood pressure carefully, and report increases to the provider. Question the client about frequency and severity of headaches, which could be an indication of increasing blood pressure or a simple adverse effect.
Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 27

Blood and Blood Products

Blood and blood products replace deficient components: packed RBCs (anemia, blood loss), platelets (thrombocytopenia, bleeding), fresh frozen plasma (clotting factor deficiency), cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen, factor VIII). Strict transfusion protocols prevent acute and delayed reactions.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Verify identity with 2 people, 2 identifiers, blood band match. Y-site only with 0.9% NS — never D5W or LR (hemolysis). Stay with client first 15 min; vital signs: baseline, 15 min, then per protocol. Complete within 4 hr. Acute hemolytic reaction (ABO mismatch — fever, chills, back pain, dark urine, shock) → STOP, NS, call provider. FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets for specific deficiencies.

Pre-transfusion safety

  • Verify with two licensed staff: Client identity (two identifiers), blood band, unit number, ABO/Rh, expiration, crossmatch
  • Obtain informed consent; assess history of prior reactions
  • Establish IV access with large-bore (18-20 gauge); use blood tubing with filter
  • Compatible with 0.9% NS ONLY — D5W and LR cause hemolysis
  • Baseline vital signs and temperature; complete within 4 hours of leaving blood bank

Monitoring & reactions

  • Start slowly (~2 mL/min); stay with client first 15 min — most reactions occur early
  • Vital signs: baseline, 15 min, then per facility (often hourly), at completion
  • Acute hemolytic reaction (ABO mismatch): Fever, chills, low back/flank pain, hematuria, hypotension, shock → STOP immediately, infuse NS through new line, save bag/tubing
  • Febrile non-hemolytic: Fever, chills, headache; STOP, treat symptomatically
  • Mild allergic: Hives, itching → slow rate, give diphenhydramine, may resume
  • Anaphylaxis: Severe — STOP, epinephrine, support
  • TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury): Dyspnea, hypoxia within 6 hr — STOP, respiratory support
  • Circulatory overload (TACO): Slow rate, sit up, diuretic

Component therapy

  • Packed RBCs: Anemia, blood loss; raises Hgb 1 g/dL per unit
  • Platelets: Thrombocytopenia, active bleeding; rapid infusion (under 30 min); ABO ideally matched but not required
  • FFP: Clotting factor replacement (warfarin reversal urgent, DIC, liver failure); must be ABO-compatible
  • Cryoprecipitate: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF — DIC, hemophilia A
  • Albumin: Volume expander; hypovolemia, hypoalbuminemia
Walk through the pre-transfusion verification process and the IV/fluid requirements.
Two licensed staff verify at bedside: two client identifiers (name + DOB), blood band number, unit number, ABO + Rh type, expiration, crossmatch label. Obtain informed consent and recent transfusion history. IV access: large-bore 18–20 gauge; blood tubing with filter. Compatible fluid: 0.9% Normal Saline ONLY — never D5W or LR (cause hemolysis). Baseline vitals + temperature. Must complete within 4 hours of leaving blood bank.
Five minutes into a PRBC transfusion, a client reports back pain, fever, and chills with hypotension. What is happening, and what is the immediate action sequence?
Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO mismatch) — life-threatening. Action sequence: (1) STOP the transfusion immediately at the IV port (do not flush the line — could push more blood). (2) Maintain IV access with 0.9% NS through a NEW line/tubing. (3) Notify provider and blood bank. (4) Save the bag, tubing, and a fresh blood sample for the blood bank to investigate. (5) Monitor: vitals, urine output (hematuria, oliguria — risk of AKI), respiratory status. Treat shock; may need vasopressors.
Why is the first 15 minutes of any transfusion so critical, and what is the standard vital-sign timing?
Most acute transfusion reactions occur within the first 15 minutes — acute hemolytic, anaphylaxis, severe febrile non-hemolytic. The nurse stays with the client throughout these 15 minutes and runs the transfusion slowly (~2 mL/min). Vital signs: baseline → 15 minutes → per facility protocol (often hourly) → at completion → 30–60 min post. Document all values. After 15 min uneventful: increase rate to complete within the 4-hour window.
Differentiate TRALI from TACO during a transfusion: presentation, timing, and management.
TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury): non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema from donor antibodies; sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates within 6 hr; BP usually normal/low. Management: STOP transfusion, respiratory support, often intubation; diuretics NOT helpful. TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload): volume overload; dyspnea, hypertension, JVD, crackles; risk higher in cardiac/renal disease and elderly. Management: slow or stop transfusion, sit client up, O₂, IV diuretic (furosemide).

Scenario

A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to a client who has who has a GI bleed and hgb 6.0 g/dL. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Therapeutic Procedure to complete this item.

  • INDICATIONS: What assessment data would indicate to the nurse that transfusion of PRBCs is indicated in this client?
Show key

Indications

A client who lost blood from a GI bleed can need a unit of PRBCs for a hgb level below 10 g/dL especially if demonstrating manifestations of hypovolemia (increase in pulse and respiration rate; decrease in blood pressure; low oxygen saturation; cool and pale or cyanotic; increased capillary refill time; increased urinary output). If hypoxic, the client will exhibit decreased level of consciousness and confusion. PRBCs restore red blood cells and improve oxygenation. If the client has lost a large amount of fluid volume, whole blood, rather than PRBCs, can be indicated.

Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 28

Peptic Ulcer Disease

Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and GERD are treated by reducing gastric acid and protecting the mucosa. Categories: H2 receptor antagonists (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine), proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole — most effective), mucosal protectants (sucralfate, misoprostol), and antacids.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

H2 blockers (cimetidine, famotidine, ranitidine) — "-tidine": ↓ acid secretion; cimetidine has many drug interactions. PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) — "-prazole": most effective; long-term: ↓ B12, ↑ fracture risk, C. difficile, pneumonia, hypomagnesemia. Sucralfate: coats ulcer; 1 hr before meals, empty stomach. Misoprostol: NSAID-induced ulcer prevention; Category X — abortifacient.

Acid-suppressive therapy

  • H2 antagonists — Cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine ("-tidine")
  • Cimetidine: Many interactions (CYP450 inhibitor); gynecomastia, impotence; avoid in older adults
  • Famotidine = preferred H2 blocker (fewer interactions)
  • PPIs — Omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole ("-prazole")
  • Most effective — block H+/K+ ATPase pump
  • Take before meals; do not crush enteric-coated; can sprinkle granules on applesauce
  • Long-term AE: ↓ B12 absorption, ↑ hip/spine fracture, hypomagnesemia, ↑ C. diff infection, pneumonia, rebound hypersecretion when stopped

Mucosal protectants & antacids

  • Sucralfate (Carafate): Forms protective barrier over ulcer
  • Take 1 hour before meals and at bedtime on empty stomach; separate from other meds by 2 hr (decreases absorption)
  • Antacids — Aluminum hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate: Neutralize acid
  • Aluminum: Constipation; Magnesium: Diarrhea (often combined); Calcium: Rebound acid, hypercalcemia
  • Separate antacids from other meds by 1–2 hr
  • Misoprostol (Cytotec): PG E1 analog; prevents NSAID-induced ulcers; CATEGORY X — abortifacient — pregnancy test before; effective contraception

H. pylori eradication

  • Triple therapy: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole) × 10–14 days
  • Quadruple therapy: PPI + bismuth subsalicylate + tetracycline + metronidazole × 10–14 days
  • Confirm eradication with urea breath test or stool antigen 4+ weeks after
A client has been on omeprazole for 3 years for GERD. What long-term adverse effects must be monitored or counseled about?
Chronic PPI use is associated with: ↓ vitamin B12 absorption (acid needed to free B12 from food protein — check B12 levels), ↑ hip/spine fracture risk (↓ calcium absorption), hypomagnesemia (can be severe → tetany, seizures), ↑ C. difficile infection, ↑ community-acquired pneumonia, possible association with chronic kidney disease and dementia. Rebound hyperacidity when stopped abruptly → taper PPIs after long-term use. Consider periodic deprescribing if no longer indicated.
A client is prescribed sucralfate (Carafate) along with several other medications. What is the timing rule, and why?
Sucralfate works by forming a protective barrier over the ulcer crater when activated by stomach acid. Take 1 hour BEFORE meals and at bedtime, on an EMPTY stomach. Separate from other medications by at least 2 hours — sucralfate binds and reduces absorption of digoxin, warfarin, phenytoin, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine, and tetracyclines. AE: constipation. Caution in renal failure (contains aluminum which can accumulate).
What is the standard H. pylori eradication regimen, and how is treatment success confirmed?
Triple therapy × 10–14 days: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole if penicillin-allergic). Quadruple therapy (for resistance or treatment failure): PPI + bismuth subsalicylate + tetracycline + metronidazole. Confirm eradication 4+ weeks after completing therapy: urea breath test or stool antigen test (stop PPI 2 weeks before testing, or false negative). Serology stays positive after eradication — not useful for confirmation. Teach client to complete entire course.
A 28-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on chronic NSAIDs is prescribed misoprostol. What is the critical safety screen, and what is the pregnancy category?
Pregnancy test required before starting and effective contraception throughout treatment. Misoprostol is Category X — abortifacient (used off-label for medical abortion and labor induction); causes uterine contractions and bleeding. Used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers in high-risk patients. AE: diarrhea, abdominal cramps. Discuss alternative GI protection in women of reproductive age (PPI is usually preferred for this indication).

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who has a prescription for calcium carbonate. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use of calcium carbonate.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify three instructions the nurse should include regarding taking this medication. on Exercises
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Calcium carbonate is an antacid that raises the ph of gastric contents, which reduces irritation of stomach mucosa, resulting in relief of pain.

Client Education

  • Shake liquid suspensions prior to taking each dose in order to disperse the medication.
  • Take other medications at least 1 hr before or after taking aluminum hydroxide.
  • Calcium carbonate can cause constipation. Notify the provider if it persists. You might need to alternate this antacid with one that is a magnesium compound and has diarrhea as an adverse effect.
  • Report manifestations of hypercalcemia (constipation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion) to the provider.
Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 29

Gastrointestinal Disorders

GI medications include antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), antidiarrheals (diphenoxylate, loperamide), laxatives (psyllium, docusate, bisacodyl, lactulose, polyethylene glycol), prokinetic agents, IBS therapies (alosetron, lubiprostone), and IBD medications (sulfasalazine, glucocorticoids, biologics).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Antiemetics: ondansetron (5-HT3 — QT prolongation), metoclopramide (EPS, tardive dyskinesia), prochlorperazine (EPS, sedation), scopolamine (motion sickness). Antidiarrheals: loperamide, diphenoxylate. Laxatives: bulk (psyllium), surfactant (docusate), stimulant (bisacodyl), osmotic (lactulose, PEG), saline (Mg hydroxide). IBS: alosetron (women, severe IBS-D — black box for ischemic colitis); lubiprostone. IBD: sulfasalazine, biologics.

Antiemetics

  • 5-HT3 antagonists — Ondansetron (Zofran), granisetron, palonosetron: Chemo-induced N/V, post-op
  • Ondansetron AE: Headache, constipation, QT prolongation — caution with other QT-prolonging drugs
  • Metoclopramide (Reglan): Prokinetic; for diabetic gastroparesis, post-op; EPS reactions, tardive dyskinesia (black box); limit to 12 weeks
  • Phenothiazines — Prochlorperazine, promethazine: Sedation, EPS, anticholinergic; IV promethazine = tissue damage if extravasates
  • Scopolamine: Anticholinergic patch behind ear for motion sickness; dry mouth, drowsiness
  • Cannabinoids — Dronabinol: Chemo-induced N/V, AIDS-related anorexia

Diarrhea, constipation, IBS

  • Antidiarrheals — Loperamide (Imodium), diphenoxylate/atropine (Lomotil): Slow GI motility
  • Bulk-forming laxatives — Psyllium, methylcellulose: Take with plenty of water (obstruction risk)
  • Surfactant — Docusate: Stool softener
  • Stimulant — Bisacodyl, senna: Short-term; risk of dependence with chronic use
  • Osmotic — Lactulose, polyethylene glycol (PEG/MiraLAX), magnesium hydroxide: Draw water into bowel; lactulose also reduces ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy
  • Alosetron (Lotronex): Severe IBS-D in women only; BLACK BOX — ischemic colitis; restricted prescribing
  • Lubiprostone (Amitiza): Chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS-C

IBD & emetic agents

  • Sulfasalazine (Azulfidine): Mild-moderate UC, RA; sulfa allergy contraindicated; folic acid deficiency; orange-yellow body fluids
  • Mesalamine: 5-ASA derivative; UC
  • Glucocorticoids — Prednisone, budesonide: Acute exacerbations
  • Biologics — Infliximab, adalimumab: Refractory IBD; infection risk
  • Emetics — Syrup of ipecac: No longer recommended for most ingestions
What is the black-box warning for metoclopramide (Reglan), and what is the maximum treatment duration?
Tardive dyskinesia — involuntary, repetitive movements (lip-smacking, tongue protrusion, choreoathetoid limbs) — often irreversible even after stopping the drug. Risk increases with cumulative dose and duration. Maximum recommended duration: 12 weeks. Other EPS reactions (acute dystonia, parkinsonism) can also occur. Used for diabetic gastroparesis, post-op N/V, GERD; avoid in Parkinson disease. Diphenhydramine can treat acute dystonia.
Ondansetron is highly effective for chemo-induced N/V. What is the major cardiac concern, and what drugs combine dangerously with it?
QT prolongation → risk of torsades de pointes, especially at higher IV doses. Single IV dose limit was reduced to 16 mg by FDA for this reason. Higher risk combinations: other QT-prolonging drugs — methadone, haloperidol, fluoroquinolones, macrolides (azithromycin), azole antifungals, amiodarone/sotalol, TCAs. Baseline ECG and electrolytes (K, Mg) for high-risk patients; correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia before dosing. Other AE: headache, constipation.

Scenario

Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis

Complications

Complications that occur with the use of sulfasalazine include agranulocytosis, and hemolytic and macrocytic anemia.

Medication Administration

The client should take sulfasalazine four times per day in divided doses.

Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 30

Vitamins and Minerals

Vitamins and minerals correct deficiencies: iron (ferrous sulfate) for iron-deficiency anemia, B12 (cyanocobalamin) for pernicious anemia, folic acid for megaloblastic anemia and pregnancy, potassium chloride for hypokalemia. Each has specific administration considerations and monitoring needs.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Iron (ferrous sulfate): empty stomach with vitamin C; dark/tarry stools normal; liquid stains teeth (use straw); IM by Z-track only. B12 (cyanocobalamin): pernicious anemia → lifelong IM/intranasal. Folic acid: pregnancy 600–800 mcg/day to prevent neural tube defects; megaloblastic anemia. K+ (KCl): NEVER IV push; max 10 mEq/hr peripheral, 20 mEq/hr central; PO with food to avoid GI upset.

Iron

  • Ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, ferrous fumarate (PO): Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Take on empty stomach for max absorption (or with food if GI upset)
  • Vitamin C (orange juice) ↑ absorption; antacids, dairy, tea, coffee ↓ absorption
  • Dark/tarry stools are NORMAL (not melena)
  • Liquid forms stain teeth — dilute, use straw, rinse mouth
  • IM iron dextran: Z-track injection to prevent staining; risk of anaphylaxis (test dose first)
  • Monitor reticulocyte count (responds in 1 week)

B12 & folic acid

  • Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin): Pernicious anemia (lack of intrinsic factor)
  • Pernicious anemia = LIFELONG IM (or intranasal); PO ineffective for malabsorption
  • Monitor reticulocytes; treat hypokalemia that may occur with reticulocyte response
  • Folic acid (folate): Megaloblastic anemia, malabsorption, pregnancy
  • Pregnancy: 600–800 mcg/day — prevents neural tube defects (start before conception)
  • NEVER give folic acid alone for B12 deficiency — masks anemia but neurologic damage progresses

Electrolytes — Potassium chloride

  • NEVER push IV potassium — fatal cardiac arrhythmia
  • Peripheral IV: max 10 mEq/hr
  • Central line: max 20 mEq/hr (or per facility)
  • Always use infusion pump
  • Burning at IV site = slow rate, change site, evaluate concentration
  • PO KCl: Take with full glass of water, with food; do not crush sustained-release
  • Monitor for hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, arrhythmias
A client is prescribed ferrous sulfate (PO) for iron-deficiency anemia. What enhances absorption, what reduces it, and what side effects should be expected?
Enhances absorption: take on an empty stomach with vitamin C (orange juice) — acidic environment ↑ ferrous form absorption. Reduces absorption: antacids, dairy, tea, coffee, calcium, fiber, certain antibiotics — separate by 2 hr. Expected: dark or tarry stools are NORMAL (not melena), GI upset (may take with food if needed). Liquid forms stain teeth — dilute, use a straw, rinse mouth after. IM iron dextran: Z-track technique only + test dose first (anaphylaxis risk).
What are the absolute rules for IV potassium chloride administration?
NEVER IV push — fatal cardiac arrhythmia (asystole). Always use an infusion pump, never gravity. Peripheral line: max 10 mEq/hr. Central line: max 20 mEq/hr (or per facility/critical care protocol). Always dilute. Burning at the IV site: slow the rate, evaluate concentration, consider site change. PO KCl: take with a full glass of water and food; do not crush sustained-release. Monitor for hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, wide QRS, weakness, paresthesias. Antidote for hyperkalemic emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilization) + insulin/D50 + albuterol + Kayexalate/Lokelma.

Scenario

A nurse is educating a client about a new prescription for cyanocobalamin. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe four teaching points for the client.
  • EVALUATION OF MEDICATION EFFECTIVENESS: Describe two nursing interventions.
Show key

Expected Pharmacological Action

Cyanocobalamin converts folic acid from an inactive form to an active form. It corrects megaloblastic anemia related to a deficiency of vitamin B12.

Client Education

  • Review manifestations of hypokalemia.
  • Discuss the use of potassium supplements, if prescribed.
  • Discuss dietary sources of potassium.
  • Consume foods high in vitamin B12.
  • Administer intranasal cyanocobalamin 1 hr before or after eating hot foods when nasal secretions are decreased.
  • Periodic laboratory testing of hgb, hct, RBC, reticulocyte count, and folate levels is advised.

Evaluation Of Medication Effectiveness

  • Review laboratory values for increased reticulocyte count and macrocytes and hgb and hct levels within the expected reference range.
  • Assess for improvement of neurologic manifestations (numbness, tingling of hands and feet).
Unit 7 · Reproductive · Chapter 31

Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract

Reproductive medications include: estrogens and progestins (combined oral contraceptives, HRT), androgens (testosterone), drugs for BPH (finasteride, tamsulosin), erectile dysfunction (sildenafil, tadalafil), and infertility agents (clomiphene, gonadotropins).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Combined OCPs (estrogen + progestin): ACHES warning (Abdominal pain, Chest pain, Headache, Eye changes, Severe leg pain); avoid in smokers > 35 yo, history of VTE/MI/stroke. Progestin-only: safer in lactation. HRT: shortest duration possible; ↑ DVT/stroke/breast cancer. Testosterone: controlled substance; gel — risk of transfer to others. BPH: finasteride (5α-reductase), tamsulosin (α1 blocker). ED: sildenafil — NEVER with nitrates.

Oral contraceptives & HRT

  • Combined OCPs (estrogen + progestin): Most effective with consistent use
  • ACHES warning signs: Abdominal pain (liver/gallbladder), Chest pain (PE/MI), Headache (stroke), Eye changes (stroke/clot), Severe leg pain (DVT)
  • Contraindicated: Smokers > 35 yo, history of VTE/MI/stroke, breast cancer, severe HTN, migraine with aura, pregnancy
  • Progestin-only ("mini-pill"): Less effective; safer during lactation; must take same time every day
  • HRT (post-menopause): Shortest effective dose, shortest duration; ↑ DVT, stroke, breast cancer (combined), endometrial cancer (estrogen alone — protect with progestin if uterus intact)
  • Long-acting: Depo-Provera (medroxyprogesterone IM q3mo), Nexplanon implant, IUDs (hormonal Mirena, copper)

Androgens

  • Testosterone: Hypogonadism, gender-affirming care; Schedule III
  • Gel: Apply to dry skin (chest/shoulders); wash hands; cover with clothing to prevent transfer to others (especially children, women)
  • AE: ↑ lipids, polycythemia (monitor H&H), acne, prostatic enlargement, gynecomastia
  • Patch: Rotate sites; do not apply to scrotum (most products)

BPH & erectile dysfunction

  • 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors — Finasteride, dutasteride: Shrink prostate over months
  • Pregnant women should not handle crushed/broken tablets — Category X teratogen
  • Alpha-1 blockers — Tamsulosin (Flomax), doxazosin, terazosin: Relax bladder neck; orthostatic hypotension; cataract surgery interaction (intraoperative floppy iris)
  • PDE-5 inhibitors — Sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), vardenafil: Vasodilation in penis
  • NEVER combine with nitrates or alpha-blockers (severe hypotension)
  • Priapism > 4 hr = emergency
  • Vision changes (NAION) — discontinue
A woman calls her clinic with new-onset severe headache while on combined OCPs. What mnemonic identifies serious warning signs, and what are the absolute contraindications to combined OCPs?
ACHES mnemonic — call provider/seek care immediately for: Abdominal pain (liver/gallbladder), Chest pain (PE/MI), Headache (stroke), Eye changes (stroke/clot), Severe leg pain (DVT). Absolute contraindications: smoker > 35 yo, history of VTE/MI/stroke, breast cancer, severe HTN, migraine with aura, pregnancy. Progestin-only pill (mini-pill) is safer in lactation but must be taken at the exact same time daily.
A pharmacy tech is asked to crush a finasteride tablet for a man with swallowing difficulty. Why is this a safety problem?
Finasteride and dutasteride (5-α-reductase inhibitors for BPH) are Category X teratogens. Pregnant or potentially pregnant women must NOT handle crushed/broken tablets — the drug can absorb through skin and cause genital malformations in a male fetus. Same caution applies to women planning pregnancy when handling a partner's medication. Tablets should be swallowed whole. Tamsulosin (α-1 blocker for BPH): teach orthostatic hypotension precautions, alert ophthalmologist before cataract surgery (floppy iris syndrome).
A 60-year-old man with stable angina is prescribed sildenafil for erectile dysfunction. What two drug classes must be absolutely avoided, and what emergency must clients be taught to recognize?
NEVER combine PDE-5 inhibitors with (1) nitrates (any form — SL, IV, patch, ointment, recreational "poppers") or (2) alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, doxazosin) without strict timing — both cause severe, prolonged, potentially fatal hypotension. Emergency to teach: priapism > 4 hours — painful erection that won't resolve; requires emergent urology care to prevent permanent tissue damage. Also: sudden vision loss (NAION) → discontinue and seek care.

Show key

Expected Pharmacological Action

Finasteride slows the production of testosterone, which reduces the size of the prostate and subsequently promotes urinary elimination.

Complications

  • Decreased libido
  • Decreased ejaculate volume
  • Gynecomastia
  • Orthostatic hypotension
Unit 7 · Reproductive · Chapter 32

Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery

Labor and delivery medications: oxytocin (induction, augmentation, postpartum hemorrhage), tocolytics (terbutaline, magnesium sulfate, nifedipine), prostaglandins for cervical ripening (misoprostol, dinoprostone), and analgesics (fentanyl epidural, opioid IV).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Oxytocin (Pitocin): Induction/augmentation of labor, postpartum hemorrhage; tachysystole (>5 contractions/10 min) — stop; uterine rupture; water intoxication. Tocolytics: magnesium sulfate (preterm labor, eclampsia prophylaxis — antidote calcium gluconate); terbutaline (β2 agonist — tachycardia, hyperglycemia); nifedipine; indomethacin. Cervical ripening: misoprostol, dinoprostone (no concurrent oxytocin within hours).

Oxytocin

  • Uses: Induce/augment labor, treat postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), milk ejection
  • Administration: IV piggyback diluted; titrate to effective contraction pattern
  • Tachysystole (more than 5 contractions in 10 min averaged over 30 min): Stop infusion, reposition, IV fluid bolus, O2; tocolytic if needed
  • Non-reassuring FHR: Stop oxytocin immediately
  • Uterine rupture: Sudden severe pain, loss of contractions, fetal distress, hypotension — emergency C-section
  • Water intoxication (with prolonged high doses): Headache, confusion, hyponatremia — limit IV fluids
  • Postpartum oxytocin: 20 units in 1 L LR/NS at brisk rate after delivery to control bleeding

Tocolytics

  • Magnesium sulfate (IV): Tocolysis (preterm labor up to 32 wk), seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia, fetal neuroprotection
  • Magnesium therapeutic 4–7 mEq/L; toxicity = ↓ reflexes, ↓ RR <12, ↓ urine output, mental status changes
  • Antidote: Calcium gluconate IV
  • Terbutaline (β2 agonist): SC for preterm labor; AE: maternal tachycardia, palpitations, hyperglycemia, pulmonary edema; FDA black box — not for prolonged use (>48–72 hr)
  • Nifedipine (CCB): Preterm labor; maternal hypotension
  • Indomethacin (NSAID): Preterm labor <32 wk; risk premature ductus arteriosus closure

Cervical ripening & analgesia

  • Misoprostol (Cytotec): PG E1; cervical ripening, induction, PPH; cheap and effective
  • Dinoprostone (Cervidil insert, Prepidil gel): PG E2; cervical ripening
  • Prostaglandins: Watch for tachysystole, fetal distress; wait 4–6 hr after prostaglandin before oxytocin
  • Methylergonovine (Methergine): IM for PPH; contraindicated in HTN, preeclampsia
  • Carboprost (Hemabate): IM for PPH; contraindicated in asthma
  • Labor analgesia: Epidural fentanyl/bupivacaine; IV opioids (limit late in labor — neonatal respiratory depression)
During an oxytocin induction, the FHR strip shows 6 contractions in a 10-minute period averaged over 30 minutes. What is this called, and what is the action sequence?
Tachysystole (>5 contractions/10 min averaged over 30 min). Action sequence: (1) Stop the oxytocin infusion, (2) reposition to left lateral, (3) IV fluid bolus of LR, (4) administer oxygen via face mask at 10 L/min if non-reassuring FHR, (5) notify provider. If persistent: tocolytic (terbutaline 0.25 mg SC). Watch for uterine rupture (sudden severe pain, loss of contractions, fetal distress, maternal hypotension → emergency C-section).
A woman is receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia. What are the toxicity signs by mag level, and what is the antidote?
Therapeutic range: 4–7 mEq/L. Toxicity signs (in order as level rises): loss of deep tendon reflexes (first warning — assess patellar reflex frequently), respiratory depression (RR <12), decreased urine output (<30 mL/hr — mag is renally cleared), mental status changes, cardiac arrest at very high levels. Antidote: IV calcium gluconate 10% (1 g IV over 3 min). Always have calcium gluconate at the bedside during mag infusions. Also used for fetal neuroprotection in preterm labor.
A nurse is preparing to give methylergonovine (Methergine) for postpartum hemorrhage. What single vital sign must always be checked first, and what other PPH agent is contraindicated in asthma?
Check BP before every dose — methylergonovine is contraindicated in HTN, preeclampsia, eclampsia because it causes severe vasoconstriction. Hold if BP > 140/90 and notify provider. Causes nausea — antiemetic often given with. Carboprost (Hemabate) is the other major PPH med — contraindicated in asthma (causes bronchospasm). Oxytocin remains first-line, then methylergonovine, then carboprost. Tranexamic acid (TXA) increasingly used early. Misoprostol is heat-stable and useful in low-resource settings.
Why does terbutaline carry an FDA black-box warning, and what is the time limit for its use as a tocolytic?
Black-box warning: increased risk of maternal cardiac events and death with prolonged use (injectable or oral). FDA limit: NOT for use beyond 48–72 hours as tocolytic, and no oral terbutaline for tocolysis at all. Mechanism: β2 agonist → uterine relaxation but also maternal tachycardia, palpitations, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema. Used as a rescue tocolytic for tachysystole and brief preterm-labor delay (e.g., to allow steroid administration for fetal lung maturity).

Prevent postpartum hemorrhage

Complications

Hypertensive crisis

Contraindications / Precautions
