Unit 8 · Joint & Bone · Chapter 33

Connective Tissue Disorders

Connective tissue disorders are treated with: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen — Ch 35), DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine), biologic DMARDs (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab), glucocorticoids (prednisone), and gout-specific agents (colchicine, allopurinol, probenecid).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

NSAIDs (covered in Ch 35) = first-line for symptoms. DMARDs: Methotrexate (folic acid daily; hepatotoxic; teratogenic Category X), hydroxychloroquine (retinal toxicity — annual eye exam), sulfasalazine, leflunomide. Biologic DMARDs (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab) — "-mab" or "-cept"; TB screening before, infection risk. Gout: colchicine (acute), allopurinol (long-term — never start during acute attack), probenecid.

DMARDs (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs)

  • Methotrexate (Rheumatrex): First-line for RA, also used for psoriasis, cancer chemotherapy
  • WEEKLY dose for RA (not daily); supplement with folic acid daily
  • AE: Hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), bone marrow suppression, mucositis, pulmonary fibrosis, photosensitivity
  • Category X — teratogenic, abortifacient
  • Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil): RA, SLE; retinal toxicity — annual eye exams
  • Sulfasalazine, leflunomide: Alternative DMARDs

Biologic DMARDs

  • TNF-alpha inhibitors — Etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab
  • SCREEN FOR TB (PPD or quantiferon) before initiating — reactivates latent TB
  • Avoid live vaccines while on therapy
  • Infection risk: Hold if active infection, scheduled surgery
  • Other biologics: Rituximab (anti-CD20), abatacept (T-cell modulator), tocilizumab (IL-6)
  • JAK inhibitors — Tofacitinib (Xeljanz): Oral; similar infection precautions

Gout therapy

  • Acute gout — Colchicine: Most effective if started within 24 hr; AE: severe GI (diarrhea, N/V), bone marrow suppression
  • Acute gout — NSAIDs (indomethacin classic; ibuprofen, naproxen) or glucocorticoids
  • Long-term — Allopurinol: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor; ↓ uric acid production
  • DO NOT start allopurinol during acute attack — can precipitate flare; take with food, plenty of water
  • Allopurinol AE: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hepatotoxicity
  • Probenecid: Uricosuric — ↑ renal excretion; encourage fluids 3 L/day
  • Febuxostat (Uloric): Alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor
A client newly started on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. What is the critical dosing frequency difference vs. cancer use, and what supplement is mandatory?
Methotrexate for RA is WEEKLY (not daily!) — a critical medication error point. Daily dosing causes fatal bone marrow suppression. Often given as a single weekly dose with day-of-week reminders. Folic acid 1 mg daily (except on MTX day) is mandatory — reduces GI/oral side effects and hepatic toxicity without losing efficacy. Other key points: Category X — teratogenic and abortifacient; both partners stop 3 months before conception. Monitor LFTs, CBC, renal function. Watch for pulmonary fibrosis (cough, dyspnea).
Before starting etanercept, what is the mandatory screening, and what immunizations must be addressed?
Screen for latent TB (PPD or QuantiFERON-Gold) before initiating any TNF-α inhibitor (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab, golimumab). TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent TB — treat latent TB first if positive. Also screen hepatitis B/C. Update immunizations BEFORE starting — particularly pneumococcal, influenza, shingles (Shingrix is non-live and OK on therapy). NO live vaccines while on biologic. Hold for active infection or scheduled surgery.
A client experiencing an acute gout attack asks about starting allopurinol. What is the timing rule, and what is the long-term teaching?
Do NOT initiate allopurinol during an acute gout attack — abrupt changes in uric acid can worsen or prolong the flare. Start after acute attack resolves (typically 2–4 weeks). For acute flare: NSAIDs (indomethacin classic), colchicine (most effective within 24 hr), or glucocorticoids. Long-term teaching: take with food, drink ≥3 L water/day (prevent stones), report any rash (Stevens-Johnson risk), avoid alcohol and purine-rich foods (organ meats, anchovies, beer). Hydroxychloroquine for SLE/RA → annual ophthalmology exam (retinal toxicity).

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has rheumatoid arthritis (RA) about a new prescription for etanercept. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for etanercept in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe at least three adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one for each of the adverse effects above.
  • MEDICATION ADMINISTRATION: Describe at least three important factors.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Etanercept is a biologic DMARD classified as a tumor necrosis factor antagonist. It suppresses manifestations of moderate to severe RA and slows the progression of the disorder.

Complications

  • Severe infections, including tuberculosis or reactivation of hepatitis B
  • Heart failure
  • Severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Hematologic disorders

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct clients to monitor for infection, and to report sore throat and other manifestations.
  • Discuss reasons for TB testing and possible hepatitis B testing.
  • Clients should notify the provider for edema, shortness of breath, and other manifestations of heart failure.
  • Report skin rash to provider.
  • Report easy bruising, bleeding, or unusual fatigue to provider.

Medication Administration

  • Teach clients to administer by subcutaneous injection twice weekly.
  • Discard solutions that are discolored or that contain particulate matter.
  • Monitor for injection-site reactions, and report them to provider.
  • Rotate injection sites.
  • Avoid skin areas that are bruised or reddened when injecting.
Unit 8 · Joint & Bone · Chapter 34

Bone Disorders

Bone disorders are treated with: calcium and vitamin D supplements (foundation), bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate), selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene), calcitonin-salmon, monoclonal antibodies (denosumab), and parathyroid hormone analogs (teriparatide).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Calcium + vitamin D: foundation of bone health; calcium 1000–1200 mg/day; vit D 600–800 IU. Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, zoledronate) — strict admin: take with 8 oz plain water, empty stomach AM, stay upright 30+ min, wait 30 min before any food/drink/meds; esophagitis, atypical fractures, jaw osteonecrosis (dental work). Raloxifene (SERM): ↑ DVT risk; hot flashes. Calcitonin-salmon: intranasal alternate nostrils. Denosumab: SC q6mo; monitor calcium.

Calcium & Vitamin D

  • Calcium 1000–1200 mg/day total intake (diet + supplement)
  • Vitamin D 600–800 IU/day (more if deficient)
  • Calcium carbonate (Tums): Take with food; cheapest; constipation
  • Calcium citrate: Take with or without food; preferred if PPI/H2 blocker user or low stomach acid
  • Divided doses (max 500–600 mg per dose) — absorption limited
  • Separate from levothyroxine, iron, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones

Bisphosphonates

  • Alendronate (Fosamax), risedronate, ibandronate (PO); zoledronic acid (IV q1y)
  • Strict administration:
  • • Take with FULL glass of plain water (no other fluid)
  • • First thing in the morning, empty stomach
  • • Stay upright (sit, stand, walk) for at least 30 minutes (60 for ibandronate)
  • • Wait 30 min before any food, drink, or other medication
  • AE: Esophagitis, GI distress, musculoskeletal pain, atypical femur fractures, osteonecrosis of the jaw (especially after dental procedures)
  • Dental clearance before starting; avoid invasive dental work during therapy

Other osteoporosis agents

  • Raloxifene (Evista) — SERM: Estrogen agonist on bone, antagonist on breast; ↑ DVT/PE risk; hot flashes; lowers breast cancer risk
  • Calcitonin-salmon (Miacalcin): Intranasal — alternate nostrils daily; rhinitis; less effective than bisphosphonates
  • Denosumab (Prolia) — RANKL inhibitor: SC q6mo; monitor for hypocalcemia; risk of infection, jaw osteonecrosis
  • Teriparatide (Forteo) — PTH analog: Daily SC × 2 yr max; rebuilds bone (anabolic); ↑ osteosarcoma risk in animals; not for pediatric/Paget
  • Romosozumab: Newer anabolic; monthly SC × 12 doses
What is the strict administration protocol for oral bisphosphonates like alendronate, and what major AE relates to dental procedures?
Take with a FULL 8 oz glass of PLAIN water (not coffee, juice, mineral water), first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach. Remain upright (sit, stand, walk) for at least 30 minutes (60 min for ibandronate) — prevents esophagitis/esophageal ulceration. Wait 30 min before any food, drink, or other medication. Major AE: osteonecrosis of the jaw — get dental clearance BEFORE starting and AVOID invasive dental work during therapy. Other: atypical femur fractures (thigh pain warning).
A client on omeprazole asks which calcium supplement to use. Which form is preferred, and what is the max absorption per dose?
Calcium citrate is preferred — absorption does not require gastric acid, so it works in clients on PPIs/H2 blockers or with achlorhydria. Calcium carbonate (Tums) requires acid and is best taken WITH food. Max absorption per dose: 500–600 mg — split larger total daily doses (1000–1200 mg/day total intake including diet). Separate from levothyroxine, iron, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, bisphosphonates by 2–4 hr (calcium binds these). Pair with vitamin D 600–800 IU/day. Calcium carbonate causes constipation; citrate causes less GI upset.
A client receives denosumab (Prolia) SC for osteoporosis. What lab must be checked before each dose, and what is the consequence of discontinuing without follow-up therapy?
Check calcium and 25-OH vitamin D before each dose; supplement to maintain normocalcemia. Pre-existing hypocalcemia is a contraindication — denosumab can cause severe, life-threatening hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia). Also check renal function. Discontinuation risk: stopping denosumab without transitioning to another antiresorptive (e.g., bisphosphonate) causes a rebound increase in bone turnover and risk of multiple vertebral fractures within months. Plan continuation/transition before initiation. Also: jaw osteonecrosis risk (dental clearance).

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse in a provider's office is teaching a client who is postmenopausal and at high risk for osteoporosis about a new prescription for alendronate. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for alendronate.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects of this medication. NURSING INTERVENTIONS ● Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor. ● Describe two nursing actions.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

In this client who is at high risk for osteoporosis, the purpose of alendronate is to prevent osteoporosis from occurring by decreasing resorption of bone. The medication also is used to treat existing osteoporosis and Paget's disease.

Complications

Alendronate can cause esophagitis and esophageal ulceration; other GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, and constipation); muscle pain; and visual disturbances. Rarely, it can cause atraumatic femoral fracture.

Nursing Interventions

Diagnostic tests: Blood calcium, bone density scans Nursing interventions

  • Assess the client's ability to follow administration directions (must be able to sit upright or stand for at least 30 min after taking alendronate).
  • Teach the client to take this medication first thing in the morning with at least 240 mL (8 oz) water and wait 30 min before eating or drinking anything else or taking any other medications or supplements.
  • Teach the client other ways to help prevent osteoporosis, such as performing weight-bearing exercises daily and obtaining adequate amounts of calcium and vitamin D.
Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 35

Non-Opioid Analgesics

Non-opioid analgesics include acetaminophen (no anti-inflammatory effect, hepatotoxic in overdose) and NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib). NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever via COX inhibition. Aspirin also has antiplatelet effects.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Acetaminophen: analgesic + antipyretic, NO anti-inflammatory; max 4 g/day adult (3 g if liver disease); hepatotoxic in overdose — antidote acetylcysteine. Aspirin: antiplatelet; Reye syndrome in kids; tinnitus = salicylism. Ibuprofen/naproxen: GI ulcer/bleed, renal, CV events. Celecoxib: COX-2 selective; less GI bleed but ↑ CV risk.

Acetaminophen

  • Mechanism: Inhibits CNS prostaglandins only (no peripheral anti-inflammatory)
  • Max dose: 4 g/day adult (3 g if older, alcohol use, liver disease)
  • Hepatotoxic in overdose — antidote N-acetylcysteine (within 8–10 hr most effective)
  • Check for hidden acetaminophen in combo products (Percocet, NyQuil)
  • Safe in pregnancy and children

NSAIDs

  • Aspirin: Irreversible COX inhibition; antiplatelet; Reye syndrome in children with viral illness
  • Salicylism toxicity: Tinnitus, hyperventilation, sweating, dizziness
  • Ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, indomethacin: Non-selective
  • Major AE: GI ulceration/bleeding, renal impairment, MI/stroke, HTN, decreased platelets
  • Take with food; avoid in late pregnancy (premature ductus closure)
  • Ketorolac: Limit to 5 days (bleed risk)
  • Celecoxib (COX-2): Less GI bleed; sulfa structure caution

Key interactions & warnings

  • NSAIDs ↑ lithium and warfarin effects
  • NSAIDs ↓ ACE inhibitor/diuretic efficacy
  • NEVER combine multiple NSAIDs
  • BLACK BOX CV risk for all NSAIDs (varies by drug)
What is the maximum daily acetaminophen dose for adults, and what are the "hidden APAP" combo products that cause unintentional overdose?
Max 4 g/day adult (reduce to 3 g/day in older adults, chronic alcohol use, or liver disease; 2 g/day in active liver disease). Hidden APAP combo products — clients commonly stack these unknowingly: Percocet (oxycodone+APAP), Vicodin/Norco/Lortab (hydrocodone+APAP), Tylenol PM (APAP+diphenhydramine), NyQuil/DayQuil, Excedrin, many cold/flu products. Teach clients to read every label and add up total APAP. Acetaminophen has no anti-inflammatory effect — but it IS analgesic and antipyretic and is safe in pregnancy.
A client presents 6 hours after intentional acetaminophen overdose. What is the antidote, and what is the critical timing window for maximal effectiveness?
N-acetylcysteine (NAC, acetylcysteine) — PO or IV. Maximally effective within 8–10 hours of ingestion; still beneficial up to 24 hr and may help even later in established hepatotoxicity. Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram: plot serum APAP level (drawn ≥4 hr after ingestion) against time to determine treatment need. NAC replenishes hepatic glutathione, neutralizing the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Monitor LFTs (AST/ALT may rise 24–48 hr post-ingestion), INR, ammonia, mental status. Liver transplant is the only definitive treatment for fulminant failure.
A client on chronic aspirin reports tinnitus, dizziness, and hyperventilation. What is happening, and what is the classic pediatric concern with aspirin?
Salicylism (aspirin toxicity) — early signs: tinnitus, hyperventilation, sweating, dizziness, vertigo. Severe: hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis, seizures, coma. Action: stop aspirin, supportive care, alkalinize urine with sodium bicarbonate, hemodialysis for severe cases. Pediatric concern: Reye syndrome — fulminant hepatic failure + encephalopathy associated with aspirin use in children with viral illness (chickenpox, flu). NEVER give aspirin to children with viral illness; use acetaminophen instead.
Which medications have dangerous interactions with NSAIDs, and why?
↑ NSAIDs raise levels of: lithium (toxicity), warfarin (bleeding — INR rises plus platelet inhibition). ↓ NSAIDs blunt: ACE inhibitors and diuretics (loss of BP control, ↑ acute kidney injury). Never combine multiple NSAIDs simultaneously (additive GI, renal, CV risk). Other major concerns: GI bleeding (worse with concurrent steroids, anticoagulants, SSRIs), renal impairment, ↑ MI/stroke risk (FDA black box — varies by drug; naproxen lowest CV risk). Avoid in 3rd trimester pregnancy — premature closure of ductus arteriosus.

Scenario

A nurse at a provider's office is providing teaching to a client who has osteoarthritis and is starting long-term therapy with NSAIDs. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three nursing actions, including two laboratory values the nurse should monitor.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

NSAIDs will treat mild to moderate joint pain and stiffness, and decrease inflammation in the client who has osteoarthritis.

Complications

  • Gastrointestinal effects can occur, including anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn.
  • GI bleeding can occur because NSAIDs affect platelet function.
  • Nephrotoxicity can occur.
  • NSAIDs can cause CNS effects (dizziness, headache, blurred vision, and tinnitus).
  • Allergy can occur, including cross allergy with other NSAIDs (aspirin).

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor hgb/hct and kidney function tests.
  • Assess the client for previous allergy to NSAIDs.
  • Assess the GI system, and ask about any history of GI bleed or peptic ulcer disease.
  • Advise the client to take the medication with food, milk, or an 8 oz glass of water to prevent GI distress.
  • Advise the client to tell provider about any over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements before taking them.
Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 36

Opioid Agonists and Antagonists

Opioid analgesics activate mu receptors for severe pain. Three categories: pure agonists (morphine — prototype, oxycodone, fentanyl, codeine), agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine), and antagonists (naloxone — overdose reversal, naltrexone — addiction therapy).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Morphine (prototype): severe pain; respiratory depression (sedation precedes it); universal constipation (prophylactic bowel regimen); urinary retention; pruritus (histamine). Naloxone: antidote — short half-life, may need repeats. Fentanyl patch: opioid-tolerant only; NEVER heat. Tramadol: seizure risk; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. Schedule II for most strong opioids.

Pure opioid agonists

  • Morphine (IV, PO, IM, SC, epidural) — prototype
  • Others: Oxycodone, hydromorphone (Dilaudid), fentanyl, hydrocodone, codeine, methadone, meperidine (avoid in renal failure)
  • Sedation precedes respiratory depression — assess sedation level
  • Hold if RR < 12; have naloxone available
  • Constipation universal — start senna + docusate prophylactically
  • Other AE: Urinary retention, pruritus, N/V, miosis (pinpoint pupils), hypotension

Special opioids

  • Fentanyl patch: Opioid-tolerant chronic pain only; 12+ hr to peak; remove old before new
  • NEVER apply heat to fentanyl patch — fatal overdose
  • Tramadol: Weak agonist + serotonin/NE reuptake; seizure risk; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs
  • Methadone: Long half-life; for OUD treatment, chronic pain
  • Buprenorphine: Partial agonist; OUD, chronic pain; ceiling effect on respiratory depression
  • Agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine): Ceiling effect on analgesia

Naloxone & overdose

  • Naloxone (Narcan): Pure opioid antagonist — IV/IM/intranasal
  • Half-life shorter than most opioids — may need repeat dosing
  • Precipitates withdrawal in opioid-dependent: agitation, tachycardia, N/V, abdominal pain
  • Naltrexone: Long-acting; OUD/AUD maintenance — must be opioid-free 7–10 days
  • Reassess respiratory status frequently after naloxone

Opioid administration & monitoring details

  • Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA): Client self-administers via pump; lockout interval prevents overdose
  • PCA safety: ONLY the client presses button (not family — "PCA by proxy" causes deaths); document pain score and sedation regularly
  • Equianalgesic dosing: Conversion between opioids and routes (e.g., morphine 10 mg IV = 30 mg PO); reduce dose 25–50% when switching due to incomplete cross-tolerance
  • Breakthrough pain: Acute exacerbation of pain in someone on stable scheduled opioid — give immediate-release opioid 10–15% of 24-hour scheduled dose
  • Around-the-clock dosing for chronic pain (not "as needed") prevents pain valleys
  • Opioid-induced respiratory depression: Pasero opioid-induced sedation scale (POSS); RR < 12, ↓ O2 sat, lower sedation score; treat: O2, stimulate, naloxone if necessary
  • Tolerance vs dependence vs addiction:
  • • Tolerance: Need ↑ dose for same effect (physiologic, normal)
  • • Physical dependence: Withdrawal symptoms if stopped abruptly (physiologic, normal)
  • • Addiction: Compulsive use despite harm (psychologic, disease)
  • Opioid withdrawal: Restlessness, anxiety, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, abdominal cramping, diarrhea — distressing but rarely fatal (unlike alcohol/benzo withdrawal)
A nurse is assessing a postoperative client receiving IV morphine. Which clinical finding is the most sensitive early warning of impending respiratory depression?
Increasing sedation — sedation almost always precedes respiratory depression. Use the Pasero Opioid-Induced Sedation Scale (POSS) at every assessment: 1 = awake/alert; 2 = slightly drowsy, easily aroused; 3 = frequently drowsy, drifts off mid-conversation (STOP additional opioid, monitor closely); 4 = somnolent, minimal response (consider naloxone). Hold opioid if RR < 12. Other contributors: concurrent benzos, sleep apnea, opioid-naive status. Have naloxone available; use lowest effective dose.
A client uses a fentanyl transdermal patch for chronic pain. What environmental exposures must be avoided, and which patient population should NEVER receive a fentanyl patch?
AVOID any heat source over the patch — heating pads, electric blankets, hot tubs, saunas, sunbathing, hot baths, fever — all dramatically accelerate fentanyl absorption, causing fatal overdose. Never apply to a patient who is opioid-naive — fentanyl patches are only for clients already tolerant to opioids (≥60 mg PO morphine equivalents/day). Remove old patch before applying new one (folded sticky-sides together, flushed or sequestered per facility policy). Effect peaks ~12–24 hr after application; residual effect ~12–24 hr after removal.
A family member offers to "help" by pressing the PCA button when the client falls asleep. Why is this dangerous, and what is the patient teaching?
"PCA by proxy" — pressing the button for a sleeping/sedated client defeats the built-in safety: the requirement that the client be awake enough to self-administer. Reported deaths have occurred from this. Teaching: ONLY the client may press the button — never family, friends, or staff. Place a "PCA by Patient Only" sign at bedside. Assess sedation/pain regularly. The PCA pump has a lockout interval (commonly 6–10 min) to prevent rapid overdose, but proxy dosing on a sedated patient bypasses this protection. Always have naloxone available.

Therapeutic Uses

Opioid medication is indicated for relief of moderate to severe pain.

Complications

  • Sedation
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Constipation
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Urinary retention

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client not to drive or perform other hazardous activities while using this medication.
  • Notify the provider for severe nausea or vomiting.
  • Prevent constipation by increasing intake of liquids and foods with fiber. Consider use of a stool softener or laxatives if necessary.
  • Move the client slowly from lying or sitting to standing to minimize effects of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Instruct the client to void every 4 hr. Contact the provider for manifestations of dysuria.

Adjuvant Medications for Pain

Adjuvant pain medications enhance pain relief in specific conditions: anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain (gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine), tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine), and topical agents (lidocaine patches, capsaicin).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Neuropathic pain (diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic, fibromyalgia): gabapentin, pregabalin (sedation, weight gain, edema; renal dosing); duloxetine (SNRI); amitriptyline (TCA — anticholinergic). Topical: lidocaine patch (12 on/12 off), capsaicin (gloves; transient burning). Trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine first-line.

Anticonvulsants for pain

  • Gabapentin, pregabalin (Lyrica — Schedule V): Neuropathic pain prototype
  • AE: Sedation, dizziness, peripheral edema, weight gain
  • Renal dosing required; titrate slowly
  • Carbamazepine: Trigeminal neuralgia drug of choice; CBC; Stevens-Johnson risk; HLA-B*1502 testing in Asian descent

Antidepressants for pain

  • Duloxetine (Cymbalta) — SNRI: Diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic musculoskeletal pain
  • TCAs — Amitriptyline, nortriptyline: Neuropathic pain, migraine prevention
  • TCA AE: Anticholinergic, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, cardiotoxic in overdose
  • Beers Criteria: Avoid TCAs in older adults
  • Lower doses for pain than for depression

Topical agents

  • Lidocaine 5% patch: Post-herpetic neuralgia; 12 hr on, 12 hr off
  • Capsaicin cream: Wear gloves; transient burning; avoid eyes/mucous membranes
  • Glucocorticoids: Reduce inflammation in nerve compression
A client with diabetic neuropathy is started on gabapentin. What two patient factors require dose adjustment, and what side effects should be expected?
Renal dosing required — gabapentin and pregabalin are renally cleared. Reduce dose for CrCl < 60; can accumulate dangerously in renal impairment causing severe sedation/myoclonus. Titrate slowly over days-weeks to minimize side effects. Expected AE: sedation, dizziness, peripheral edema, weight gain, ataxia. Driving caution during titration. Pregabalin (Lyrica) is Schedule V due to abuse potential. Both are also used for fibromyalgia (pregabalin), post-herpetic neuralgia, and partial seizures.
What is the first-line medication for trigeminal neuralgia, what genetic screen is recommended in certain populations, and what monitoring is required?
Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia. Genetic screen: test for HLA-B*1502 in clients of Asian descent before starting — strongly associated with Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. Monitoring: baseline + periodic CBC (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia), LFTs (hepatotoxicity), serum sodium (SIADH/hyponatremia), serum drug level. Therapeutic level: 4–12 mcg/mL. Carbamazepine is a CYP450 INDUCER → ↓ OCP, warfarin, many other drugs (auto-induces its own metabolism in first weeks).
A client is prescribed topical capsaicin cream for osteoarthritis pain. What three teaching points prevent injury or unintended exposure?
(1) Wear gloves to apply (or wash hands thoroughly with soap immediately after) — capsaicin transferred to eyes, mucous membranes, or genitals causes severe burning. (2) Expected transient burning/stinging at application site — typically subsides over the first 1–2 weeks of regular use; full effect takes 2–4 weeks of consistent application. (3) Avoid heat (heating pads) or occlusive dressings over the area — increases absorption and irritation. Don't apply to broken skin. The lidocaine 5% patch is different: 12 hours on, 12 hours off, for post-herpetic neuralgia.

Therapeutic Uses

Carbamazepine relieves neuropathic (nerve) pain, which can be described as sharp, burning, or aching.

Complications

Adverse effects of carbamazepine include GI manifestations (abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting). It also can cause bone marrow suppression, affecting all blood cell types.

Interactions

  • The medication can cause hypertensive crisis if taken within 14 days of an mAOI antidepressant.
  • Toxicity can result if the client drinks grapefruit juice while taking carbamazepine.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor CBC, including platelet counts.
  • Assess for abnormal bleeding, bruising, or infection.
  • Monitor for GI manifestations, and advise the client to take the medication with food.
Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 38

Miscellaneous Pain Medications

Miscellaneous pain medications include migraine-specific agents (triptans, ergot alkaloids), antiemetics for migraine, prophylactic agents (propranolol, topiramate), and newer CGRP inhibitors (erenumab, fremanezumab) for migraine prevention.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Migraine acute: triptans (sumatriptan SC/PO/intranasal); contraindicated in CAD, uncontrolled HTN; not with MAOIs or 2 triptans/24 hr. Migraine prevention: propranolol, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline, CGRP inhibitors (-mab; monthly SC). Cluster headache: 100% O2, sumatriptan SC.

Acute migraine therapy

  • Triptans — Sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan: 5-HT1B/1D agonists
  • Contraindicated: CAD, uncontrolled HTN, peripheral vascular disease, ischemic stroke, hemiplegic/basilar migraine, pregnancy
  • Interactions: No MAOIs (within 2 weeks); SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome); no ergot within 24 hr; no 2nd triptan within 24 hr
  • AE: Chest pressure (usually benign), tingling, flushing
  • Ergot alkaloids — Ergotamine, DHE: Category X; ergotism (peripheral ischemia)
  • Antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) for migraine nausea

Migraine prevention

  • Indicated if > 4 attacks/month or significant disability
  • Beta blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, timolol)
  • Anticonvulsants (topiramate, valproate)
  • TCAs (amitriptyline)
  • CGRP antagonists ("-mab"): Erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab — monthly SC; eptinezumab IV q3mo
  • Oral CGRP ("-gepants"): Ubrogepant, rimegepant (acute); atogepant (prevention)
  • Lasmiditan: 5-HT1F selective; no vasoconstriction (safer in CAD); 8 hr driving restriction
  • OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox): Chronic migraine (>15 days/month)
A client on phenelzine (MAOI) wants to use sumatriptan for migraine. What is the issue, and what other timing rules apply to triptans?
NEVER combine triptans with MAOIs — wait 2 weeks after stopping MAOI before any triptan (serotonin syndrome + hypertensive crisis risk). Other timing rules: no second triptan within 24 hours of the first; no ergotamine within 24 hours before or after a triptan (both vasoconstrict). With SSRIs/SNRIs: theoretical serotonin syndrome risk — use cautiously, watch for symptoms. Triptan contraindications: CAD, uncontrolled HTN, recent MI/stroke, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic/basilar migraine, pregnancy. Lasmiditan is an alternative without vasoconstriction (but 8-hr driving restriction).
A client with cluster headaches asks about treatment. What are the two first-line acute therapies, and how do they differ from migraine acute care?
(1) High-flow 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask at 12–15 L/min for 15–20 min — uniquely effective for cluster headaches (~70% relief). (2) Sumatriptan subcutaneous injection (faster onset than oral/intranasal — within 10–15 min). Cluster headaches: severe unilateral pain, often around one eye, with autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, ptosis); attacks cluster over weeks. Prevention: verapamil is first-line. Migraines, by contrast, use oral triptans more often and don't respond as well to oxygen.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has frequent migraine headaches about a new prescription for sumatriptan. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for sumatriptan in this client.

Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Sumatriptan is used to abort a migraine headache and associated manifestations (nausea and vomiting) after it begins by causing cranial artery vasoconstriction.

Complications

The nurse should monitor for chest and arm heaviness/pressure, angina caused by coronary vasospasm, dizziness, and vertigo.

Interactions

Toxicity can result if sumatriptan is given concurrently or within 2 weeks of an mAOI antidepressant. Sumatriptan should not be given concurrently with other triptan medications or within 24 hr of ergotamine or dihydroergotamine.

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach clients to take sumatriptan at the first finding of migraine manifestations.
  • Teach client how to administer sumatriptan if it is prescribed intranasally or by subcutaneous injection.
  • Monitor cardiovascular risk factors and vital signs while taking this medication.
  • Advise clients to notify the provider immediately for onset of angina pain. Teach clients to distinguish transient chest or arm heaviness caused by sumatriptan from angina pain.
Unit 10 · Endocrine · Chapter 39

Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes mellitus is managed with insulin (Type 1, advanced Type 2) and oral antidiabetic agents (Type 2). Insulin categories: rapid-acting, short-acting, intermediate, long-acting. Oral agents include biguanides (metformin — first-line), sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

T1DM: insulin required. T2DM: metformin first-line. Insulins: rapid (lispro/aspart — 15 min); short (regular — 30–60 min, only IV insulin); intermediate (NPH — 1–2 hr); long (glargine/detemir — peakless). Mix "clear before cloudy." Hypoglycemia <70: rule of 15. Sick days: never skip insulin. Metformin: lactic acidosis (rare); hold for IV contrast.

Insulin types

  • Rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine): Onset 15 min, peak 30–90 min, duration 3–5 hr; give immediately before/with meals
  • Short (Regular): Onset 30–60 min, peak 2–4 hr, duration 5–8 hr; ONLY insulin given IV
  • Intermediate (NPH): Onset 1–2 hr, peak 6–12 hr, duration 14–24 hr; cloudy — gently roll
  • Long (glargine, detemir, degludec): Peakless basal; do not mix
  • Mixing: "clear before cloudy" — draw up Regular before NPH
  • Rotate sites within same anatomic region; abdomen absorbs fastest/most consistent
  • Storage: Unopened in fridge; opened — room temp 28–30 days
  • Sick days: Never skip insulin — illness raises blood sugar

Oral & injectable T2DM agents

  • Metformin (biguanide) — FIRST-LINE T2DM: ↓ hepatic glucose; AE: GI distress, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (rare); hold 24–48 hr before/after IV contrast
  • Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride): Hypoglycemia, weight gain, sulfa allergy
  • Glinides (repaglinide): With meals; skip if skipping meal
  • Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone): ↑ insulin sensitivity; fluid retention/HF; fractures
  • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose): Flatulence; treat hypoglycemia with glucose, NOT sucrose
  • DPP-4 ("-gliptin"): Sitagliptin; weight-neutral; pancreatitis
  • GLP-1 agonists (exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide): SC (semaglutide also PO); weight loss; pancreatitis; thyroid C-cell tumors
  • SGLT2 inhibitors ("-flozin"): Empagliflozin; renal glucose excretion; GU infections, DKA possible with normal glucose

Hypoglycemia & DKA

  • Hypoglycemia < 70: Sweating, tremor, tachycardia, hunger, confusion
  • Rule of 15: 15 g rapid carbs (4 oz juice, 3–4 glucose tabs) → wait 15 min → recheck → repeat if still low → then complex carb + protein
  • Unconscious: Glucagon IM/SC at home; D50W IV in hospital
  • Somogyi effect: Nocturnal hypoglycemia → AM rebound — give bedtime snack, ↓ evening insulin
  • Dawn phenomenon: Early AM glucose rise — ↑ evening NPH
  • DKA: IV insulin (regular), aggressive fluids, K+ replacement

Newer agents & complete diabetes drug list

  • Canagliflozin (SGLT2) AE: Cystitis, candidiasis (males AND females), polyuria, dehydration, hypotension; ↑ amputation risk historically reported
  • Pramlintide (Symlin) — amylin analog: Adjunct to insulin in T1DM and insulin-using T2DM; SC before meals; severe hypoglycemia risk when added to insulin (reduce mealtime insulin by 50%); do not mix with insulin (separate syringe)
  • Pregnancy Risk categories: Metformin = B (often preferred PO if needed); Insulin = B (preferred overall); avoid most other PO agents during pregnancy
  • Bariatric surgery can resolve T2DM in many cases — insulin doses often substantially reduced post-op
  • DKA vs HHS: DKA — T1DM, ↑ ketones, ↓ pH, glucose 250–800; HHS — T2DM, no/minimal ketones, glucose > 600, severe dehydration, ↑ osmolality
List the onset, peak, and duration for the four major insulin types (rapid, short, intermediate, long).
Rapid (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset 15 min, peak 30–90 min, duration 3–5 hr. Give immediately before/with the meal. Short (Regular): onset 30–60 min, peak 2–4 hr, duration 5–8 hr. The only insulin given IV. Intermediate (NPH): onset 1–2 hr, peak 6–12 hr (highest hypoglycemia risk window), duration 14–24 hr. Cloudy — gently roll, don't shake. Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec): peakless basal coverage, duration 24 hr. Do NOT mix with other insulins.
A nurse is mixing Regular and NPH insulin in one syringe. What is the correct order, and why does it matter?
"Clear before cloudy" — draw up Regular insulin first, then NPH. Reason: prevents contamination of the Regular vial with the longer-acting NPH. Steps: (1) Inject air into NPH vial (don't draw any insulin yet); (2) inject air into Regular vial; (3) draw Regular insulin into syringe; (4) draw NPH insulin into same syringe. Mix only insulins approved to mix — NEVER mix long-acting glargine or detemir with anything. Insulins must be at room temperature before injecting. Rotate sites within same anatomic area (abdomen most consistent absorption).
A conscious diabetic client checks blood glucose at 58 mg/dL. Walk through the "rule of 15" management.
Rule of 15: (1) Give 15 g rapid-absorbing carbohydrate — 4 oz juice, regular soda (NOT diet), 3–4 glucose tabs, 1 tablespoon honey/sugar. (2) Wait 15 minutes. (3) Recheck glucose. (4) If still < 70 → repeat 15 g carbs. Once >70: give complex carb + protein (peanut butter crackers) to prevent rebound. If unconscious: NEVER give PO. Use glucagon IM/SC (home) or D50W IV push (hospital). For acarbose-induced hypoglycemia: must use pure glucose (acarbose blocks sucrose breakdown).
A client on metformin is scheduled for a CT scan with IV iodinated contrast. What is the action and why?
Hold metformin 24–48 hours before (depending on renal function and protocol) and 48 hours after IV contrast administration. Resume only after renal function (creatinine) is confirmed normal. Reason: IV contrast can cause acute kidney injury → metformin accumulates → rare but potentially fatal lactic acidosis. Also hold for major surgery, sepsis, or any acute illness causing hypoperfusion. Other key metformin points: take with food (GI distress most common AE), monitor B12 (long-term deficiency), and it does NOT cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy (mechanism is insulin-sensitizing).
A diabetic client calls because they have a stomach flu and can't eat. What are the "sick-day rules" — should they hold their insulin?
NEVER skip insulin during illness — even with reduced intake, illness raises blood sugar via stress hormones and risks DKA. Sick-day rules: (1) Continue basal insulin at usual dose. (2) Check blood glucose every 2–4 hr. (3) Check urine/blood ketones if glucose > 240 or with N/V. (4) Drink fluids — sugar-free if glucose high, sugar-containing if low or normal. (5) Substitute liquids/soft foods with similar carb counts if can't eat solid food. (6) Call provider if: ketones moderate/large, glucose persistently >240, vomiting/diarrhea >6 hr, can't keep fluids down, mental status change.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has type 2 diabetes mellitus and is taking exenatide along with an oral antidiabetic agent. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI active learning template: Medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for exenatide in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two laboratory tests the nurse should monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe teaching points to give a client taking exenatide.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Exenatide is prescribed along with an oral antidiabetic medication (metformin or a sulfonylurea medication) for clients who have type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve diabetes control. exenatide improves insulin secretion by the pancreas, decreases secretion of glucagon, and slows gastric emptying.

Complications

  • Gi effects (nausea and vomiting)
  • Pancreatitis manifested by acute abdominal pain and possibly severe vomiting
  • Hypoglycemia, especially when taken concurrently with a sulfonylurea medication (glipizide)

Nursing Interventions

Monitor daily blood glucose testing by the client, periodic Hba1c tests, and periodic kidney function testing. exenatide should be used cautiously in clients who have any renal impairment.

Client Education

  • Inject exenatide subcutaneously.
  • Take exenatide within 60 min before the morning and evening meal but not following the meal.
  • Withhold exenatide and notify the provider for severe abdominal pain.
  • Recognize and treat hypoglycemia.
  • Exenatide should not be given within 1 hr of oral medications, particularly antibiotics, acetaminophen, or contraceptives due to its ability to slow gastric emptying.
Unit 10 · Endocrine · Chapter 40

Endocrine Disorders

Endocrine disorders covered: thyroid (hypothyroid — levothyroxine; hyperthyroid — methimazole, PTU, RAI), pituitary (somatropin, vasopressin), and adrenal (glucocorticoids — prednisone, hydrocortisone). Each has specific monitoring and lifelong implications.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Hypothyroid — levothyroxine: empty stomach AM (1 hr before food); lifelong; never abruptly stop; monitor TSH. Hyperthyroid: methimazole (preferred); PTU (1st trimester pregnancy, thyroid storm); radioactive iodine (avoid pregnancy/breastfeeding). Lugol's: pre-thyroidectomy; straw to avoid teeth staining. Vasopressin/DDAVP: DI; watch for hyponatremia. Glucocorticoids: taper; Cushingoid with long-term.

Hypothyroidism — Levothyroxine

  • Levothyroxine (Synthroid) — T4: Drug of choice
  • Administration: AM, empty stomach, 30–60 min before food/other meds; same time daily
  • Lifelong therapy; never stop abruptly
  • Monitor TSH q6–8 weeks during titration, then annually
  • Overdose signs: Tachycardia, palpitations, weight loss, insomnia, heat intolerance, tremor
  • ↓ Absorption: Antacids, calcium, iron, fiber, coffee — separate by 4 hr
  • Liothyronine (T3): For myxedema coma

Hyperthyroidism

  • Methimazole (Tapazole): Preferred for most adults; inhibits T4 synthesis
  • Propylthiouracil (PTU): Preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm; hepatotoxicity
  • Both: Agranulocytosis (sore throat, fever) — discontinue; weeks to effect
  • Radioactive iodine (131I): Destroys thyroid; contraindicated pregnancy/breastfeeding; radiation precautions × few days
  • Strong iodine (Lugol's, SSKI): Pre-thyroidectomy, thyroid storm; use straw (stains teeth); dilute in juice
  • Beta blockers (propranolol): Symptomatic relief of tachycardia, tremor

Pituitary & adrenal

  • Somatropin (GH): GH deficiency; SC injection
  • Vasopressin/desmopressin (DDAVP): Central diabetes insipidus; also bedwetting, hemophilia A
  • Monitor for hyponatremia/water intoxication — restrict fluids
  • Glucocorticoids — Prednisone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone: Multiple uses
  • Cushingoid: Weight gain, moon face, buffalo hump, thin skin, easy bruising, muscle wasting, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, HTN, mood changes
  • NEVER stop abruptly — taper to prevent adrenal crisis
  • Take with food, AM dosing mimics circadian; calcium + vit D for bone protection
  • Fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid): Addison disease

Pituitary & growth hormone disorders

  • Octreotide (Sandostatin) — somatostatin analog: Treats acromegaly, gigantism, severe diarrhea (carcinoid, VIPoma), variceal bleeding
  • Octreotide AE: Gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis), hyperglycemia/hypoglycemia, GI distress, bradycardia
  • Lanreotide, pegvisomant: Other agents for acromegaly
  • Somatropin (GH): For pediatric GH deficiency; SC injection; monitor growth; avoid in active malignancy
  • SIADH treatment: Fluid restriction, demeclocycline, tolvaptan, conivaptan (vaptans) — caution rapid sodium correction (central pontine myelinolysis)
  • Adrenal crisis treatment: IV hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef), IV fluids, glucose; emergency situation
A client is newly started on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. What is the administration protocol, and which common substances reduce absorption?
Take in the morning, on an empty stomach, 30–60 min before food or any other medications. Same time daily; consistent brand (small bioavailability differences between brands matter at this narrow TI). Lifelong — never abruptly stop. Monitor TSH every 6–8 weeks during titration, then annually once stable. ↓ Absorption substances (separate by 4 hr): antacids, calcium supplements, iron, fiber, soy, coffee, PPIs (chronic use). Overdose signs (TSH suppressed): tachycardia, palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance, insomnia, tremor → reduce dose.
A client has been on prednisone 40 mg/day for 6 weeks for autoimmune disease. Why must it never be stopped abruptly, and what teaching addresses Cushingoid effects?
Chronic glucocorticoids suppress the HPA axis; abrupt discontinuation causes adrenal crisis (hypotension, weakness, hypoglycemia, shock — can be fatal). Taper slowly per provider plan, often weeks to months. Stress doses (ER, surgery, severe illness) may be needed for up to a year after stopping. Cushingoid effects: moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, thin skin, easy bruising, muscle wasting, hyperglycemia, HTN, osteoporosis, mood changes. Teach: take in AM with food (mimics circadian), calcium + vitamin D for bone protection, monitor glucose and BP, medical alert ID, never stop without provider.
A client receives desmopressin (DDAVP) for central diabetes insipidus. What is the major adverse effect to monitor for, and what fluid teaching applies?
Water intoxication / hyponatremia — DDAVP acts as ADH analog → kidneys retain free water. Excess water + low sodium causes headache, confusion, lethargy, nausea, seizures, coma. Monitor: daily weights, I&O, serum sodium, mental status. Fluid teaching: only drink to thirst while on therapy — do not push fluids; restrict free water during dosing if instructed. Also used for primary nocturnal enuresis and bleeding in mild hemophilia A / vWD. Caution: severe symptomatic hyponatremia must be corrected slowly to prevent central pontine myelinolysis.

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse in a provider's office is providing instructions to a client who has a new prescription for levothyroxine to treat hypothyroidism. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use of levothyroxine in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two laboratory tests the nurse should monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe teaching points for a client taking levothyroxine.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Levothyroxine replaces T4 and is used as thyroid hormone replacement therapy. Replacement of T4 also raises T3 levels, because some T4 is converted into T3.

Complications

Adverse effects are essentially the same as manifestations of hyperthyroidism: cardiac manifestations (hypertension and angina pectoris); insomnia; anxiety; weight loss; heat intolerance; increased body temperature; tremors; and menstrual irregularities.

Nursing Interventions

Monitor thyroid function tests: T3, T4, and TSh.

Client Education

  • Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, usually 1 hr before breakfast.
  • Thyroid replacement therapy is usually required for life
  • Monitor for adverse effects that indicate that the dosage needs to be adjusted.
Unit 11 · Immune · Chapter 41

Immunizations

Immunizations confer active immunity through live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, intranasal flu) or inactivated/subunit vaccines. Schedule based on CDC recommendations. Live vaccines contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Live attenuated (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG, intranasal flu): contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise. Inactivated/subunit: safe in immunocompromised. Two live vaccines: same day OR ≥ 4 weeks apart. Egg allergy: caution with influenza/yellow fever. Common AE: injection site, low-grade fever. Severe AE: anaphylaxis (rare) — don't repeat vaccine.

Vaccine types

  • Live attenuated: MMR, varicella, rotavirus (oral), BCG, intranasal flu (FluMist), yellow fever, oral typhoid
  • Inactivated: Influenza (injection), polio (IPV), Hep A, rabies
  • Subunit/recombinant: HPV, Hep B, Tdap, Hib, Shingrix (zoster)
  • Toxoid: Tetanus, diphtheria
  • Adult schedule: Flu annual; Tdap q10y; Shingrix > 50 (2 doses); pneumococcal > 65 or risk factors
  • HPV: Routine ages 11–12; catch-up to 26; eligible to 45

Contraindications & precautions

  • Live vaccines contraindicated: Pregnancy, severe immunocompromise (chemo, high-dose steroids, HIV/CD4 < 200, transplant), SCID infants
  • Egg allergy: Most flu vaccines OK; cell-based/recombinant alternatives; yellow fever produced in eggs
  • Defer: Moderate-severe acute illness (mild illness OK)
  • Anaphylaxis to previous dose = absolute contraindication
  • Pediatric aspirin: Avoid varicella + live flu (Reye risk)

Administration & reactions

  • Routes: Most IM (deltoid adult; vastus lateralis infant); some SC (MMR, varicella); intranasal/PO for specific vaccines
  • Common AE: Injection site soreness, low-grade fever, fussiness
  • Severe AE to report: Anaphylaxis, encephalopathy, seizures, persistent crying > 3 hr
  • Document: Vaccine name, lot #, manufacturer, date, site, route, VIS
  • Immunoglobulin/blood products: Delay live vaccine 3+ months
Name the major live-attenuated vaccines, and list the absolute contraindications.
Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, rotavirus (oral), BCG, intranasal influenza (FluMist), yellow fever, oral typhoid, MMRV. Absolute contraindications: pregnancy, severe immunocompromise (active chemotherapy, high-dose corticosteroids, HIV with CD4 < 200, organ/stem-cell transplant, SCID), prior anaphylactic reaction to vaccine component. Defer (not absolute contraindication): moderate-severe acute illness (mild illness like cold is OK). After IVIG/blood product → delay live vaccine ≥3 months.
A child needs MMR and varicella vaccines but missed the appointment. What spacing rules apply between two live vaccines, and what is the post-exposure rule for blood products?
Two live parenteral vaccines: give SAME DAY or wait ≥ 4 weeks apart — if given less than 4 weeks apart, the second one may not "take" because of immune response interference. After receiving IVIG, immunoglobulin, or any blood product: delay live vaccine 3+ months (passive antibodies neutralize the vaccine virus). Inactivated/subunit vaccines have no spacing restrictions and can be given simultaneously with anything. Adult routine: flu annual; Tdap q10y; Shingrix >50 (2 doses); pneumococcal >65.
A client with a documented egg allergy needs the influenza vaccine. Can it be given safely, and which vaccine is the one true egg-allergy contraindication?
Yes — flu vaccines are safe for egg-allergic clients (recommendation updated by ACIP): even severe egg-allergic individuals can receive standard inactivated influenza vaccine; observe per usual post-vaccination protocols. Cell-based or recombinant flu vaccines (Flucelvax, Flublok) are completely egg-free options. Yellow fever vaccine is the one to specifically flag — produced in eggs, may require allergy specialist consultation or skin testing. Any prior anaphylactic reaction to a previous vaccine dose is always an absolute contraindication regardless of egg status.

A nurse at a community health clinic is planning to administer the human papilloma virus (9vHPV) vaccine to an 11-year-old client. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should monitor for.

Show key

Complications

  • The 9vHPV vaccine can cause redness, tenderness, and swelling at the injection site.
  • It has caused fainting in some clients shortly after the vaccine is administered.
  • Headache and mild to moderate fever are also possible adverse effects the client should monitor for.

Contraindications / Precautions

Contraindications to receiving the 9vHPV vaccine include pregnancy and a severe allergy to yeast.

Client Education

  • Monitor for adverse effects; the common adverse effects are mild and temporary.
  • The adolescent will require a second dose in 6 to 12 months since this one occurred before age 16. Initial administration after 16 years of age requires a three dose series.
Unit 11 · Immune · Chapter 42

Chemotherapy Agents

Chemotherapy agents target rapidly-dividing cells. Categories include alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide), antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-FU), antitumor antibiotics (doxorubicin — cardiotoxic), mitotic inhibitors (vincristine), hormonal agents, and targeted therapies. Severe toxicity requires careful monitoring.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

All chemo: bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia), N/V, alopecia, mucositis, fatigue, ↑ infection risk. Doxorubicin: cardiotoxicity (cumulative); red urine (harmless); vesicant. Cyclophosphamide: hemorrhagic cystitis — ↑ fluids, mesna. Methotrexate: leucovorin rescue. Vincristine: peripheral neuropathy; FATAL if intrathecal. PPE required; hazardous waste disposal.

Major drug categories

  • Alkylating agents — Cyclophosphamide, cisplatin, carboplatin:
  • • Cyclophosphamide: Hemorrhagic cystitis — ↑ fluids, mesna; secondary leukemia
  • • Cisplatin: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe N/V
  • Antimetabolites — Methotrexate, 5-FU, cytarabine, mercaptopurine:
  • • Methotrexate: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue; hepatotoxic; teratogenic
  • Antitumor antibiotics — Doxorubicin, daunorubicin, bleomycin:
  • • Doxorubicin: Cardiotoxicity (dose-limited; baseline echo); red/orange urine (harmless); vesicant — extravasation = necrosis
  • • Bleomycin: Pulmonary fibrosis (dose-limited)
  • Mitotic inhibitors — Vincristine, vinblastine, paclitaxel:
  • • Vincristine: Peripheral neuropathy; NEVER intrathecal — fatal
  • Hormonal — Tamoxifen, raloxifene, anastrozole, leuprolide
  • Targeted/biologics — Imatinib, trastuzumab, bevacizumab, rituximab

Universal toxicities

  • Myelosuppression: Nadir at 7–14 days; monitor CBC
  • Neutropenia: ANC < 1500; precautions if < 500 (neutropenic precautions)
  • Fever in neutropenic: EMERGENCY — pan-culture, broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • N/V: Pre-medicate with ondansetron, dexamethasone, aprepitant
  • Alopecia: Begins 2–3 weeks; grows back when therapy ends
  • Mucositis: Soft toothbrush; saline rinses; avoid alcohol-based mouthwash; acidic foods
  • Tumor lysis syndrome: Hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, AKI; allopurinol or rasburicase prophylaxis

Safety in handling chemo

  • PPE required: Double gloves, gown, eye protection, mask
  • Closed system transfer devices for preparation
  • Spill kits readily available; specialized cleanup
  • Hazardous waste disposal per facility protocol
  • Pregnant or trying to conceive nurses: Avoid handling
  • Body fluids contaminated 48–72 hr after admin; flush toilet twice

Additional chemo subcategories

  • Nitrosoureas — Carmustine, lomustine: Cross BBB (brain tumors); cumulative bone marrow toxicity; topical Gliadel wafer for brain tumor resection
  • Topoisomerase inhibitors — Topotecan, irinotecan, etoposide: Topotecan (ovarian, small-cell lung); irinotecan: cholinergic diarrhea (give atropine)
  • Asparaginase, hydroxyurea: Specific leukemias
  • Hormonal/anti-androgens — Flutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide: Prostate cancer; GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin)
  • Aromatase inhibitors — Anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane: Postmenopausal breast cancer
  • Immunomodulators — Interferon alfa, interleukin-2: Hairy cell leukemia, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma; flu-like symptoms
  • Monoclonal antibodies — Trastuzumab (HER2+ breast), bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), rituximab (CD20), cetuximab (EGFR): Infusion reactions; cetuximab — acneiform rash
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors — Imatinib, erlotinib, sorafenib: "-tinib"/"-fenib"; oral; targeted therapy for specific mutations
A client starts doxorubicin chemotherapy. What baseline cardiac test is required, what dose-limiting toxicity does this monitor, and what harmless side effect is expected?
Baseline echocardiogram or MUGA scan to assess left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) — doxorubicin causes cumulative, dose-related cardiomyopathy that can progress to irreversible heart failure. Lifetime cumulative dose limit: ~450–500 mg/m². Repeat cardiac imaging during therapy. Dexrazoxane may be used as cardioprotective in some regimens. Harmless expected effect: red/orange urine, tears, and sweat for 1–2 days after each dose. Doxorubicin is also a vesicant — extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis; administer through central line when possible, have antidote (dexrazoxane IV) ready.
What is the absolute medication-administration rule for vincristine, and what is the most common dose-limiting toxicity?
VINCRISTINE IS NEVER GIVEN INTRATHECALLY — FATAL. Intrathecal vincristine causes ascending paralysis and death in nearly 100% of cases. Multiple sentinel events have occurred from confusion with methotrexate (which IS given intrathecally). ISMP-recommended safeguards: (1) administer only via mini-bag (not syringe) which physically prevents intrathecal use, (2) label clearly with bright warning, (3) two-nurse verification, (4) never store with intrathecal medications. Dose-limiting toxicity: peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, weakness, constipation/ileus) — sensory loss often persists.
A client on chemotherapy presents with fever 38.5°C (101.3°F) and an ANC of 400. What is this called, and what is the immediate action sequence?
Neutropenic fever (febrile neutropenia) — a medical EMERGENCY in cancer care. ANC < 500 with fever ≥38.3°C (or 38.0°C sustained 1 hr). Risk of sepsis is extremely high; mortality climbs with delay. Action: (1) Pan-culture (blood × 2 sets, urine, sputum, line tip if applicable, wound), (2) Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR — do NOT delay for culture results (typical: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem ± vancomycin). (3) Neutropenic precautions: private room, no fresh flowers, no raw fruits/vegetables, meticulous hand hygiene. Avoid rectal temps, suppositories, or IM injections.

Therapeutic Uses

Leuprolide is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist of luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormones. It is used instead of surgical ca

Complications

  • Hot flashes (or flashes), decreased libido, gynecomastia
  • Cardiac manifestations (dysrhythmias) and increased edema, which can lead
  • Decreased bone density, which can lead to fractures

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 43

Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

Antimicrobial principles include identifying causative organism (culture before starting), selecting narrow-spectrum when possible, avoiding superinfection and resistance, completing full course, and addressing hypersensitivity. Empiric vs targeted therapy.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Before antibiotics: obtain cultures (blood, sputum, urine, wound) BEFORE first dose. Empiric therapy until cultures return; narrow once organism identified. Complete entire course even if feeling better. Resistance prevention: appropriate selection, adequate dosing, full course. Hypersensitivity: ask about prior reactions; cross-reactivity (PCN-cephalosporin minimal). Superinfection: C. difficile, yeast.

Selection principles

  • Culture & sensitivity BEFORE first dose (when possible)
  • Empiric therapy: Best guess based on likely organism, site, local resistance
  • Targeted therapy: Switch to narrow-spectrum once culture returns
  • Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic — choose bactericidal if immunocompromised or serious infection
  • Host factors: Age, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function, allergies
  • Site factors: Penetration (CNS, prostate, biofilm)

Resistance prevention

  • Use antibiotics only when truly bacterial (not viral)
  • Use narrowest spectrum effective
  • Adequate dosing (avoid subtherapeutic)
  • Complete full course as prescribed
  • Do not save antibiotics for later use
  • MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE: Healthcare-associated; contact precautions

Adverse effects & monitoring

  • Hypersensitivity: Most common AE; PCN most common allergen
  • Penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity: < 1% with modern cephalosporins (was overestimated)
  • Superinfection: Eradication of normal flora → opportunistic — C. difficile (severe diarrhea), oral/vaginal yeast
  • C. difficile: Stop offending antibiotic; treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (NOT metronidazole first-line anymore)
  • Renal/hepatic adjustments often required
A client with suspected sepsis has a fever and orders for blood cultures plus IV ceftriaxone. What is the correct order of these tasks, and why?
Obtain blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (cultures of urine, sputum, wound, CSF — whatever applies). Even one dose of antibiotic can sterilize cultures and prevent organism identification, which then prevents narrowing therapy. BUT — in suspected sepsis, do not delay antibiotics waiting for cultures: if cultures can be obtained within 45 minutes, do them first; otherwise, give antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition (each hour of delay increases mortality). Two peripheral blood culture sets from different sites are standard. After cultures return: narrow spectrum to the targeted organism.
A client on clindamycin develops profuse watery diarrhea with cramping. What is the likely diagnosis, and what is the current first-line treatment (not metronidazole)?
Clostridioides difficile colitis (C. diff) — antibiotic-associated colitis from disruption of normal gut flora. Clindamycin and fluoroquinolones carry the highest risk. Action: (1) stop the offending antibiotic if possible. (2) First-line treatment (updated IDSA): oral vancomycin OR oral fidaxomicin — NOT IV vancomycin (doesn't reach gut lumen). Metronidazole is NO LONGER first-line (used only in non-severe cases when others unavailable). Strict contact precautions, soap-and-water hand hygiene (alcohol-based does NOT kill spores), single-patient room. Recurrent or fulminant C. diff: fecal microbiota transplant or bezlotoxumab.
A client with documented penicillin allergy needs cefazolin for surgical prophylaxis. What is the actual cross-reactivity rate, and what factors guide the decision?
The "10% cross-reactivity" figure is outdated and overestimated. True cross-reactivity is < 1% with modern cephalosporins, especially 3rd–5th generation. Decision-making: get a detailed allergy history — was it a true IgE reaction (urticaria, anaphylaxis, angioedema) or just GI upset (not an allergy)? If non-severe PCN allergy: cephalosporins generally safe (especially later generations); modern guidelines allow administration with monitoring. If true anaphylaxis to PCN: consider alternative (e.g., clindamycin or vancomycin for surgical prophylaxis) or do allergy consultation/desensitization. Document the actual reaction in the chart.
What infection-control precautions apply to MRSA, VRE, ESBL, and CRE — and what are typical treatment options?
All are healthcare-associated multidrug-resistant organisms requiring CONTACT precautions: private room (or cohort), gown + gloves on entry, dedicated equipment, hand hygiene with soap and water. Treatment options: MRSA → IV vancomycin (mainstay), or linezolid, daptomycin, ceftaroline. VRE → linezolid, daptomycin, quinupristin-dalfopristin, tigecycline. ESBL gram-negatives → carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem). CRE (carbapenem-resistant) → very limited: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, plazomicin. Antimicrobial stewardship: narrow spectrum, complete course, do not save antibiotics, hand hygiene.

Scenario

A staff educator is providing information to a group of nurses about ways to prevent the spread of micro-organisms. What information should the educator include? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Basic Concept to complete this item.

Related Content

Preventive nursing measures

Underlying Principles

Controlling the spread of infection to staff and clients in a health care setting

Nursing Interventions

  • Perform hand hygiene before and after each client contact to prevent the spread of infection.
  • Recognize invasive procedures that increase the risk of infection (indwelling urinary catheter, IV catheter, cardiac catheterization).
  • Encourage prevention by having clients maintain an up-to-date immunization status.
  • Instruct clients to take the full course of antimicrobials the provider prescribes to prevent medication resistance and recurrence of infection.
  • Use infection-control procedures to prevent transmission of resistant micro-organisms.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of treatment.
Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 44

Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall

Cell wall antibiotics include penicillins (penicillin G, amoxicillin, piperacillin), cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone — generations), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem), monobactams (aztreonam), and vancomycin. All bactericidal.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Penicillins (PCN G, amoxicillin, piperacillin): bactericidal; cross-reactivity with cephalosporins rare with modern; rash to anaphylaxis. Cephalosporins (cephalexin oral; cefazolin, ceftriaxone IV; cefepime broader): 5 generations of increasing gram-neg coverage. Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem): broad-spectrum, last-line. Vancomycin: MRSA, C. diff (PO); red man syndrome with rapid IV; nephro/ototoxic; trough monitoring.

Penicillins

  • Penicillin G: Narrow-spectrum gram-positive (Strep)
  • Amoxicillin, ampicillin: Broader spectrum; PO
  • Piperacillin, ticarcillin: Extended spectrum (Pseudomonas)
  • Beta-lactamase inhibitor combos: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin), piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn), ampicillin-sulbactam
  • AE: Allergic reaction (rash → anaphylaxis), GI upset, diarrhea (C. difficile risk)
  • Document allergies clearly; ask about specific reaction
  • PCN + aminoglycoside synergy for serious gram-positive (endocarditis)

Cephalosporins

  • 1st gen — Cephalexin (PO), cefazolin (IV): Gram-positive; cefazolin = surgical prophylaxis
  • 2nd gen — Cefuroxime, cefoxitin: More gram-negative
  • 3rd gen — Ceftriaxone (IM/IV), cefotaxime, ceftazidime: Broad; CNS penetration (meningitis); ceftriaxone — incompatible with calcium IV; bilirubin displacement (avoid in neonates)
  • 4th gen — Cefepime: Broad gram-pos AND gram-neg + Pseudomonas
  • 5th gen — Ceftaroline: MRSA coverage
  • Cross-reactivity with PCN: Rare (< 1% with modern cephalosporins)
  • AE: Same as PCN; some cause disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Carbapenems, monobactams, vancomycin

  • Carbapenems — Imipenem-cilastatin, meropenem, ertapenem, doripenem: Very broad-spectrum; last-line for resistant gram-negative
  • Imipenem: Lower seizure threshold
  • Monobactams — Aztreonam: Gram-negative only; safe in PCN allergy
  • Vancomycin (IV): MRSA, severe gram-positive
  • Vancomycin (PO): C. difficile colitis — not absorbed, stays in gut
  • Red man syndrome: Flushing, hypotension with rapid IV — infuse over ≥ 60 min
  • Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity: Monitor trough levels (10–20 mcg/mL; higher for serious infection)
  • Monitor BUN/Cr, urine output, hearing
A client receiving IV vancomycin develops flushing, pruritus, and erythematous rash on the face and neck during infusion. What is this, and what is the management?
"Red man" / vancomycin infusion reaction (now called vancomycin infusion reaction or VFS) — NOT a true allergy. Caused by direct histamine release from rapid infusion. Management: slow the infusion to ≥ 60 minutes (and ≥90 min for higher doses); pretreat with diphenhydramine if recurrent. Not a contraindication to future vancomycin (rechallenge with slower rate). Differentiate from anaphylaxis (hypotension, dyspnea, wheezing — would require stopping infusion and treating as allergy). Also monitor for true vancomycin AEs: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neutropenia.
What is the target vancomycin trough level for serious infections, when is the trough drawn, and what labs are monitored?
Target trough: 15–20 mcg/mL for serious infections (endocarditis, meningitis, MRSA pneumonia, osteomyelitis); 10–15 for less severe. Some institutions are moving to AUC-based dosing instead of troughs. Trough timing: 30 minutes BEFORE the 4th or 5th dose (steady state). Monitor: BUN/creatinine (nephrotoxicity — additive with other nephrotoxins like aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast), hearing/tinnitus (ototoxicity), CBC (neutropenia), and trough levels. Adjust dose based on trough + renal function. Note: oral vancomycin is NOT absorbed — used only for C. diff colitis; no monitoring needed.
A neonate needs ceftriaxone for sepsis. What is the absolute contraindication regarding concurrent IV solutions, and why is this drug avoided in the very young?
NEVER co-administer ceftriaxone with IV calcium-containing solutions (LR, calcium gluconate, calcium chloride, TPN with calcium) — forms a fatal calcium-ceftriaxone precipitate in the lungs and kidneys. Even Y-site at separate ports is problematic in neonates. Avoid ceftriaxone in neonates < 28 days, especially hyperbilirubinemic — ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin from albumin → kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy). Cefotaxime is the preferred 3rd-gen cephalosporin alternative in neonates. Some cephalosporins (cefotetan, cefoperazone) also cause a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
Why is oral vancomycin used for C. difficile but IV vancomycin is not? What about the reverse — IV vancomycin for MRSA bacteremia?
Oral vancomycin is NOT absorbed from the GI tract — it stays in the gut lumen where C. diff lives, achieving high local concentrations. IV vancomycin doesn't reach the gut lumen well, so it can't treat C. diff colitis. The reverse: Oral vancomycin can't be used for MRSA bacteremia, endocarditis, or any systemic infection — it never enters the bloodstream. IV vancomycin is the workhorse for serious MRSA infections. The takeaway: route of administration determines tissue distribution and indication. Same drug, completely different uses.

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is administering vancomycin IV to a client who has a serious wound infection. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for vancomycin for this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two nursing actions for clients receiving vancomycin.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Vancomycin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria by disrupting their cell wall. The IV form treats serious infections due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and streptococci.

Complications

  • Infusion reactions (red man syndrome: rashes, flushing, tachycardia, and hypotension)
  • Ototoxicity (rare and reversible)
  • Renal toxicity
  • Thrombophlebitis at the IV site
  • Im and IV injection-site pain

Nursing Interventions

  • Infuse vancomycin over at least 60 min/dose to prevent an infusion reaction.
  • Monitor the IV site for redness, pain, or other manifestations of thrombophlebitis.
  • Monitor I&O, and notify the provider for oliguria or other findings of acute renal injury.
  • Monitor for hearing loss.
  • Ask the client about allergy to antibiotics before administering the medication. Watch for allergic manifestations during and after the infusion.
Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 45

Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis

Protein synthesis inhibitors include tetracyclines (doxycycline), macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin), aminoglycosides (gentamicin — narrow TI, nephro/ototoxic), and others (clindamycin, linezolid). Mostly bacteriostatic except aminoglycosides.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline): not in children < 8 yo or pregnancy (tooth staining, bone growth); photosensitivity; ↓ absorption with calcium/iron/dairy. Macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin): GI distress; QT prolongation; CYP450 interactions. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin): narrow TI; nephrotoxic, ototoxic; peaks and troughs. Clindamycin: high C. difficile risk. Linezolid: MRSA/VRE; thrombocytopenia.

Tetracyclines

  • Doxycycline (most used), tetracycline, minocycline
  • Uses: Acne, Lyme disease, rickettsial, atypical pneumonia, malaria prophylaxis
  • AVOID in children < 8 yo, pregnancy, breastfeeding — permanent tooth discoloration, bone growth inhibition
  • Photosensitivity — sunscreen, protective clothing
  • ↓ Absorption: Calcium (dairy), iron, antacids, magnesium — separate by 2 hr
  • Esophagitis: Take with full glass of water; sit upright 30 min

Macrolides

  • Azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin
  • Uses: Respiratory infections, atypical pneumonia, STIs (chlamydia), pertussis
  • Alternative for PCN-allergic
  • AE: GI distress (erythromycin most), QT prolongation (especially erythromycin, clarithromycin), hepatotoxicity, hearing loss
  • CYP450 interactions (erythromycin, clarithromycin): ↑ warfarin, statins, theophylline, digoxin
  • Azithromycin: Z-Pak; longer half-life; better tolerated

Aminoglycosides

  • Gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin
  • Uses: Serious gram-negative infections (gram-positive synergy with PCN/vanc)
  • NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX — monitor peak & trough
  • Nephrotoxicity: ATN; monitor BUN/Cr, urine output
  • Ototoxicity: Vestibular AND auditory — hearing loss may be permanent; baseline audiogram
  • Neuromuscular blockade (with anesthetics) — respiratory arrest possible
  • IV only: Not absorbed PO; neomycin = oral pre-bowel surgery (gut sterilization)

Other protein synthesis inhibitors

  • Clindamycin: Anaerobes, gram-positive; highest C. difficile risk
  • Linezolid (Zyvox): MRSA, VRE; thrombocytopenia (CBC monitoring); serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; MAOI activity
  • Daptomycin: MRSA, VRE; myopathy (CK monitoring)
  • Quinupristin-dalfopristin: VRE
  • Tigecycline: Multi-drug resistant infections
Doxycycline is prescribed for a 7-year-old child with Lyme disease. What are the major concerns, and what reduces absorption?
Caution in children < 8 yo — historically avoided due to permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia plus bone growth inhibition. However, for serious indications like Rocky Mountain spotted fever or anaphylaxis-risk Lyme disease, doxycycline can be given even in young children (short courses appear lower-risk per modern data). Also avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding. ↓ Absorption substances (separate by 2 hr): dairy products, calcium supplements, iron, antacids, magnesium, sucralfate. Photosensitivity — use sunscreen and protective clothing. Esophagitis — take with full glass of water, sit upright 30 min after.
A client on IV gentamicin needs peak and trough levels. When are each drawn, what are the major toxicities to monitor, and what baseline test is recommended?
Trough: 30 min BEFORE the next dose (target < 2 mcg/mL for most aminoglycosides). Peak: 30 min AFTER the END of the infusion (target 5–10 mcg/mL for gentamicin/tobramycin; higher for amikacin). Many centers now use extended-interval (once-daily) dosing with random levels and Hartford nomogram. Major toxicities — both can be permanent: (1) Nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis) — monitor BUN/Cr, urine output. (2) Ototoxicity — both vestibular AND auditory; baseline audiogram recommended for long courses. (3) Neuromuscular blockade with concurrent anesthetics — respiratory arrest possible.
Which antibiotic carries the highest risk for C. difficile infection, and what symptoms should prompt the client to stop and call?
Clindamycin historically has the highest C. diff risk among common antibiotics (also high: fluoroquinolones, broad-spectrum cephalosporins, carbapenems, broad-spectrum penicillins). Symptoms to teach the client to recognize and report immediately: profuse watery diarrhea (≥3 loose stools/day, especially if foul-smelling), abdominal cramping and tenderness, fever, blood/mucus in stool. Action: stop antibiotic if possible, obtain C. diff toxin/PCR testing, start oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin if positive. Diarrhea can develop weeks AFTER stopping the antibiotic — keep the warning current.
