From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for oral erythromycin every 6 hr to treat pneumonia. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for erythromycin in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor for clients taking erythromycin.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include two teaching points for clients taking erythromycin.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Erythromycin inhibits protein synthesis in the cells of susceptible micro-organisms, usually gram-positive bacteria. Erythromycin can be either bacteriostatic or bactericidal, depending on the organism and on the medication's dosage. It also treats infections for clients who are allergic to penicillin.

Complications

  • The most common adverse effects of erythromycin are GI manifestations, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
  • Hepatotoxicity with abdominal pain, anorexia, fatigue, and possibly jaundice can occur after 1 to 2 weeks of erythromycin therapy.
  • Erythromycin can cause a prolonged QT interval on ECG, which can lead to potentially fatal tachydysrhythmias.
  • Ototoxicity can occur with high doses, especially after prolonged periods.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor liver function tests for clients who take erythromycin over a period of several weeks.
  • If the client is concurrently taking warfarin or digoxin with erythromycin, carefully monitor PT and INR or digoxin levels.
  • Monitor WBC counts for effectiveness of erythromycin treatment.

Client Education

  • Take erythromycin on an empty stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals with 8 oz of water.
  • Observe for adverse effects, and call the provider for severe GI distress, manifestations of liver toxicity, and ototoxicity.
  • Take the entire course of the medication and not to stop when feeling better.
Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 46

Urinary Tract Infections

UTIs are treated with TMP/SMX (Bactrim), nitrofurantoin for uncomplicated cystitis, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) for complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, and urinary tract analgesics (phenazopyridine — turns urine red-orange).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Uncomplicated cystitis: TMP/SMX (Bactrim) — sulfa allergy contraindicated; or nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) — turns urine brown, take with food, do not crush. Complicated UTI/pyelo: ciprofloxacin (FQ) — tendon rupture (black box), C. diff, photosensitivity; not in < 18 yo or pregnancy. Phenazopyridine (Pyridium): urinary analgesic — orange-red urine; stains clothes/contacts; max 2 days; treats symptoms not infection.

First-line UTI antibiotics

  • TMP/SMX (Bactrim, Septra) — sulfa drug:
  • • Uncomplicated cystitis first-line (3 days)
  • • AE: Stevens-Johnson, hyperkalemia, photosensitivity, crystalluria (↑ fluids)
  • • Sulfa allergy = contraindicated
  • • Avoid in late pregnancy (kernicterus risk) and G6PD deficiency (hemolysis)
  • Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid, Macrodantin):
  • • Concentrates in urine — UTI only (not systemic infections)
  • • Turns urine brown/dark yellow (harmless)
  • • Take with food; do not crush
  • • Avoid if CrCl < 60 mL/min
  • • Avoid in late pregnancy (term/labor) and infants < 1 mo
  • • Pulmonary toxicity with long-term use (suppressive therapy)

Fluoroquinolones

  • Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin
  • Uses: Complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, prostatitis; respiratory; anthrax; some STIs
  • BLACK BOX warnings:
  • • Tendinitis and tendon rupture (Achilles); ↑ risk: older adults, corticosteroids, post-transplant
  • • Peripheral neuropathy (possibly permanent)
  • • CNS effects (psychosis, depression, suicidal thoughts)
  • • QT prolongation
  • • C. difficile (high risk)
  • • Aortic aneurysm/dissection risk
  • Avoid in: Children < 18 yo (cartilage damage in animals), pregnancy
  • Photosensitivity
  • ↓ Absorption: Calcium, iron, antacids, dairy, sucralfate — separate 2 hr
  • ↑ warfarin, theophylline levels

Urinary tract analgesia & teaching

  • Phenazopyridine (Pyridium): Local anesthetic; orange-red urine; stains clothing, soft contact lenses
  • Maximum 2 days with antibiotic; doesn't treat infection
  • Take after meals
  • UTI teaching: ↑ fluids; cranberry products may help; void after intercourse; wipe front to back; avoid bubble baths/feminine sprays; complete full antibiotic course
A pregnant woman at 38 weeks has a UTI. Why is TMP/SMX contraindicated, and what populations should also avoid it?
Late pregnancy (3rd trimester): TMP/SMX causes kernicterus in newborns by displacing bilirubin from albumin. Also a folic acid antagonist → fetal harm in early pregnancy. Other contraindications: sulfa allergy (true cross-reactivity exists), G6PD deficiency (hemolytic anemia), severe renal/hepatic disease. Other AEs: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hyperkalemia (↑ in clients on ACE/ARB/spironolactone), photosensitivity, crystalluria (↑ fluids to prevent). Safer alternatives in pregnancy: nitrofurantoin (avoid at term/labor due to neonatal hemolysis), cephalexin, fosfomycin (single dose).
A client is prescribed nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) for uncomplicated cystitis. What are the four key teaching points, and what is the renal function cutoff?
(1) Take with food — improves absorption and reduces GI upset. (2) Brown/dark-yellow urine is NORMAL — not blood, not concerning. (3) Do NOT crush sustained-release capsules (Macrobid). (4) Limited to lower UTI only — nitrofurantoin concentrates in urine but does NOT achieve systemic levels — useless for pyelonephritis or systemic infection. Avoid if CrCl < 60 mL/min (per IDSA; some guidelines say < 30) — won't reach therapeutic urinary levels and risk of peripheral neuropathy. Also avoid at term/labor (neonatal hemolysis) and infants <1 mo. Long-term suppressive therapy → rare pulmonary fibrosis (cough, dyspnea).
List the black-box warnings for fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) and the populations at highest risk for tendon rupture.
FQ black-box warnings: (1) Tendinitis and tendon rupture (especially Achilles — can occur during therapy or weeks after). (2) Peripheral neuropathy (may be permanent). (3) CNS effects (psychosis, depression, suicidality, seizures). (4) QT prolongation, (5) C. difficile, (6) Aortic aneurysm/dissection risk, (7) Avoid in myasthenia gravis (worsens weakness). Tendon rupture risk highest in: age >60, concurrent corticosteroids, post-transplant, kidney/heart transplant recipients. Stop FQ at first sign of tendon pain/swelling. Avoid in: children <18 (cartilage damage in animal models), pregnancy. ↓ Absorption: calcium, iron, antacids, dairy, sucralfate — separate by 2 hr.

Scenario

A client who has a UTI has a prescription for phenazopyridine. What information should the nurse review? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe four.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include three teaching points.
Show key

Expected Pharmacological Action

Phenazopyridine is an azo dye, which acts as a local anesthetic on the mucosa of the urinary tract. It is not an antibiotic.

Therapeutic Uses

Relieves urinary burning, urgency, pain, and frequency

Client Education

  • Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease are contraindications.
  • It changes urine to an orange-red color.
  • Tell clients that the urine can stain clothes.
  • Instruct clients to take it with or after meals to minimize GI discomfort.
Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 47

Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections

Mycobacterial, fungal, and parasitic infections require specialized therapy. TB: 4-drug RIPE regimen (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). Fungal: amphotericin B (nephrotoxic), azoles, echinocandins. Parasitic: metronidazole.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

TB — RIPE × 2 mo intensive, then RI × 4–7 mo continuation. Isoniazid: peripheral neuropathy (give B6), hepatotoxic. Rifampin: red-orange body fluids; CYP inducer; OCPs ineffective. Ethambutol: optic neuritis. Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxic, hyperuricemia. Antifungals: amphotericin B (nephrotoxic, infusion reactions); azoles (hepatotoxic, many interactions); nystatin (oral candidiasis). Metronidazole: disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; metallic taste.

Tuberculosis — RIPE regimen

  • Rifampin: Red-orange body fluids (urine, sweat, tears — stains contacts); potent CYP inducer — ↓ OCPs, warfarin, methadone, antiretrovirals
  • Isoniazid (INH): Peripheral neuropathy (give vitamin B6/pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily); hepatotoxic (LFTs); avoid alcohol; lupus-like syndrome
  • Pyrazinamide: Hepatotoxic; hyperuricemia (gout flare); arthralgia
  • Ethambutol: Optic neuritis — baseline + monthly eye exams (visual acuity, color vision)
  • Duration: Intensive phase 2 months (all 4), then continuation 4–7 months (rifampin + INH)
  • Directly observed therapy (DOT): Often used to ensure adherence
  • Latent TB: INH alone × 6–9 months; or rifampin × 4 months; or INH + rifapentine weekly × 12 doses

Antifungals

  • Amphotericin B (IV) — "amphoterrible": Systemic fungal infections
  • • Nephrotoxicity (most serious — preload with NS, monitor BUN/Cr, K+, Mg)
  • • Infusion reactions: Fever, chills, rigors, hypotension — pretreat with diphenhydramine, acetaminophen, hydrocortisone
  • • Lipid formulations less toxic
  • Azoles — Fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole:
  • • Hepatotoxic; many drug interactions (CYP inhibitors)
  • • Fluconazole: Vaginal/oropharyngeal candidiasis; PO or IV
  • Echinocandins — Caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin: IV; invasive Candida and Aspergillus
  • Topical/oral: Nystatin (oral candidiasis — swish and swallow); clotrimazole, miconazole (topical)
  • Terbinafine: Onychomycosis (toenail fungus); hepatotoxic; long course

Antiparasitic & metronidazole

  • Metronidazole (Flagyl): Anaerobic bacterial infections, C. difficile (no longer first-line), Trichomonas, giardiasis, amebiasis
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — avoid alcohol during and 48 hr after
  • Metallic taste, dark urine, peripheral neuropathy
  • Antimalarials: Chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine (retinal toxicity), mefloquine, doxycycline, atovaquone-proguanil
  • Antihelminthics: Mebendazole, albendazole, ivermectin, praziquantel
Pair each RIPE drug with its signature adverse effect and the matching monitoring or supplement.
Rifampin → orange-red body fluids (urine, sweat, tears, will stain contacts — harmless); potent CYP450 inducer → counsels OCP backup contraception. Isoniazid (INH) → peripheral neuropathy (B6 deficiency-mediated) → give pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily; also hepatotoxic — monitor LFTs and avoid alcohol. Pyrazinamide → hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia (may trigger gout flare); arthralgia. Ethambutol → optic neuritis (color vision changes, ↓ visual acuity) → baseline + monthly eye exams. Duration: intensive 2 mo all 4 drugs; continuation 4 mo INH + rifampin (longer if cavitary or culture-positive at 2 mo).
Why must a woman of reproductive age on rifampin be counseled about contraception, and what other drugs are affected?
Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer (also induces P-glycoprotein) — it accelerates the metabolism of many drugs, reducing their effectiveness. Counseling: oral contraceptives fail on rifampin — use a non-hormonal backup method (condom, copper IUD) throughout therapy and for ≥1 month after. Other drugs with reduced effect: warfarin (INR drops dramatically — adjust dose), methadone (may precipitate withdrawal — increase dose), antiretrovirals (HIV — major problem), digoxin, beta blockers, sulfonylureas, tacrolimus/cyclosporine, glucocorticoids, theophylline. Also turns urine, sweat, tears orange-red — alert client to expected color and contact-lens staining.
Why is amphotericin B called "ampho-terrible," and what pre-medication and monitoring strategies reduce its toxicity?
Major toxicities: (1) Nephrotoxicity (most serious — dose-related, sometimes irreversible); (2) Infusion reactions (fever, rigors, hypotension, sometimes severe). Strategies to reduce nephrotoxicity: pre-hydrate with 0.9% NS 500–1000 mL before each dose, monitor BUN/Cr daily, replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺ losses (renal wasting). Use lipid-formulation amphotericin (liposomal/AmBisome) when available — much less nephrotoxic. Pre-medication for infusion reactions: diphenhydramine, acetaminophen, ± hydrocortisone, ± meperidine for rigors. Slow infusion. Azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole) are alternatives for many indications.
A client on metronidazole for trichomoniasis asks if it's safe to have one drink at dinner. What is the issue, and how long after stopping should they continue to avoid alcohol?
Disulfiram-like reaction — metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase. Drinking even small amounts of alcohol causes severe flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting, palpitations, hypotension, dyspnea. Reaction can occur within minutes. Avoid all alcohol during treatment AND for 48–72 hours after completing the course. Also check for hidden alcohol: mouthwash, cold medicines, vanilla extract, hand sanitizer (if licked/swallowed). Other key metronidazole points: metallic taste, dark urine (harmless), peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use. Same disulfiram-like reaction occurs with certain cephalosporins (cefotetan, cefoperazone) and tinidazole.

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse in a public health department is teaching a client who has latent tuberculosis (TB) and a new prescription for isoniazid twice weekly for 6 months. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for isoniazid in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one test to monitor for clients taking isoniazid.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe two teaching points for clients taking isoniazid.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

A client who has latent tuberculosis has been infected by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is at risk for (but has not yet developed) active tuberculosis. Some clients who have latent tuberculosis (those who are immunocompromised or who have recently immigrated to the U.S. from a country where active TB is common) can require treatment with isoniazid, with or without rifapentine, in order to prevent the onset of active TB. The client who has latent TB has a positive tuberculin test but a negative sputum culture and negative chest x-ray for TB. The client cannot infect others with tuberculosis unless the infection becomes active.

Complications

  • Paresthesias in the extremities caused by vitamin B6 deficiency
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • Hyperglycemia (if client has diabetes mellitus)

Nursing Interventions

The client who starts isoniazid should have baseline liver function testing and be tested periodically throughout treatment.

Client Education

  • Teach the client to watch for paresthesias, and to take pyridoxine daily to reverse the effect if they occur.
  • Teach the client about indications of hepatitis (anorexia, fatigue, nausea, jaundice) and to notify the provider if these occur.
  • Teach the client to take isoniazid as prescribed, and not to stop until the entire course of treatment is completed.
  • The client who has latent tuberculosis does not feel ill. The nurse should be sure that the client understands why it is important to continue with treatment.
Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 48

Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS

Viral infections: HIV uses multi-class HAART (NRTIs like zidovudine, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors like ritonavir, integrase inhibitors, entry inhibitors like maraviroc). Herpes: acyclovir, valacyclovir. Influenza: oseltamivir. Hepatitis: interferons, direct-acting antivirals.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

HIV — HAART: at least 3 drugs from ≥ 2 classes; lifelong; adherence critical to prevent resistance. NRTIs (zidovudine, tenofovir): bone marrow suppression. Protease inhibitors (ritonavir): metabolic effects, many drug interactions. Integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir): well-tolerated, often first-line. Acyclovir (herpes): ↑ fluids (crystalluria). Oseltamivir (flu): within 48 hr of symptom onset.

HIV antiretrovirals (ART/HAART)

  • NRTIs (Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors):
  • • Zidovudine (AZT/ZDV), tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir, lamivudine
  • • AE: Bone marrow suppression, lactic acidosis, hepatic steatosis
  • • Abacavir: HLA-B*5701 testing (hypersensitivity)
  • NNRTIs — Efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine: Hepatotoxic; rash (Stevens-Johnson)
  • • Efavirenz: CNS effects (dreams, dizziness) — take at bedtime; teratogenic
  • Protease inhibitors ("-navir") — Ritonavir, atazanavir, darunavir, lopinavir:
  • • Many CYP450 interactions; metabolic: ↑ glucose, ↑ lipids, lipodystrophy
  • • Ritonavir often used as "booster" for other PIs
  • Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) — Dolutegravir, raltegravir, bictegravir, elvitegravir:
  • • Often first-line — well-tolerated, high barrier to resistance
  • Entry inhibitors: Maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist), enfuvirtide (fusion inhibitor — SC)
  • Critical: STRICT ADHERENCE — missed doses → resistance
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): Start within 72 hr; 28-day course
  • Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP): Tenofovir/emtricitabine daily for high-risk individuals

Herpes, varicella, CMV

  • Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir: Herpes simplex (genital, oral), varicella-zoster (shingles, chickenpox)
  • ↑ Fluids with acyclovir IV to prevent crystalluria/AKI
  • Topical acyclovir: Limited efficacy; wear gloves
  • Ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir: CMV (especially immunocompromised, transplant); bone marrow suppression

Influenza, hepatitis, other

  • Oseltamivir (Tamiflu), zanamivir (inhaled), peramivir (IV), baloxavir: Influenza A and B
  • Start within 48 hours of symptom onset for best effect
  • Hepatitis B: Tenofovir, entecavir (NRTIs); interferon alfa; pegylated interferons
  • Hepatitis C: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) — sofosbuvir, ledipasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir; cure rates > 95%
  • Ribavirin: RSV (inhaled), Hep C combo; hemolytic anemia; Category X — teratogenic
  • Remdesivir: SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19); IV
A client newly diagnosed with HIV is starting antiretroviral therapy. Why is adherence the single most critical teaching point?
HIV mutates rapidly. Missing doses → drug levels drop below MIC → resistance develops within weeks, and resistance to one drug often extends to the entire class. Each subsequent regimen is more complex and toxic. Goal: ≥ 95% adherence for sustained viral suppression. Strategies: simplified regimens (often single-tablet once-daily integrase combos like Biktarvy), pill boxes, smartphone reminders, address barriers (cost, mental health, substance use), regular viral load monitoring. PEP within 72 hr (28-day course) after exposure; PrEP daily for high-risk individuals. U=U: undetectable viral load = untransmittable sexually.
A client receives IV acyclovir for severe HSV encephalitis. What is the major adverse effect to prevent, and what is the nursing action?
Crystalluria → acute kidney injury — acyclovir crystallizes in renal tubules when dehydrated. Action: aggressive IV hydration BEFORE and DURING infusion — typically 1 mL of D5W or NS for every 1 mg of acyclovir given. Infuse over ≥ 1 hour (never IV push). Monitor BUN/Cr, urine output, urinalysis. Renal dose adjustment required for CrCl < 50. Other AEs: phlebitis at IV site (extravasation causes tissue necrosis), CNS effects (confusion, tremor, seizures) particularly in renal impairment. Oral acyclovir/valacyclovir/famciclovir have much less nephrotoxicity but still benefit from good hydration.
When is oseltamivir (Tamiflu) most effective for influenza, and when should it still be given despite being outside that window?
Most effective when started WITHIN 48 HOURS of symptom onset — shortens illness by ~1 day and reduces complications. After 48 hr, benefits in otherwise-healthy outpatients are marginal. Still give beyond 48 hr in: hospitalized patients, severe/complicated influenza, pregnancy, high-risk groups (age >65, chronic lung/heart/kidney/liver disease, immunocompromised, morbid obesity), nursing-home residents, children <2. Pediatric formulation available. Renal dosing required. Resistance can develop — monitor outbreaks. Baloxavir is a single-dose alternative; zanamivir is inhaled (avoid in asthma/COPD).

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is caring for a client who is immunocompromised and has a new prescription for ganciclovir iV twice per day to prevent cytomegalovirus. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ati active learning template: Medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for ganciclovir in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two for clients taking ganciclovir, and two tests the nurse should monitor.
Show key

Therapeutic Uses

Ganciclovir prevents reproduction of viral dna and thus prevents viral cell replication. it is used is to prevent or treat cytomegalovirus in clients who are immunocompromised.

Complications

  • Minor discomforts (fever, headache, and nausea)
  • Suppresses the bone marrow, causing a decrease in WBcs, especially granulocytes
  • Causes thrombocytopenia frequently
  • The client should report any discomforts and be sure to report new onset of fatigue, easy bruising, or sore throat.
  • Advise the client to report manifestations of infection or bleeding, and to avoid crowds or individuals who have respiratory infections.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor client blood counts, especially WBc, absolute neutrophil count, and thrombocyte count. expect ganciclovir therapy to be interrupted for an absolute neutrophil count less than 500/mm3 or a thrombocyte count less than 25,000/mm3.
  • Monitor blood counts.
  • Prepare to administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factors for a low absolute neutrophil count.
  • Monitor i&o, and encourage the client to increase fluid intake.
  • Avoid direct contact with the powder from oral ganciclovir or the iV solution, and wash well if contact occurs.
  • Advise clients to use a barrier contraception (condoms) during treatment and for 3 months following treatment.
Unit 13 · Other Medications · Chapter 49

Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies

Complementary and alternative therapies include herbal supplements (echinacea, ginkgo, ginseng, St. John's wort, garlic, valerian, black cohosh, saw palmetto), megavitamins, glucosamine/chondroitin, and probiotics. Not FDA-regulated as drugs; many drug interactions.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

CAM products are NOT FDA-regulated as drugs; quality and potency vary. Major interactions: St. John's wort = CYP450 inducer (↓ OCPs, warfarin, digoxin, antiretrovirals); garlic, ginkgo, ginger, ginseng = bleeding risk (avoid with anticoagulants/antiplatelets); kava + valerian = hepatotoxic with sedatives. Always ask about supplement use during med reconciliation. Discontinue most herbals 2 weeks before surgery.

Common herbal supplements

  • Echinacea: Cold/flu prevention (evidence weak); avoid in autoimmune disease, immunosuppression
  • Ginkgo biloba: Memory, peripheral circulation; ↑ bleeding (avoid with anticoagulants, antiplatelets)
  • Ginseng: Energy, immune; ↓ blood glucose (caution with diabetes meds); ↑ bleeding
  • Garlic: ↓ BP, ↓ cholesterol; ↑ bleeding
  • Ginger: N/V; ↑ bleeding at high doses
  • St. John's wort: Depression; POTENT CYP3A4 inducer — ↓ OCPs (pregnancy risk), warfarin, digoxin, antiretrovirals, cyclosporine; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/MAOIs
  • Valerian: Sleep; ↑ effects of CNS depressants
  • Kava: Anxiety; hepatotoxic — avoid
  • Black cohosh: Menopausal symptoms; hepatotoxic; avoid with breast cancer history
  • Saw palmetto: BPH symptoms; may affect PSA levels; bleeding risk

Other CAM categories

  • Glucosamine/chondroitin: Osteoarthritis (evidence mixed); shellfish allergy caution (glucosamine often from shellfish)
  • Probiotics: Restore GI flora; especially with antibiotic use; avoid in severely immunocompromised
  • Melatonin: Sleep, jet lag; may interact with anticoagulants, immunosuppressants
  • Coenzyme Q10: May help statin-induced myopathy; may ↓ warfarin effect
  • Fish oil (omega-3): Triglyceride reduction; ↑ bleeding at high doses
  • Megavitamins: Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) accumulate — toxicity possible

Nursing implications

  • ALWAYS ask about supplements/herbals during med reconciliation
  • Discontinue most herbals 2 weeks before elective surgery (bleeding risk)
  • Document supplement use; report to provider
  • Pregnancy/breastfeeding: Most supplements not studied — avoid unless specifically recommended
  • Children: AVOID most herbal supplements
  • Quality issues: Look for USP verification mark
  • Teach clients that "natural" does NOT mean "safe"
A woman on combined OCPs and warfarin reports taking St. John's wort for mild depression. What are the consequences, and what other drug classes interact?
St. John's wort is a POTENT CYP3A4 inducer — accelerates the metabolism of many drugs, dramatically reducing their effectiveness. Critical interactions: ↓ oral contraceptives → unintended pregnancy; ↓ warfarin → INR drops → thromboembolism; ↓ digoxin, antiretrovirals, cyclosporine/tacrolimus, certain chemo agents (life-threatening reductions in transplant or HIV patients). Pharmacodynamic risk: serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans, tramadol. Counseling: stop St. John's wort; discuss safer prescribed antidepressants with provider; check INR; ensure backup contraception until next cycle off the herb.
A client is scheduled for elective surgery in 3 weeks and takes garlic, ginkgo, ginger, ginseng, and fish oil supplements. What is the pre-operative advice and why?
Discontinue most herbal supplements ≥ 2 weeks before elective surgery — the "4 G's" (garlic, ginkgo, ginger, ginseng) plus ginger, vitamin E, and high-dose fish oil all increase bleeding risk by inhibiting platelet aggregation. Other surgical concerns: kava and valerian → ↑ effect of anesthetics (oversedation); ephedra → cardiovascular instability (banned but variants exist); St. John's wort → many anesthetic drug interactions. Always include supplements in medication reconciliation at every encounter; teach clients "natural ≠ safe," look for USP verification, and report ALL supplements to anesthesia and surgical teams.

Active Learning Scenario

From the book — uses the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication. Practice answering before reviewing the key.

Scenario

A nurse is educating a client about the use of the dietary herbal supplement St. John's Wort. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USE: Describe the potential uses of this supplement.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify four potential adverse effects of this supplement.
  • MEDICATION INTERACTIONS: Identify four medication interactions that can occur with this supplement.
Show key

Therapeutic Use

  • Affects serotonin, producing antidepressant effects
  • Mild depression
  • Oral analgesic to relieve pain and inflammation
  • Applied topically to treat infection

Complications

  • Mild adverse effects, including dry mouth, lightheadedness, constipation, GI discomfort
  • Skin rash with client exposure to sunlight

Interactions

  • Can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with other antidepressants, amphetamine, and cocaine
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, warfarin, digoxin, calcium channel blockers, steroids, HIV protease inhibitors, and some anticancer medications
